title: Course Overview
text:
Levels
The aim of this series of practical sessions is to develop the skills to independently perform biological and mathematical analyses using the programming language R. There will be eight two hour practicals, four in Michaelmas term and four in Lent term.
Materials and exercises are labelled as follows:

title: Course Overview
text:
Icon
Level
Description





Core
Essential material that everyone should read and complete, unless you are already very comfortable with the topic.



Recommended
Everyone should read and understand this material, and ideally do the exercises, but if you’re running short of time you can move on without completing the exercises yourself.



Extension
Provides either extra depth on a topic or additional skills which are not essential for other practicals. Exercises will have a little less guidance than the core and recommended exercises.



Bonus
Extra challenges just for fun, for people who are working quickly or are very comfortable with the topic. Exercises will have much less guidance than the other levels.

title: Course Overview

Exams and assessment
The material in these practicals is not in itself examinable. Each practical is recorded as either completed or not completed.






Important 1: Completion



At the end of each practical, to be marked as having completed the practical, please show a demonstrator the main Quarto file you have been working on.


Some of the material does overlap with or build upon material from the lectures, and in these cases you may be examined on the lecture material.

title: Installing R and RStudio
text:
Installing R and RStudio
Prior to the practicals, you need to install two pieces of software on your computer - R, a programming language, and RStudio, which acts as a graphical interface for R.
Please try to do this, following the instructions below, before the first practical.
You will need: - R - at least version 4.6.1 (2026-06-24) - RStudio - at least version 2026.06.0

Windows 10/11macOSLinux


You can install R and RStudio using winget. Click the Windows key and search for Windows PowerShell, right-click on the app and choose Run as administrator. Then run the following commands:
winget install --id=RProject.R -e
winget install --id=RProject.Rtools -e
winget install --id=Posit.RStudio -e
Alternatively, you can manually download and install these programs using default options:

R
RTools
RStudio



To open a terminal, do one of the following:

Click the Launchpad icon in the Dock, type Terminal in the search field, then click Terminal.
In the Finder , open the /Applications/Utilities folder, then double-click Terminal.

Once you open a Terminal window, you can execute commands and run tools.

Xcode Command Line Tools
We recommend installing the Xcode Command Line Tools, which makes several useful software utilities available.
In your terminal, run:
xcode-select --install


Homebrew
On macOS the brew package manager is a popular choice for installing packages as a user.
First, make sure to install Xcode as instructed in the previous section. Then, in your terminal, run:
/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"
Then run type the following command:
uname -m
Your screen should either say arm64 or x86_64.
If it says arm64, run the following two commands:
echo 'eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"' >> ~/.zprofile
eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"
If it says x86_64, run the following two commands instead:
echo 'eval "$(/usr/local/bin/brew shellenv)"' >> ~/.zprofile
eval "$(/usr/local/bin/brew shellenv)"
Test your brew installation by installing the wget utility, which is used to download files from the internet:
brew install wget
You can now install R and RStudio using brew. In your terminal, run:
brew install --cask r
brew install --cask rstudio
Alternatively, you can manually download and install these programs using default options:

R
RStudio





Go to the R installation folder and look at the instructions for your distribution.
Download the RStudio installer for your distribution and install it using your package manager.

Installing Packages
Now that you have RStudio installed, please download this file and open it in RStudio using File > Open File....
Run all of the code in the file by clicking the  button.
Lots of text will appear in the Console section at the bottom of your screen while the packages are being installed. Don’t worry — this is normal!
If you are asked:
Update all/some/none? [a/s/n]:

Installation may take a while (potentially up to 30 minutes). Most of the GitHub setup in the following section can be carried out in the meantime, if you like (as far as Cloning a repository with RStudio).
If a package cannot be installed, you may see a message such as:

There will usually be more information about the problem above this message in the Console. If you feel confident, you can search online for the error message and try to resolve the problem yourself. If this doesn’t work, or you are unsure what to do, please bring your computer to the Practical 0 session and we will help you.

title: Setting Up RStudio and GitHub
text:
Git
Before we start running code, we should make sure our RStudio session is set up correctly.
In this course, we will use Git and GitHub to track changes to our code and store the code online. We can use these tools directly in RStudio.
Git is a version control system for code (and other files). It keeps track of changes you make to your files over time, allowing you to return to earlier versions if something goes wrong. It also makes it easier for multiple people to work on the same project.
Usually, Git is used to track all the changes within a folder, called a Git Repository.

text:
Installing Git
↑ top
Follow the instructions below for your operating system.

WindowsmacOSLinux



Go to the Git for Windows website.
Download the installer for your computer.
Run the installer.
You will be offered lots of installation options. You can leave these at their default settings.







Note



During installation, you may be asked to choose the default editor used by Git. You can leave this at its default setting, as we will normally interact with Git through RStudio.




Git may already be installed on your computer.
Open Terminal (Applications → Utilities → Terminal) and enter:
git --version
If Git is installed, you should see something similar to:
git version 2.51.0
If macOS asks whether you would like to install the Command Line Developer Tools, agree to the installation. These include Git.
Alternatively, you can download Git from the Git website.


Git may already be installed on your computer.
Open a terminal and enter:
git --version
If Git is installed, you should see something similar to:
git version 2.51.0
If Git is not installed, follow the appropriate instructions for your Linux distribution.
For Ubuntu or Debian, enter:
sudo apt update
followed by:
sudo apt install git
For Fedora, enter:
sudo dnf install git




Check that RStudio can find Git
Open RStudio and go to:
Tools → Global Options → Git/SVN
You should see a file path next to Git executable.






Tip



If you have just installed Git, make sure you close and reopen RStudio before checking whether RStudio can find it.

Setting up your GitHub account
Throughout this course, you’ll use Git to record the history of your code and GitHub to store a copy of your work online.
This means you’ll always have a backup of your work, you’ll be able to recover previous versions if you make a mistake, and you’ll be learning to use the same tools that are widely used in research and industry.
For the MB1A practicals, we would like you to create a free GitHub account (unless you already have an account you’re happy to use).






Important



Please set up a GitHub account now, preferably using your University email address.
You will not need Copilot for these practicals.
Feel free to turn off or reroute notifications.
When you have set up your account, please send us your CRSID and GitHub username using this form.

↑ top
You will also need to set up a personal access token which allows your GitHub account to connect to your RStudio session.
To do so, go to the GitHub Personal Access Tokens settings page and click on Generate New Token.

title: Setting Up RStudio and GitHub
text:
Cloning a repository with RStudio
↑ top
Now we’re ready to load this repository in RStudio. You should already have installed R and RStudio on your computer, following the instructions here: Installation
Now we want to import our new fork of the Git repository into RStudio.
To do this, in your RStudio session, select File > New Project.






Figure 3.8: File > New Project



In the window which pops up, choose Version Control.






Figure 3.9: New Project Version Control



Select Git - Clone a project from a Git repository.






Figure 3.10: New Project Git



Copy and paste the URL of your forked repository into the Repository URL box. It should be something similar to https://github.com/githubid/MB1A_Students_2026_2027, but with your GitHub ID instead of githubid.






Important



Make sure you are using the URL for your forked repository, not the original! Your username should be in the URL. If you’re not sure, please talk to a demonstrator.


The rest of the boxes should fill in automatically.
Click Create Project.






Figure 3.11: New Project Clone



RStudio will download a copy of your repository (known as a clone) and open it as a new project.
You now have a local copy of the practical repository on your computer, where you can edit files, save your work and upload your changes to GitHub.
To see where this folder is saved on your computer, go to the Files panel - the bottom right corner of the RStudio interface. You may need to click on the Files tab.
Click on More then Show Folder in a New Window






Figure 3.12: Find Project Folder



Inside this folder there should be a file called MB1A_Students_2026_2027.Rproj.
At the start of each practical session, you should follow the instructions below (we will remind you!).






TipSync your Git Repository



At the beginning of each practical, make sure to sync any changes in the main copy of online repository from GitHub.

Open RStudio
Choose File > Open Project
Navigate to your MB1A_Students_2026_2027 folder and then to the directory for Practical_1_Introduction_to_R, then load Practical_1_Introduction_to_R.Rproj.
In a web browser, log in to GitHub and navigate to your fork of the MB1A_Students repository.
Click on Sync Fork. If it shows “This branch is not behind the upstream” there is nothing else you need to do.
Otherwise, click Update Branch. Do not click Discard commits.
Go to your RStudio session and open the Git tab.
Click Pull to update your local copy of the repository.



At the end of each session, you should follow the instructions below (again, we will remind you!).






TipPush your changes



Now you are at the end of the practical, commit your changes with Git and push them to GitHub.

Click Push in the Git panel to save the changes to GitHub.
Enter your UserName and your Personal Access Token. If you don’t have your token or it doesn’t work, visit this page while logged into your GitHub account, click on the MB1A token and choose Regenerate token.
Visit your GitHub account and check that your changes are there.



Although this seems like a lot of steps, you’ll quickly get used to the workflow. Using Git and GitHub from the start of the course will help you keep your work organised and introduce you to tools that are widely used in research and industry.

title: Part 1: Using R and RStudio
text:
The R language
Core
↑ top






Figure 5.1: The R Logo. Source



In this session, we will learn the basics of using the programming language R, which we will use for data analysis and visualisation throughout the MB1A course.






ImportantLevels



If you’ve never programmed before, don’t worry about the extension and bonus material in this practical! The material marked core is all you will need to progress through this course. You should also read the material and exercises marked recommended, but if you are running short of time, don’t worry about completing all of the recommended exercises.
If you are an experienced programmer, please still read all of the core and recommended materials to understand some of the differences between R and other programming languages, and how we will interact with R in these practicals. However, if you are confident, you do not need to complete all of the introductory exercises. Instead, there are extension and bonus exercises for you to try (but there is no requirement to complete all of them).
If you are somewhere in between, please read all of the core and recommended materials and choose whichever exercises feel more helpful to you.


The R language was initially developed by two programmers, Ross Ihaka and Robert Gentleman, in 1993, for teaching introductory statistics. It has become one of the most commonly used languages in scientific computing, particularly amongst biologists.

Why learn R?
R provides many of the same capabilities as spreadsheet tools such as MS Excel and Google Sheets, and statistics and graphing software like SPSS and GraphPad.
However, R has lots of advantages over these tools:

It provides thousands of functions for statistics, visualisation and data analysis.
It allows you to automate repetitive tasks rather than repeating the same steps manually.
It creates reproducible workflows: every step of your analysis can be recorded, checked and repeated by yourself or others.

title: Part 1: Using R and RStudio
text:
Coding in the console
Core
↑ top
Before we go any further, let’s try writing some R code.
When you first open your RStudio project, your screen will look like this.






Figure 5.2: The welcome screen of RStudio



We will look at other parts of the screen shortly, but for now let’s focus on the Console.
In the console, R commands can be typed and executed immediately by the computer. When you type a line of code and press EnterEnter, it is transferred to the R interpreter. Results are shown straight after the command is executed. However, unlike code saved in a script or Quarto document, you do not have a clear, reproducible record of your analysis.
Try typing the following text (everything in the grey box), into the console, then press EnterEnter.

print("Hello! First contact with R successful!")

[1] "Hello! First contact with R successful!"


You should immediately see the message on the screen.
Now, try the following. Here, you are creating a new variable, x, with a value of 8. In R, the operator <- associates a specific name (here the name is x) with a specific value (we will discuss this in more detail later).

x <- 3 + 5

To see the value of x, type print (x) into the console, then press EnterEnter.

print(x)

[1] 8


Usually in these practicals, we won’t run most of our code directly in the console like this, because we want to keep a record of the code we write. Instead, we will use Quarto documents, as we will discuss in Part 2. Coding in the console is a bit like cooking without a recipe - the results can be great, but if you want to make the same thing again, you may not remember exactly what you did.
However, it can be useful to use the console, for example to quickly try something out or check the value of a variable.






ExerciseExercise 1 - Create a variable






Core

In your console, create a variable with your first name. The syntax you will need to use is as follows - replace “Mary” with your own name.


my_name <- "Mary"

Then, have R write you a message as follows:

print(paste("Hi", my_name, "- welcome to R!"))

[1] "Hi Mary - welcome to R!"












ImportantThe R prompt



If R is ready to accept commands, the R console shows a > symbol.
If the console shows a + symbol, this means it is waiting for something - you have most likely not ‘closed’ a parenthesis or quotation e.g. you have opened a parenthesis ( but not closed it ). When this happens, and you thought you finished typing your command, click inside the console window and press EscapeEscape. This will cancel the incomplete command and return you to the > prompt.

The RStudio interface
Core
↑ top
Now we will learn a bit about the rest of RStudio.
RStudio is an interactive development environment (IDE) - a piece of software designed to make working with R as easy as possible. It’s free, open-source and well-supported.






Figure 5.3: The welcome screen of RStudio



In the image above you can see that the window is divided into three main parts, each with various tabs. In clockwise order we have:

Console / Terminal / Background jobs
Environment / History / Connections / Tutorial / Git
Files / Plots / Packages / Help / Viewer / Presentation

In orange we’ve highlighted the tabs we’ll be using most.

In the Console we can directly run code, as you did above.
The Environment shows any information that is stored in R’s memory (empty in the figure above).

Click on the environment now - you should see two variables: x, with a value of 8 and my_name, with whatever you entered as your name above.






Figure 5.4: The environment tab




The Git tab allows you to interact with Git and GitHub, as we saw above.
Help is where you can go for help.







ExerciseExercise 2 - Using help






Core
In the search box on the Help tab, search for the function sum.
Using the Examples section as a guide, calculate the sum of the numbers 2, 3, 4 in the console.

sum(2, 3, 4)

title: Part 1: Using R and RStudio
text:
R Scripts
Core
↑ top
The basis of programming is that we create or code instructions for the computer to follow.
Next, we tell the computer to follow the instructions by executing or running those instructions.
In your RStudio window, choose File > New File > R Script. This will add a new panel to your RStudio session, the Source panel.






Figure 5.5: The source and console panels



Here, we can save our code as a script. This is a list of commands which can be sent to R to execute in order. The script represents a complete record of what we did, and anyone (including our future selves) can easily replicate the results on their computer. We can also use a script to repeatedly perform the same or similar tasks.



Console
Script




runs code directly
in essence, a text file


interactive
needs to be told to run


no record
records actions


difficult to trace progress
transparent workflow




Creating a script
To create a script, we put a list of commands for R to run into the Source panel.
Try entering the following into the Source panel, then press the  button. The  button runs all of the code in the Source panel, while the  button will only run the active line - the line where your cursor is currently or anything which is highlighted. The answer should show in the console.

x <- 8
y <- 10
z <- x + y

print(z)

[1] 18








ExerciseExercise 3 - Writing an R script






Core
Here is the code we wrote in the console above:

my_name <- "Mary"
print(paste("Hi", my_name, "Welcome to R!"))

[1] "Hi Mary Welcome to R!"


Write a script based on this code but to display, for example, “My name is Jeremy and I am 27 years old”, but with your own (or another) name and age. Run your script using the  button.
Save your script as my_first_script.R (using File > Save As). You can save it directly into the Practical_1_Introduction_to_R folder.






AnswerAnswer







my_name <- "Jeremy"
my_age <- 27
print(paste("My name is", my_name, "and I am", my_age, "years old"))

[1] "My name is Jeremy and I am 27 years old"

title: Part 2: Reproducible Analysis with Quarto
text:
Introduction to Quarto
Core
↑ top
Throughout this course, we will write our code in Quarto documents (with the suffix .qmd) rather than using the R Console or standalone R scripts.
Quarto allows you to create quite complex documents, for example, these teaching materials are written in Quarto.
The main reason to use Quarto is to make your research reproducible. You will likely have learned about this previously for lab-based research, but reproducibility is just as important for computer-based research.
Optional homework: There is an interesting lecture here about the importance of reproducibility in computational biology.
crumbs: Practical 1 - Basics of R and RStudio
6  Part 2: Reproducible Analysis with Quarto

title: Part 2: Reproducible Analysis with Quarto
text:
The console is useful for trying out individual commands, but anything you type there is easily lost.
R scripts allow you to save your code, but it is not easy to include explanations, figures, or results in the same file.
Quarto documents combine text, code and output into a single file, making it easy to explain what you are doing, present your results, and reproduce your analysis. This helps you keep an organised record of your work and is widely used for teaching, research and data science.

Creating a Quarto document
Core
↑ top
To create a new Quarto document in RStudio, select File > New File > Quarto Document. Give the document a title and add your own name as the author, then uncheck the box next to Use visual markdown editor and select Create empty document.






Figure 6.1: New quarto document



You should see something like this:






Figure 6.2: Empty quarto document



In this document, we can combine code, text and images.
We can type explanatory text directly into the document.
To add code, click on the Insert a New Code Chunk  button and choose R. Anything within this chunk will be interpreted as R code.






ExerciseExercise 1 - Create your first Quarto document






Core
Type the following into your Quarto document, below the header.
I have measured the diameter of four bacterial colonies.
The results were as follows: 2.2mm, 1.6mm, 3.3mm, 4.0mm.

I want to calculate the total diameter of these colonies.
Then, using the  button, add the following code chunk.

total_colony_diameter <- sum(2.2, 1.6, 3.3, 4.0)
print(total_colony_diameter)

[1] 11.1


You can run just this code chunk by clicking the small play button in the corner of the chunk, or by clicking on it and then pressing ControlControl + ShiftShift + EnterEnter.






Figure 6.3: Run button



Below your code chunk, type the following:
The total diameter of my colonies is 11.1 mm.
Your whole document should look something like this:






Figure 6.4: Quarto document



Running a code chunk with the play button executes only that piece of code. Rendering a Quarto document runs all the code and creates the final report.
You can produce a report based on your document by clicking the Render button - . This runs all of the code and formats the document into HTML format, so it is easy to read and share.
Save your document in the Practical_1_Introduction_to_R folder as my_first_quarto.qmd. Then click on the .
Your first Quarto report should open in a new window. A HTML file will also be created in the same folder as your Quarto file, which you can open in a web browser.






Figure 6.5: Rendered quarto document



As our code becomes more complicated, the value of using Quarto will become much clearer.

text:
Documenting and formatting your code
Core
↑ top

Documentation
It’s always a good idea to add explanations to your code. We can do so in Quarto, by writing a description of what we’re trying to do, as you did above.
Within a code chunk, we can also use the hash tag # symbol to add comments, as shown below.

# This code calculates the sum of two numbers
1 + 9

Documenting your code is almost always helpful. What makes sense to you in that moment, might not a week later. Similarly, when sharing code with colleagues and collaborators, it’s always good to be as clear as possible.


Formatting your code
Writing code that is well formatted - arranged neatly on the page with appropriate line breaks and spaces - makes it easier for you and others to understand, check, and reuse.
Good formatting:

Helps you to structure your code
Makes mistakes easier to spot
Allows collaborators to quickly see what your code is doing.

In research and industry, code is often shared between people and revisited months or years later, so clear and consistent formatting is an important part of writing reproducible and maintainable analyses.
In this course, we will use the tidyverse style guide where possible. This document contains lots of references to things we haven’t covered yet. However, RStudio has an option to automatically style code, which we’ll use for now.
In the HPA Quarto document you created above, click on Addins on the menu and then Style active file - this will automatically change your code to the tidyverse style where possible.






Important



This function will only work if your code is able to run without errors and you’ve saved your Quarto document.








Figure 6.8: Style Active File



For example, the Style active file feature removes the extraneous spaces from the following code.
Before:






Figure 6.9: Bad formatting



After:






Figure 6.10: Good formatting



Also, where you need to give something a name in R, it is helpful to use a name which describes what it is. For example, rather than x <- 12 it is preferable to write e.g. mean_size <- 12.

Recommended

title: Part 3: Functions and Variables
text:
Functions
For parts 3 and 4 of the practical, we recommend that you keep track of your progress in a new Quarto document, Practical_1_Introduction_to_R/prac1_exercises.qmd.
You can describe the code if you wish, or just label it with the exercise name. It is recommended to use a different code chunk for each exercise.
For the data analysis exercises in Part 4, we will create a second Quarto document Practical_1_Introduction_to_R/ukhsa_data_analysis.qmd. As you perform your analysis in this document, please very briefly describe it.
Core
↑ top
Functions take an input (called an argument), perform an action, and often return an output. They allow us to perform common tasks without writing the same code repeatedly.
We have used some functions already:
Functions allow us to do the same thing multiple times without rewriting code. We can also write our own functions, we’ll come to this in a later practical.
A function usually takes one or more inputs called arguments. They often (but not always) return an output.
A typical example would be the function sqrt(). The input (the argument) must be a number, and the output is the square root of that number.
sqrt(9)

[1] 3
Here, the input 9 is given as an argument to the sqrt() function. The function calculates the square root, and returns the value. This function is very simple, because it takes just one argument and has no additional options.
crumbs: Practical 1 - Basics of R and RStudio

title: Part 3: Functions and Variables
text:
Figure 7.1: Functions





The print() function outputs text to the screen.
The sum() function adds together a series of numbers.










Figure 7.2: Functions











ExerciseExercise 1 - Using functions






Core
The function round() rounds a number, by default into the nearest whole number.
In your prac1_exercises.qmd Quarto file, write some code to round the number 3.14159 to the nearest whole number.






AnswerAnswer







round(3.14159)

[1] 3
crumbs: Practical 1 - Basics of R and RStudio

title: Part 3: Functions and Variables
text:
Arguments
Core
↑ top
Arguments allow you to control the behaviour of a function. They can be anything, not only numbers. Exactly what each argument means differs per function and can be looked up in the documentation.
Some functions take arguments which may either be specified by the user, or, if left out, take on a default value.
Arguments can be used to provide something to the function, such as the input data, or to alter the way the function operates.
Let’s look at the round() function again.






Figure 7.3: Functions




round(3.14159)

[1] 3


This gives us an integer, 3.






Figure 7.4: Functions



However, if we want e.g. two digits after the decimal point, we can type digits = 2 (or however many we want). For example:

round(3.14159, digits = 2)

[1] 3.14



Ordering arguments
When a function has several arguments, there are two common ways to provide them. You can either give the arguments in the correct order, or you can name each argument explicitly.
For example, let’s take the function seq().
This function generates a sequence of numbers. The arguments are, in order, from, to and by, where from is the number you want the sequence to start from, to is the number you want it to end at and by is the increment. If you search in the Help panel for seq you’ll see this order - from, to, by.
We can call the function with these three arguments:
For example:

print(seq(1, 10, 2))

[1] 1 3 5 7 9



print(seq(5, 15, 5))

[1]  5 10 15


However, we can also use their names, and then put them in any order:

print(seq(by = 2, from = 1, to = 10))

[1] 1 3 5 7 9



print(seq(by = 5, to = 15, from = 5))

[1]  5 10 15








ExerciseExercise 2 - Argument order






The function rep() repeats a value, x a specific number of times. The order of arguments is: rep(x, times) - so you first specify x, then the number of times you want it to be repeated.
For example:

print(rep(2, 5))

[1] 2 2 2 2 2



print(rep(x = 2, times = 5))

[1] 2 2 2 2 2


In your prac1_exercises.qmd Quarto file, write some code to repeat the number 5, 7 times, first by specifying arguments in order and then using their names.






AnswerAnswer







# ordered
print(rep(5, 7))

[1] 5 5 5 5 5 5 5

# keywords
print(rep(times = 7, x = 5))

[1] 5 5 5 5 5 5 5
















Note



When writing a function call in RStudio, press the Tab key after the opening bracket (() to see a list of the arguments available for that function. You can then select an argument from the list rather than having to remember or type its name in full. This is particularly useful when you can’t remember the exact name of an argument.
crumbs: Practical 1 - Basics of R and RStudio

title: Part 3: Functions and Variables
text:
Variables
Core
↑ top
Another fundamental concept in programming is a variable.
Basically, a variable associates a specific name with a specific value. In R, we use the operator <- to assign a value to a name, we’ve done this several times already.
For example, by running the code below, we are saying that the name my_variable refers to the value 12. When you run the code, it will seem like nothing has happened, but, internally, R now knows that my_variable is equal to 12.

my_variable <- 12

To check this has worked, we can use the function, print() to show the value of our variable on the screen.

my_variable <- 12
print(my_variable)

[1] 12


We can change the value of our variable by assigning it a new value. Although the first line of the code below is run, the value is then replaced in the second line, so when we reach the third line, the value is 10.

my_variable <- 12
my_variable <- 10
print(my_variable)

[1] 10








ExerciseExercise 3 - Assigning values to variables






Core
Without trying it in R, what do you think the value of whatsmynumber would be after running all of the code in the box below?

whatsmynumber <- 1
whatsmynumber <- 5







AnswerAnswer






5









Variable Names
You can have as many variables as you like, and use any name, with a few exceptions.
Your variable names should be one word, without spaces and ideally without punctuation except underscores (“_“), so the following won’t work:

my-var <- 12

Error:
! object 'my' not found



my var <- 12

Error in parse(text = input): <text>:1:4: unexpected symbol
1: my var
       ^


In R, variable names can’t start with a number.

1var <- 12

Error in parse(text = input): <text>:1:2: unexpected symbol
1: 1var
     ^


Some words have a special meaning in R and cannot be used as variable names. For example:

if <- 12

Error in parse(text = input): <text>:1:4: unexpected assignment
1: if <-
       ^
crumbs: Practical 1 - Basics of R and RStudio

title: Part 3: Functions and Variables
text:
Types of variable
Core
↑ top

Numeric, character and logical variables
Different types of data can be stored as variables.
There are many types of variable in R.
Some of the most important are:

Numeric
(You may sometimes see the term double used for numeric values in R — you don’t need to worry about the distinction yet.)
All variables which are numbers can be classed as numeric (there are some more specific number types but you don’t need these yet)

x <- 1
print(x)

[1] 1

x <- 1.74
print(x)

[1] 1.74

x <- 4e-3
print(x)

[1] 0.004




Character
(sometimes called a string)
A character variable consists of text - it can be one or multiple words.

x <- "hello"
print(x)

[1] "hello"

x <- "I am a variable"
print(x)

[1] "I am a variable"




Logical
(sometimes called boolean)
These can only be TRUE or FALSE.

x <- TRUE
print(x)

[1] TRUE

x <- FALSE
print(x)

[1] FALSE




Identifying types of variables
We can find out what type of variable we have using the function class().

x <- "hi there"
print(class(x))

[1] "character"

x <- 1513871
print(class(x))

[1] "numeric"

x <- FALSE
print(class(x))

[1] "logical"








ExerciseExercise 4 - Character, numerical and logical variables






Core
In your prac1_exercises.qmd Quarto file, create character, numerical and logical variables, print them, then check their classes.






AnswerAnswer







# for example
my_favourite_number <- 11
my_favourite_word <- "hullabaloo"
is_this_true <- FALSE

print(class(my_favourite_number))

[1] "numeric"

print(class(my_favourite_word))

[1] "character"

print(class(is_this_true))

[1] "logical"

The attributes of your two batches of cells are in this table:

title: Part 3: Functions and Variables
text:
Exploring the quirks of R






ExerciseExercise 6 - Explore the quirks of R






Bonus
If you have programmed before, some of R’s behaviour may be different from languages you have previously used.
Predict the outcome of the following expressions, then test them in R in your prac1_exercises.qmd Quarto file. Are they as you expected?

print(TRUE + TRUE)
print(TRUE + FALSE)
print(5 + TRUE)







AnswerAnswer






Logical values can behave like numbers
When logical values are used in arithmetic, R converts TRUE to 1 and FALSE to 0. Therefore:

TRUE + TRUE gives 2
TRUE + FALSE gives 1
5 + TRUE gives 6





Predict the outcomes of the following chunks of code, then test them in R.

x <- NA
print(x == NA)
print(is.na(x))







AnswerAnswer






Missing values are unknown
NA represents a missing or unknown value. Asking whether an unknown value is equal to another unknown value does not give TRUE or FALSE — the answer is also unknown (NA).
For this reason, use is.na() to test whether a value is missing rather than == NA.





x <- 0 / 0
print(x)
print(is.na(x))
print(is.nan(x))







AnswerAnswer






NaN is a special kind of missing value
0 / 0 has no defined numerical value, so R returns NaN (“Not a Number”). NaN is considered missing, so is.na(NaN) is TRUE, but is.nan() can be used to distinguish NaN from other missing values.





print(round(2.5))
print(round(3.5))







AnswerAnswer






R may round halves differently than you expect
R uses “round to even” for numbers exactly halfway between two possibilities. Therefore round(2.5) gives 2, while round(3.5) gives 4.
This reduces systematic bias that could result from always rounding .5 upwards.




R has several other special values and objects. Use the R Help system to find out what Inf, -Inf and NULL represent. Can you write an expression that produces Inf and -Inf? How does NULL differ from NA and NaN?






AnswerAnswer






Other special values and objects
Inf and -Inf represent positive and negative infinity. For example:

print(1 / 0)

[1] Inf

print(-1 / 0)

[1] -Inf


NULL represents the absence of a value or object. This is different from NA, which represents a value that exists but is missing or unknown.

title: Part 4: Vectors, data frames and plots
text:
Packages
↑ top
Core
R comes with many useful functions, but additional functions are available in packages. Packages are collections of functions and other resources designed for particular purposes.
Normally, you need to install a package once before you can use it, and load it each time you start a new R session in which you want to use it.
Let’s install the package fortunes, to demonstrate.
install.packages("fortunes")

Installing package into '/home/katy/R/x86_64-pc-linux-gnu-library/4.6'
(as 'lib' is unspecified)
We can then load the package into R using the function library():
library(fortunes)
This package just includes one function, fortune(), which outputs a random quote about R.
fortune()


The urge to imitate other statistical packages that rely on profusion of
dummies should be resisted. R repression functions can handle factor variables.
   -- David (Muphry) Winsemius (about factors in regressions...and the dangers
      of drinking and deriding)
      R-help (September 2015)
You have already installed all the packages you will need for this practical by following the instructions in Installation.
However, we will often need to load a package.
For example, for this practical we will use some functions from the tidyverse package collection for data science and from the gt package for visualising data frames.
Therefore, you need to include the following code at the beginning of your prac1_exercises.qmd Quarto document.

title: Part 4: Vectors, data frames and plots
text:
Vectors
↑ top
All of the variables we’ve created so far just have a single element - one number, one section of text, or one TRUE/FALSE.
However, we can also create variables which contain multiple elements.
One of the most common ways of storing multiple values in R is a vector.
Vectors in R are (usually) specified using the function c().

my_first_vector <- c(1, 5, 9)
print(my_first_vector)

[1] 1 5 9


You can have vectors with all numbers, all text, or all logical values, but everything needs to be the same type.

character_vec <- c("hello", "this", "is", "a", "character", "vector")
print(character_vec)

[1] "hello"     "this"      "is"        "a"         "character" "vector"   

logical_vec <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)
print(logical_vec)

[1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE


If you have existing variables, you can put them into a vector using their variable names.

x <- 1
y <- 2
z <- 3

xyz_vec <- c(x, y, z)







ExerciseExercise 1 - Vectors






Core
Let’s look again at our dataset in which you have treated one batch of cells with radiation and kept the other as a control, then counted the number of live cells before and after.
The attributes of your two batches of cells are in this table:








cell_ID
treated
num_cells_before
num_cells_after




CX1
TRUE
5415
1432


CX2
FALSE
8123
7543







In your existing prac1_exercises.qmd Quarto document, combine the variables you made earlier into four vectors, one for each column of the table.






AnswerAnswer







# You should already have this part
cell_id_1 <- "CX1"
cell_id_2 <- "CX2"

treated_1 <- TRUE
treated_2 <- FALSE

n_before_1 <- 5415
n_before_2 <- 8123

n_after_1 <- 1432
n_after_2 <- 7543

# Combine these into vectors
cell_id <- c(cell_id_1, cell_id_2)
treated <- c(treated_1, treated_2)
n_before <- c(n_before_1, n_before_2)
n_after <- c(n_after_1, n_after_2)










Accessing elements of a vector
Once our values are in a vector, we can access them using an index, which refers to the position of the value within the vector. Indices are indicated within square brackets - [].






NoteOne-based indexing



If you’ve previously used a language such as Python, you’ll notice that indexing in R is 1-based - so the first element in a vector is element 1 - rather than 0-based.



nice_food <- c("cheese", "beans", "potatoes")

print(nice_food[1])

[1] "cheese"

print(nice_food[2])

[1] "beans"

print(nice_food[3])

[1] "potatoes"








ExerciseExercise 2 - Indexing






Core
In your prac1_exercises.qmd Quarto file, isolate the fourth value in this vector and assign it to a new variable, then print its value.

all_my_pets <- c("dog", "horse", "guinea pig", "chicken", "cat")







AnswerAnswer







# for example
all_my_pets <- c("dog", "horse", "guinea pig", "chicken", "cat")
my_only_bird <- all_my_pets[4]
print(my_only_bird)

[1] "chicken"












Vectorisation
Extension
One useful feature of R is vectorisation. Many R operations can be applied to an entire vector at once.
For example, adding 10 to a vector adds 10 to every element:

x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
print(x + 10)

[1] 11 12 13 14 15


Similarly, functions will often operate on every element of a vector:

print(sqrt(x))

[1] 1.000000 1.414214 1.732051 2.000000 2.236068








ExerciseExercise 3 - Vectorisation

Create a vector as follows:

title: Part 4: Vectors, data frames and plots
text:
Data Frames
↑ top
Core
Our next variable type is a data frame, which is one of the types of data structure you’ll most commonly use. A data frame is basically a table, consisting of rows and columns. Each row is a single record, corresponding to some entity - a cell, a person, a country - and each column is a specific piece of information.
For example:








fruit
length
weight




apple
22
150


pear
30
165


banana
55
170







In this data frame, there are three columns - fruit, length and weight, and three rows, each containing information about a specific fruit.
We can build a data frame using the R function tibble() (note that there is also an R function data.frame() which you might see referenced elsewhere, usually modern applications use tibble() as it is more user-friendly).
I would specify the data frame above as follows:

my_data_frame <- tibble(
  fruit = c("apple", "pear", "banana"),
  length = c(22, 30, 55),
  weight = c(150, 165, 170)
)


print(my_data_frame)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  fruit  length weight
  <chr>   <dbl>  <dbl>
1 apple      22    150
2 pear       30    165
3 banana     55    170


You can also use existing vectors to put data into the data frame columns.

fruits <- c("apple", "pear", "banana")
lengths <- c(22, 30, 55)
weights <- c(150, 165, 170)

my_data_frame <- tibble(
  fruit = fruits,
  length = lengths,
  weight = weights
)


print(my_data_frame)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  fruit  length weight
  <chr>   <dbl>  <dbl>
1 apple      22    150
2 pear       30    165
3 banana     55    170


Although we can see our data frame using the print() function, it’s not formatted particularly nicely. Instead, we can use the function gt() to display a nicely formatted version of our data frame in our Quarto document.

my_data_frame <- tibble(
  fruit = c("apple", "pear", "banana"),
  length = c(22, 30, 55),
  weight = c(150, 165, 170)
)

gt(my_data_frame)

Downloading data via an API
Often, when we want to work with data which is regularly updated, we will use an application programming interface (API) to directly access data programmatically. UKHSA provides an API for accessing the data underlying its dashboard.
The UKHSA API is organised hierarchically. Navigating its hierarchical structure takes a little getting used to.
To find a dataset, we need to work through several levels:
theme → sub_theme → topic → geography_type → geography → metric
Start by opening this URL in your browser:
https://api.ukhsa-dashboard.data.gov.uk/themes/
Here, you need to navigate through the theme, then sub-theme, then topic, geography_type, geography. This should lead you to a list of metrics, each with a name and a link. The names of these metrics are not exactly intuitive, but you can find out what they mean by searching for them by name here.
For example, I have chosen Clostridioides. difficile monthly cases by onset type, for which the link is:
https://api.ukhsa-dashboard.data.gov.uk/themes/infectious_disease/sub_themes/gastrointestinal/topics/C-difficile/geography_types/Nation/geographies/England/metrics/c-difficile_cases_countsByOnsetType
Now we can access the data via the API.
We need to import a package, httr2.

library("httr2")

We can also assign our URL to a variable.

url <- "https://api.ukhsa-dashboard.data.gov.uk/themes/infectious_disease/sub_themes/gastrointestinal/topics/C-difficile/geography_types/Nation/geographies/England/metrics/c-difficile_cases_countsByOnsetType"

We need to append this to our URL - ?page_size=365. You have probably seen similar additions to URLs before, which tell a website more specifically what you want it to show you. These are called query parameters. Here, page_size=365 tells the UKHSA API to return up to 365 records.






Note



The API allows a maximum of 365 records per page. Some datasets contain more than 365 records, so this may not retrieve the complete dataset. For this exercise, it does not matter.


You can concatenate strings in R using the function paste0, as follows:

url <- paste0(url, "?page_size=365")
print(url)

[1] "https://api.ukhsa-dashboard.data.gov.uk/themes/infectious_disease/sub_themes/gastrointestinal/topics/C-difficile/geography_types/Nation/geographies/England/metrics/c-difficile_cases_countsByOnsetType?page_size=365"


Now we are ready to import our data. First, we structure a request for the data from the URL, using the function request().

api_request <- request(url)

Next, we use the function req_perform() to perform the request we’ve built.

response <- req_perform(api_request)

The returned data is encoded in JSON format, a common and useful data format used for storing and transferring data. The function resp_body_json() reads this JSON data into an R object.

json_response <- resp_body_json(response)

All of our data is now in this object. We can describe the object using the R function str(), which displays the structure of an R object. The argument max.level = 1 tells R to only show the top level of information (otherwise it will show us something for every data frame row).

str(json_response, max.level = 1)

List of 4
 $ count   : int 126
 $ next    : NULL
 $ previous: NULL
 $ results :List of 126


The part we are interested in is contained in $results - this is a list of observations, which will become the rows in our data frame. We haven’t encountered R lists yet. Lists are a flexible way of storing multiple objects in R, but they are trickier than vectors, so we won’t cover them until Practical 6.
We don’t want our results to be in a list, we want a data frame. We can convert a list to a data frame using the function bind_rows().

results_df <- bind_rows(json_response$results)
gt(head(results_df))

This may seem like a lot of work to do something you could do manually in two minutes! The advantage of an API is that the process can now be automated. The same code can retrieve newly updated data without somebody having to visit the website and download a new file each time. First, I read the table and initiate a blank canvas on which to put my plot.

weather <- read_csv("data/weather_data.csv")

Rows: 9 Columns: 10
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr  (3): station_id, weather_condition, wind_direction
dbl  (6): temperature_c, humidity_pct, wind_speed_kmh, pressure_hpa, precipi...
dttm (1): observation_time

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

ggplot(weather)










Adding axes
We use another function, aes(), as an argument to the ggplot() function, telling R how various attributes of the data map to the “aesthetics” of the plot.
For example, here we choose which data we will represent with the x and y axes.

ggplot(weather, aes(
  x = observation_time,
  y = temperature_c
))










Adding data
Now we can add some data to our plot. In ggplot2, we build plots by adding layers using the + symbol.
Here, we add a line representing the data using the geom_line() function.

ggplot(weather, aes(
  x = observation_time,
  y = temperature_c
)) +
  geom_line()










Adding extra features
We can add some additional features here to make the plot look nicer. For example, here I will change the colour of the line to red (with colour = "red" as an argument to geom_line()), add x (xlab()) and y (ylab()) axis labels and add a title (ggtitle()).

ggplot(weather, aes(
  x = observation_time,
  y = temperature_c
)) +
  geom_line(colour = "red") +
  xlab("Date") +
  ylab("Temp (C)") +
  ggtitle("Temperature by Date")

For example:

ggplot(rhinovirus, aes(
  x = date,
  y = metric_value
)) +
  geom_line()

Recommended
In your ukhsa_data_analysis.qmd Quarto document, edit the code you wrote above to:

Change the colour of the line and add appropriate axis labels and a title - you can go back to the UKHSA data website to see exactly what is being measured.

For example:

ggplot(rhinovirus, aes(
  x = date,
  y = metric_value
)) +
  geom_line(color = "red") +
  xlab("Date") +
  ylab("Percentage") +
  ggtitle("Percentage of positive PCR test results for rhinovirus")


















Additional plot styling






ExerciseExercise 10 - Make your plot look good






Extension
The plot you have created in ukhsa_data_analysis.qmd contains the information we need, but there are many ways we could improve its appearance.
Explore the ggplot2 documentation and improve your plot. For example, you could:

Try a different theme.
Change the appearance of the line.
Change the size and style of text.
Adjust the appearance of the axes or grid lines.

Choose changes that you think make your plot clearer or more visually appealing. You don’t need to use all of the suggestions above.










ExerciseExercise 11 - Bonus-bonus






Bonus
Still looking for a challenge? In your ukhsa_data_analysis.qmd Quarto document, extend your UKHSA analysis in any way you like. For example, retrieve and compare multiple metrics or geographical areas, automate part of the workflow, or create a more sophisticated visualisation.

Review
↑ top






NoteSummary




Concepts

Packages contain additional functions and other resources. Packages need to be installed once and loaded using the library() function in each new R session in which they are used.
A vector (c()) stores multiple values of the same type.
Indexing with square brackets ([]) allows us to access individual elements of a vector by position in the vector.
A data frame (tibble()) stores tabular data in rows and columns.
CSV (comma-separated values) is a plain-text format commonly used to store tabular data.
ggplot2 builds plots in layers. Variables are mapped to features of the plot using aesthetics.
Vectorisation allows an operation or function to be applied to all elements of a vector at once. (Extension)
An API allows data to be accessed programmatically. (Bonus)

text:
The dataset
↑ top
Core
In this practical, we will first work with a published dataset to learn how to perform various analyses in R.
For the worked example, we will use data from this Science paper, published in June 2026. This study tracked the migration of a songbird species, the pied flycatcher (Ficedula hypoleuca).






Figure 10.1: Pied flycatcher. Source



One of the most surprising findings of this study was that these birds take very different routes depending on the time of year. The authors demonstrated that:

In spring, the birds migrate north from their wintering grounds in West Africa. After crossing the Sahara, they stop over near the Mediterranean before continuing to their breeding sites in the north (Fig. 1B in the paper).
In autumn, the birds take a much longer route. They migrate south from their breeding sites, but — regardless of how far east their breeding site is — they all travel via the Iberian Peninsula (Spain and Portugal) before following the west coast of Africa to their wintering grounds (Fig. 1A in the paper). Why they take this detour is currently unknown.
As a result, spring migration routes are shorter and more variable than autumn migration routes.

In our worked example, we will reproduce Figures 1A and 1B from this paper, illustrating this phenomenon.






ExerciseExercise 1 - Examining the source






Core
Have a look at the two plots in the paper and read their legends.
What are the x and y axis labels?






AnswerAnswer






x - Longitude
y - Latitude




What do the colours represent?






AnswerAnswer






The locations of the breeding populations.

Orange - Spain
Purple - Norway
Blue - Sweden
Pink - Britain
Red - Netherlands
Turquoise - western Russia
Green - Ural
Dark green - Siberia





What do the shapes represent?






AnswerAnswer






The type of site:

Circles - breeding site
Squares - non-breeding area (this is the winter location)
Filled upward triangles - autumn post-Saharan stopover location
Filled downward triangles - spring Iberian stopover location
Open downward triangles - spring westernmost location









All of the data we will use here comes from the Supplementary Data associated with this publication.
To produce this plot, we need a single data frame which contains all of the information in the plot:

Breeding site
Longitude and latitude of breeding site
Longitude and latitude of winter non-breeding site
Longitude and latitude of post-Saharan stopover
Longitude and latitude of the Iberian stopover
Longitude and latitude of the westernmost location

However, as is very common with biological datasets, the data provided with the publication is not in the ideal format for our needs. Therefore, there are various data frame operations we need to perform before we start plotting.

Starting your analysis
The first part of the data we will use for this practical contains the longitude and latitude coordinates for breeding sites for eight specific populations of pied flycatcher. This data comes from Supplementary Table 1 in the publication.
The file is in the data directory for Practical 2 and named breeding_site_locations.csv. Open this file in a text editor (for example NotePad, TextEdit) and examine it.

title: Part 1: Basic Data Frame Operations
text:
The pipe symbol
↑ top
Core
We are going to make copies of these data frames with only the columns we are interested in.
To do this, we first need to learn about the pipe symbol |>. This is an operator in R which is used to link multiple steps in an analysis.
Here, we first make a vector of numbers, then we use this vector as the input to the function sum().

my_numbers <- c(2, 4, 6, 8)

sum(my_numbers)

[1] 20


Alternatively, we can use the pipe symbol. The pipe passes the value on its left into the function on its right. Here, we pass the value of my_numbers to sum().

my_numbers <- c(2, 4, 6, 8)

my_numbers |> sum()

[1] 20


This produces the same result as above.
Pipes make it easier to perform a series of steps on the same variable:

my_numbers <- c(2, 4, 6, 8)

print(my_numbers |>
  sum() |>
  sqrt())

[1] 4.472136


You can keep adding additional steps to your pipe:

my_numbers <- c(2, 4, 6, 8)

print(my_numbers |>
  sum() |>
  sqrt() |>
  round())

[1] 4


We can assign the result to a variable using the <- operator as usual.

my_numbers <- c(2, 4, 6, 8)

my_result <- my_numbers |>
  sum() |>
  sqrt() |>
  round()

print(my_result)

[1] 4

AnswerAnswer

print(result)

title: Part 1: Basic Data Frame Operations
text:
Comparison operators
↑ top
Core
We can also filter our data frame to just see certain rows.
To do this, one option is to use comparison operators.
For example:



Operator
Meaning




==
is equal to


!=
is not equal to


>
is greater than


>=
is greater than or equal to


<
is less than


<=
is less than or equal to









Note==



The operator == means “is equal to?”. It compares two values and returns either TRUE or FALSE. This is different from assigning a value.
In these practicals, we use <- to assign values to variables:

x <- 1

We also use a single equals sign (=) to specify the values of function arguments:

round(3.123, digits = 1)

[1] 3.1


To compare two values, we therefore use two equals signs (==):

x <- 1
y <- 2
print(x == y)

[1] FALSE


This returns FALSE, because x and y are not equal.
A single equals sign cannot be used as a comparison operator:

x <- 1
y <- 2
print(x = y)

[1] 2




We can use comparison operators with single values as well as with data frame columns:

x <- 3

print(x == 2)

[1] FALSE


This shows FALSE because x is not equal to 2.

x <- 3

print(x == 3)

[1] TRUE


This shows TRUE because x is equal to 3.

Review
↑ top






NoteSummary




Concepts

The pipe operator (|>) passes the result of one step to the next, allowing us to link multiple steps in an analysis.
We can select particular columns (select()) from a data frame, remove duplicate rows and rename columns.
Comparison operators compare values and return TRUE or FALSE. These include ==, !=, >, >=, < and <=.
We can filter (filter()) a data frame to keep only rows that meet particular conditions.

Selects particular columns from a data frame.
Core

Removes duplicate rows from a data frame.
Core

Renames columns in a data frame.

Selects rows of a data frame that meet specified conditions.

title: Part 2: Complex Data Frame Operations
text:
Grouping and summarising data
Core
↑ top
At the moment, the data frame bird_breeding_exc has seven rows, one for each breeding site - as the breeding sites are small, fixed locations. However, the data frame bird_migration_exc has multiple measurements for each location for each bird population - as the numerous birds were tracked as they migrated.
For our visualisation, it’s sufficient to just take the median values for the migration locations in bird_migration_exc.
To do this, we can group our data by the values in a specific column, then calculate summary statistics for each group.
We group data using the group_by() function, then summarise for each group using the summarise() function.
First, let’s group our migration frame by the Site column.
bird_migration_grouped <- bird_migration_exc |> group_by(Site)
We can’t really visualise the grouped data frame, but we can check it has worked using the glimpse function:
glimpse(bird_migration_grouped)

Rows: 94
Columns: 9
Groups: Site [7]
$ Site               <chr> "Vomb", "Vomb", "Vomb", "Vomb", "Vomb", "Vomb", "Vo…
$ Winter_Longitude   <dbl> -12.708132, -11.279293, -10.624196, -11.401071, -12…
$ Winter_Latitude    <dbl> 10.436439, 7.111185, 11.010127, 12.490454, 8.010118…
$ Stopover_Longitude <dbl> -7.1964231, -8.3202987, -4.4147850, -2.2617310, -5.…
$ Stopover_Latitude  <dbl> 40.14848, 31.58424, 34.20548, 33.37589, 34.23834, 4…
$ Iberian_Longitude  <dbl> -5.80472833, -5.72987181, -6.70771241, -3.78472031,…
$ Iberian_Latitude   <dbl> 41.51223, 42.13779, 35.72224, 35.03179, 36.17385, 4…
$ Westmost_Longitude <dbl> -16.83263, -16.07610, -18.19715, -16.57398, -15.008…
$ Westmost_Latitude  <dbl> 32.55738, 29.28441, 30.77262, 33.41686, 24.81672, 4…
We can see Groups: Site [7] at the top, which tells us our data frame is grouped into seven different sites.
group_by() does not change the data itself. It tells R how later calculations should be applied.
We can then use the function summarise() to calculate specific statistics per group and generate a new data frame containing these values.
For example, the following code creates a new data frame, lat_df, with one column Highest_Lat_Stopover, which contains the maximum (calculated with the function max()) value in the Stopover_Latitude column for each Site.
lat_df <- bird_migration_grouped |>
  summarise(Highest_Lat_Stopover = max(Stopover_Latitude, na.rm = TRUE))

Joining with non-unique values






ExerciseExercise 4 - Joining with non-unique values






Extension
Joins do not always produce the number of rows you might expect.
In your worked_example.qmd Quarto file, create these two data frames:

birds <- tibble(
  Bird = c("Robin", "Robin", "Blackbird"),
  Mass = c(18, 19, 100)
)

observations <- tibble(
  Bird = c("Robin", "Robin", "Robin", "Blackbird"),
  Count = c(4, 7, 2, 5)
)

Before running any more code, predict how many rows you think the following join will produce:

inner_join(birds, observations, by = "Bird")

Now run the join and examine the result.
Why does the resulting data frame contain so many rows?






AnswerAnswer






When joining data frames, each matching row in one data frame is matched with every matching row in the other. Here, two Robin rows in one data frame and three in the other produce 2 × 3 = 6 rows.

title: Part 2: Complex Data Frame Operations
text:
Long and wide formats
Recommended
↑ top
Now you should have a single data frame with all the data you need for your plot.
We need to perform one more transformation before we can plot our data.
Our data is currently in what is known as wide format - with a single row per site and multiple columns for each measurement for that site. So, all our measurements for each site are on a single row in the data frame.
The plots we want to create will be simpler if we convert the data to long format. Instead of having separate columns for the breeding, stopover, Iberian, westmost and winter locations, we will have a Location_Type column containing either Breeding, Stopover, Iberian, Westmost or Winter. Each bird will therefore have multiple rows: one for each type of location.






Figure 11.1: Long and wide format. Source



We can convert our data frame to long format using the pivot_longer() function.
This is a little more complicated than some of the other functions we have used.
Basically we are instructing R to:

Select the columns to reshape: take any columns ending in _Longitude or _Latitude using cols = ends_with(c("_Longitude", "_Latitude")).
Split the column names: separate the original column names wherever there is an underscore using names_sep = "_".
Create new column names: use the first part of the original column name to create a new column called Location_Type, and use the second part (Longitude or Latitude) to create new columns containing the values. This is specified with names_to = c("Location_Type", ".value").

  pivot_longer(
    cols = ends_with(c("_Longitude", "_Latitude")),
    names_sep = "_",
    names_to = c("Location_Type", ".value")

In order to create the two plots shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1B in the publication, we need to make two subsets of our data frame, one with only the spring migration data and one with only the autumn migration data.

ExerciseExercise 6 - Subset data

In your worked_example.qmd Quarto document, generate two subsets of your combined_bird_piv data frame, one with the spring data and one with the autumn data. Store these in two variables spring_data and autumn_data.






AnswerAnswer







spring_vals <- c("Breeding", "Stopover", "Winter")
autumn_vals <- c("Breeding", "Iberian", "Westmost", "Winter")

spring_data <- combined_bird_piv |>
  filter(Location_Type %in% spring_vals)

autumn_data <- combined_bird_piv |>
  filter(Location_Type %in% autumn_vals)

We can save copies using the function write_csv(). The first argument is the variable we want to save and the second is the path to the file we want to save it into.

title: Part 2: Complex Data Frame Operations
text:
Review
↑ top






NoteSummary




Concepts

Grouping (group_by()) a data frame allows us to perform calculations separately for different groups of observations.
Summary statistics (summarise()) can be calculated for each group or the whole data frame to produce a new summary data frame.
Joins combine information from multiple data frames based on one or more shared columns.
Different types of join determine which rows are retained when values are not present in both data frames.
Data can be stored in wide format, with multiple measurements in different columns, or long format, with measurements spread across multiple rows.
The %in% operator tests whether values occur within a set of values, which is useful when filtering on several categories.



Functions








Function
What it does
Level




group_by()
Groups rows of a data frame according to the values in one or more columns.
Core


summarise()
Calculates summary values, either for a whole data frame or for groups in a grouped data frame.
Core


max()
Returns the largest value from a set of values.
Core


min()
Returns the smallest value from a set of values.
Core


median()
Calculates the median of a set of values.
Core


full_join()
Joins two data frames while retaining all rows from both.
Core


inner_join()
Joins two data frames while retaining only rows shared by both.
Core


left_join()
Joins two data frames while retaining all rows from the first data frame.
Core


right_join()
Joins two data frames while retaining all rows from the second data frame.
Core


write_csv()
Saves a data frame to a CSV file.
Core


pivot_longer()
Reshapes a data frame from wide to long format.
Recommended


ends_with()
Selects columns whose names end with specified text.
Recommended


across()
Applies the same operation to multiple columns.
Extension


pivot_wider()
Reshapes a data frame from long to wide format.
Extension

title: Part 3: Visualisation
text:
Initiating a new plot
Core
↑ top
We will visualise the spring migration paths of the birds using the R plotting package ggplot2.
We can do this in the same Quarto document used for Part 1.
ggplot2 builds figures by starting with a blank plot and then adding layers. We first tell ggplot which data frame to use, then specify the variables to plot, and finally add layers such as points, lines and axes.
As we saw in Practical 1 (Plotting in R), we first need to generate a new blank plot.
We do this using the function ggplot(), with our data frame as an argument.

ggplot(spring_data)








Based on the published plot, we know that our x axis should be Longitude and our y axis should be Latitude.






ExerciseExercise 1 - Add axes






Core
Look back at the plotting code from Practical 1 (Plotting in R).
In your worked_example.qmd Quarto document, generate a new blank plot then add the x and y axis.






AnswerAnswer







ggplot(
  spring_data,
  aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude)
)

title: Part 3: Visualisation
text:
Adding points
Core
↑ top
A plot of longitude against latitude is simply a scatter plot - longitude determines the position on the x axis and latitude determines the position on the y axis.
We can add points to our plot using the geom_point() function, just like we used geom_line() to add a line in the previous practical (Plotting in R).
To demonstrate the geom_point() function, let’s briefly revisit our fruit data frame from the previous practical.

my_data_frame <- tibble(
  fruit = c("apple", "pear", "banana"),
  length = c(22, 30, 55),
  weight = c(150, 165, 170)
)

gt(my_data_frame)







fruit
length
weight




apple
22
150


pear
30
165


banana
55
170







To plot this data as a scatter plot, with length on the x axis and weight on the y axis, we would do this:

ggplot(my_data_frame, aes(x = length, y = weight)) +
  geom_point()














ExerciseExercise 2 - Adding points






Core
Going back to your worked_example.qmd Quarto document, add a layer to your existing plot to plot all of the longitude and latitude points as a scatter plot.






AnswerAnswer







ggplot(
  spring_data,
  aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude)
) +
  geom_point()
















If you compare this with Fig 1B in the paper, you can see that the points are at the same positions.
Now, we can add some additional information to make the plot more informative.

Adding map features
There is a convenient function, annotation_borders(), to add geographical country borders to a scatter plot representing a map. We’re also going to add a second function used with map data, coord_quickmap() - this keeps the shape of the plot consistent so the map isn’t skewed.
We can add this layer to our scatter plot as follows. The argument linewidth sets the width of the lines in the map borders.






Important



The majority of the steps in this practical are useful for any scatter plot, however, this specific code chunk is specific to plotting maps.








NoteInclude this code



In your worked_example.qmd Quarto document, add this layer (starting at annotation_borders) to your existing scatterplot to add map borders.

ggplot(
  spring_data,
  aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude)
) +
  geom_point() +
  annotation_borders(linewidth = 0.2) +
  coord_quickmap()

title: Part 3: Visualisation
text:
Setting axis limits
Core
↑ top
It would be clearer to zoom in just on the region containing the points. We can do this by setting the axis limits.
It would be helpful to know the minimum and maximum longitude and latitude of the points, we can do this with the min() and max() functions and the function pull(), which pulls a single column from a data frame.
e.g. to find the minimum longitude in our data frame

min_long <- spring_data |>
  pull(Longitude) |>
  min()

print(min_long)

[1] -13.54433

Core
In your worked_example.qmd Quarto document, before your plotting code, calculate the minimum longitude, maximum longitude and the minimum and maximum latitude, and store these as variables min_lon, max_lon, min_lat and max_lat.






AnswerAnswer






Minimum longitude

min_lon <- spring_data |>
  pull(Longitude) |>
  min()

print(min_lon)

[1] -13.54433


Maximum longitude

max_lon <- spring_data |>
  pull(Longitude) |>
  max()

print(max_lon)

[1] 84.6


Minimum latitude

min_lat <- spring_data |>
  pull(Latitude) |>
  min()

print(min_lat)

[1] 4.093563


Maximum latitude

max_lat <- spring_data |>
  pull(Latitude) |>
  max()

print(max_lat)

[1] 60










We can use these numbers directly as our axis limits - but let’s subtract 2 from each minimum and add 2 to each maximum so our points are not right on the edge of the plot.
We can set the x axis limits as an argument to the coord_quickmap() function as follows:






Important



For non-map data, we would most commonly use coord_cartesian() instead of coord_quickmap() here, which works in the same way.



ggplot(
  spring_data,
  aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude)
) +
  geom_point() +
  annotation_borders(linewidth = 0.2) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(min_lon - 2, max_lon + 2))














ExerciseExercise 4 - Setting axis limits






Core
Add x and y axis limits to the plot in your worked_example.qmd Quarto document, by adding your min_lat and max_lat and min_lon and max_lon variables as arguments to coord_quickmap().






AnswerAnswer







ggplot(
  spring_data,
  aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude)
) +
  geom_point() +
  annotation_borders(linewidth = 0.2) +
  coord_quickmap(
    xlim = c(min_lon - 2, max_lon + 2),
    ylim = c(min_lat - 2, max_lat + 2)
  )
















Now we have changed the axis limits, the points look a little small. We can make them bigger by adding the argument size = 3 (for example) to the geom_point() function.

ggplot(
  spring_data,
  aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude)
) +
  geom_point(size=3) +
  annotation_borders(linewidth = 0.2) +
  coord_quickmap(
    xlim = c(min_lon - 2, max_lon + 2),
    ylim = c(min_lat - 2, max_lat + 2)
  )

We want to set the colour by the Site column and the shape by the Location_Type column.
To set colour by Site, we add color = Site as an argument to the aes() function.

ggplot(
  spring_data,
  aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude, color = Site)
) +
  geom_point(size=3) +
  annotation_borders(linewidth = 0.2) +
  coord_quickmap(
    xlim = c(min_lon - 2, max_lon + 2),
    ylim = c(min_lat - 2, max_lat + 2)
  )








Setting shape by Location_Type is very similar, we add shape = Location_Type as an argument to the aes() function.






ExerciseExercise 5 - Grouping points






Core
In the plotting code in your worked_example.qmd Quarto document, add the shape = Location_Type and color = Site arguments to the aes() function, to set both the shape and the colour of the points.

  spring_data,
  aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude, color = Site, shape = Location_Type)
) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  annotation_borders(linewidth = 0.2) +
  coord_quickmap(
    xlim = c(min_lon - 2, max_lon + 2),
    ylim = c(min_lat - 2, max_lat + 2)
  )

















Adding labels
It is good practice to always give your plots a title (ggtitle()) and axis labels (xlab() and ylab()). Where appropriate, axis labels should also include the units of measurement.
I will also always use theme_minimal() to apply the ggplot minimal theme to my plots, this changes the default plot appearance and is just personal preference - you can use any theme you wish.

ggplot(
  spring_data,
  aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude, color = Site, shape = Location_Type)
) +
  geom_point(size  = 3) +
  annotation_borders(linewidth = 0.2) +
  coord_quickmap(
    xlim = c(min_lon - 2, max_lon + 2),
    ylim = c(min_lat - 2, max_lat + 2)
  ) +
  ggtitle("Pied Flycatcher Spring Migration Routes") +
  xlab("Longitude (°)") +
  ylab("Latitude (°)") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Part 3: Visualisation
text:
Adding paths
Recommended
↑ top
Finally, we want to add paths connecting the migration locations belonging to the same breeding population.
To do this, we use the geom_path() function, grouping the points by breeding site, by adding the argument aes(group = Site):

ggplot(
  spring_data,
  aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude, color = Site, shape = Location_Type)
) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  annotation_borders(linewidth = 0.2) +
  coord_quickmap(
    xlim = c(min_lon - 2, max_lon + 2),
    ylim = c(min_lat - 2, max_lat + 2)
  ) +
  geom_path(aes(group = Site)) +
  ggtitle("Pied Flycatcher Spring Migration Routes") +
  xlab("Longitude (°)") +
  ylab("Latitude (°)") +
  theme_minimal()














ExerciseExercise 6 - Add paths






Recommended
In the plotting code in your worked_example.qmd Quarto document, add the geom_path() function with the argument aes(group = Site) to your plotting code.






AnswerAnswer







ggplot(
  spring_data,
  aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude, color = Site, shape = Location_Type)
) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  annotation_borders(linewidth = 0.2) +
  coord_quickmap(
    xlim = c(min_lon - 2, max_lon + 2),
    ylim = c(min_lat - 2, max_lat + 2)
  ) +
  geom_path(aes(group = Site)) +
  ggtitle("Pied Flycatcher Spring Migration Routes") +
  xlab("Longitude (°)") +
  ylab("Latitude (°)") +
  theme_minimal()
















Now we have our plot! Compare it to Figure 1B in the publication.

title: Part 3: Visualisation
text:
Beautifying your plot
Extension
There are various tweaks available if you want to change the appearance of your plot.
For example:

To change the width of the line, add e.g. linewidth = 0.5 as an argument to the geom_path() function.
To change the colour theme of all the data points, add an additional layer with scale_color_brewer(palette = “PALETTE”) , changing PALETTE to anything on the chart on this page.
You can change the overall theme of your plot using one of the theme options on this page

It’s worthwhile to search online for other aesthetic changes you can make to your plot, many options are available.
Add any of these that you like to the plotting code in your worked_example.qmd Quarto document.
E.g.

ggplot(
  spring_data,
  aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude, color = Site, shape = Location_Type)
) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  annotation_borders(linewidth = 0.2) +
  coord_quickmap(
    xlim = c(min_lon - 2, max_lon + 2),
    ylim = c(min_lat - 2, max_lat + 2)
  ) +
  geom_path(aes(group = Site), linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  ggtitle("Pied Flycatcher Spring Migration Routes") +
  xlab("Longitude (°)") +
  ylab("Latitude (°)") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Part 4: Visualisation Exercise
text:
The Movebank database
Extension
↑ top
In this exercise, you will apply the skills from Parts 1 to 3 to analyse a new dataset independently. You will download animal tracking data from the Movebank database, process it into a suitable format, and create a map showing the median location of each tracked individual on each day.
Movebank is a free, online database of animal tracking data hosted by the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior. It is a database of data from lots of different animal tracking studies, all stored in a standardised format.
For this part of the practical, you will choose an animal tracking dataset and plot the tracked locations of different individuals within that dataset on a map.

Read the data frame into a variable.
This data has a couple of features you’ve not come across yet, so we’ll provide some code to help you:

The column names are not in a format that R can easily use, as they contain hyphens (-). We can use an additional function, clean_names() to rename the columns. clean_names() converts column names into a consistent format by replacing spaces and punctuation with underscores and converting everything to lower case.
One of the columns contains date information which needs to be reformatted - we do this using the mutate() function and the as_date() function. The as_date() function converts values containing date information into R’s date format.

We can create an extra column in a data frame using the function mutate().
For example, let’s say I have the following data frame:

text:
Plot data
Extension
↑ top

Plot a scatter plot using ggplot() and geom_point() with longitude on the x axis and latitude on the y axis.
Add a map to the plot using annotation_borders() and coord_quickmap().
Set axis limits by subtracting 2 from the minimum longitude and latitude and adding 2 to the maximum longitude and latitude. If your study covers a small geographic area, you may find that adding 2 degrees leaves too much empty space. Adjust these values if necessary.







Note



Some of the geographic areas are very small so you might not actually see many borders on your plot - don’t worry about this.



Colour the points by individual by adding color = individual_local_identifier as an argument to the aes() function.
Add a plot title with ggtitle(), axis labels with xlab() and ylab() and, if you wish, a theme with e.g. theme_minimal().
If you wish, change the appearance of your plot to your taste.


Example solution






AnswerAnswer






Plot a scatter plot using ggplot() and geom_point() with longitude on the x axis and latitude on the y axis.

ggplot(
  loc_sum,
  aes(
    x = Longitude,
    y = Latitude,
  )
) +
  geom_point()








Add a map to the plot using annotation_borders() and coord_quickmap().

ggplot(
  loc_sum,
  aes(
    x = Longitude,
    y = Latitude,
  )
) +
  geom_point() +
  annotation_borders(linewidth = 0.2) +
  coord_quickmap()








Set axis limits by subtracting 2 from the minimum longitude and latitude and adding 2 to the maximum longitude and latitude. If 2 seems like too little or too much for your data, feel free to adjust.

min_lat <- loc_sum |>
  pull(Latitude) |>
  min()

max_lat <- loc_sum |>
  pull(Latitude) |>
  max()

min_lon <- loc_sum |>
  pull(Longitude) |>
  min()

max_lon <- loc_sum |>
  pull(Longitude) |>
  max()


ggplot(
  loc_sum,
  aes(
    x = Longitude,
    y = Latitude,
  )
) +
  geom_point() +
  annotation_borders(
    linewidth = 0.2
  ) +
  coord_quickmap(
    # as my data has a narrow y range I have used 0.2 instead of 2
    xlim = c(min_lon - 2, max_lon + 2),
    ylim = c(min_lat - 0.2, max_lat + 0.2)
  )
