title: Part 1: Loops
text:
For Loops
Core
↑ top
A loop is a way of repeating a task multiple times in a computer program.
There are two main types of loop, a for loop, which runs once for every item in a vector (or other sequence), or a while loop which runs until a certain condition is met.
In these practicals we will focus on for loops, which perform a task a fixed number of times or once for each item in a sequence.
We usually loop over a vector, meaning we perform the task once for each item in the vector.
To repeat a task n times, we can use seq_len(n). This creates a sequence from 1 to n. The loop then runs n times, once for each number in this sequence. If we run our loop as for (i in seq_len(n)), each time we pass through the loop, the value of i increases by one.






Note



We can also use the syntax 1:n to iterate through the numbers from 1 to n. We will always use seq_len(n) in these practicals, but you may see this alternative elsewhere.


We refer to each pass through the loop as an iteration - we iterate over a loop.
In a loop we use curly brackets {} to show which code is part of the loop - so everything inside the brackets will be repeated every time we iterate through the loop.
For example:

for (i in seq_len(10)) {
  print(i)
}

[1] 1
[1] 2
[1] 3
[1] 4
[1] 5
[1] 6
[1] 7
[1] 8
[1] 9
[1] 10


We can add steps to our loop to run on each iteration.

for (i in seq_len(10)) {
  # add 2 to i
  j <- i + 2
  # take the square root of j
  sj <- sqrt(j)
  # round sj to the nearest whole number
  rsj <- round(sj)
  # print rsj
  print(rsj)
}

We can use our variable i inside the loop but we don’t have to, we can just use it to set the number of iterations.

title: Part 1: Loops
text:
Storing results from loops
Core
↑ top
We sometimes want to store the results of running our loop in a vector or data frame.
For example, here we store all of the cubed numbers from our example above in a vector called cubed_nums. Before we start the loop, we create an empty vector using c(). Then, each time we pass through the loop, we use c() again to append the new result to the end of the vector. Once the loop has finished, cubed_nums contains the results from every iteration.

cubed_nums <- c()

for (i in seq_len(20)) {
  res <- i^3
  cubed_nums <- c(cubed_nums, res)
}

print(cubed_nums)

 [1]    1    8   27   64  125  216  343  512  729 1000 1331 1728 2197 2744 3375
[16] 4096 4913 5832 6859 8000


We can also store the results of each iteration of a loop in a data frame.
One way to do this is to create an empty data frame before starting the loop using tibble(). During each iteration, we create a new one-row data frame containing the results from that iteration, then add it to the results data frame using the function bind_rows().
bind_rows() combines two data frames row-wise — that is, it adds the rows of one data frame underneath the rows of the other. If the data frames do not contain exactly the same columns, the resulting data frame contains all columns present in either data frame, with NA used where a row has no value for a particular column.






Figure 15.1: bind_rows() and bind_cols()



In this case, each time the loop runs, current_row is replaced with the results for the current species, then species_df grows by one row.
For example, we can adapt our animal loop above to store both the species name and whether it starts with “s”:

species <- c("monkey", "shark", "turkey", "snowman")
species_df <- tibble()

for (spp in species) {
  has_s <- startsWith(spp, "s")
  current_row <- tibble(
    Species = spp,
    Starts_with_S = has_s
  )
  species_df <- species_df |> bind_rows(current_row)
}
gt(species_df)

title: Part 1: Loops
text:
Review
↑ top






NoteSummary




Concepts

A for loop repeats a task for each item in a vector or other sequence.
Each pass through a loop is called an iteration.
A variable can take a different value on each iteration and be used (or not) within the code inside the loop.
Curly brackets ({}) define which code is repeated during each iteration of a loop.
Results generated during a loop can be stored by adding values to a vector or rows to a data frame.
The ^ operator is used to raise a number to a power.
Data manipulation and plotting workflows can be adapted to datasets with different structures by identifying the equivalent variables and processing steps.

title: Part 2: Using simulation to understand probability
text:
Introduction to simulation
Core
↑ top
Many biological processes involve an element of chance and therefore involve probability. In R, we can use simulation to generate data that approximates a random process. These simulated data allow us to investigate probability, test hypotheses and better understand the behaviour of biological systems.
If you are studying a stochastic process, the exact probability of an event can sometimes be calculated mathematically. In these cases, simulation provides a useful way to check your calculations. In other cases, an exact solution may be difficult or impossible to obtain, and simulation allows you to estimate the answer instead.
crumbs: 16  Part 2: Using simulation to understand probability

title: Part 2: Using simulation to understand probability
text:
How to simulate data
First, let’s perform a tiny simulation, of a coin toss.
We are using the function sample(), which was introduced in the last exercise of Part 1. We will initially use two arguments with this function: x - the elements from which to sample, and size, the number of samples to take. By default, R assumes that every element is equally probable.

coin_toss <- sample(c("Heads", "Tails"), size = 1)
print(coin_toss)

[1] "Heads"


We can use a for loop to toss multiple coins.

for (i in seq_len(5)) {
  coin_toss <- sample(c("Heads", "Tails"),
    size = 1
  )
  print(coin_toss)
}

[1] "Heads"
[1] "Heads"
[1] "Heads"
[1] "Tails"
[1] "Tails"


We can also do this directly with the sample function by changing size. We need to add the argument replace = TRUE to tell R to replace the samples - otherwise after two samples, the coin has no remaining sides!

coin_tosses <- sample(c("Heads", "Tails"),
  size = 5,
  replace = TRUE
)
print(coin_tosses)

[1] "Tails" "Tails" "Heads" "Tails" "Heads"


To count how many times a specific value occurs in a vector, you can use the operator == and the sum() function:

n_successes <- sum(coin_tosses == "Heads")
print(n_successes)

[1] 2


The coin showed Heads 2 times.
crumbs: 16  Part 2: Using simulation to understand probability

title: Part 2: Using simulation to understand probability
text:
Unequal probabilities
Core
↑ top
So far, we’ve assumed a “fair coin” - with 50% probability of each outcome. However, we can change this by giving an additional argument to the sample() function.
This argument is prob - a vector of probability weights corresponding to the elements of the original vector.
So, if we want the coin to land on heads 70% of the time, we would use:

coin_tosses <- sample(c("Heads", "Tails"),
  size = 5,
  replace = TRUE,
  prob = c(0.7, 0.3)
)
print(coin_tosses)

[1] "Tails" "Tails" "Heads" "Heads" "Tails"


If we had a vector c('Badger', 'Mushroom', 'Snake') and we want to sample 100 times from this vector, with replacement, selecting Badger 95% of the time, Mushroom 4% of the time and Snake 1% of the time, we would use this function as follows:

bm_vec <- c("Badger", "Mushroom", "Snake")
bm_probs <- c(0.95, 0.04, 0.01)

my_sample <- sample(bm_vec,
  size = 100,
  replace = TRUE,
  prob = bm_probs
)
print(my_sample)

Repeating simulations
Core
↑ top
If you run this simulation several times, you’ll see that the result often changes.
We can formalise this using a for loop, running the simulation a fixed number of times.
Let’s say we have 1000 squirrels, each making 150 attempts, with the same fixed probability of success of 30%.

for (i in seq_len(1000)) {
  is_success <- sample(c("SUCCESS", "FAILURE"),
    size = 150,
    replace = TRUE,
    prob = c(0.3, 0.7)
  )
  n_successes <- sum(is_success == "SUCCESS")
  combined_successes <- c(combined_successes, n_successes)
}

title: Part 2: Using simulation to understand probability
text:
The binomial distribution
Core
↑ top
As you may have recognised, this approximates a binomial distribution:

We have a fixed number of trials - 150.
We have a binary outcome - success or failure.
Our trials are independent.
The probability of success is constant across trials.

The number of successes announced by the squirrel above is the random variable - the number of successes, k out of 150 trials.
Increasing the number of simulations reduces the random variation in our estimate, bringing it closer to the theoretical distribution. Therefore, if we run our simulation more times, our empirical approximation should get closer to a theoretical binomial distribution.
crumbs: 16  Part 2: Using simulation to understand probability

title: Part 2: Using simulation to understand probability
text:
Using probability functions in R
Core
↑ top
As you learned in the lectures, the probability mass function (PMF) for the binomial distribution is:
\[
P(X = k) =
\binom{n}{k}
p^k
(1-p)^{n-k}
\]
This is implemented in R with the function dbinom().
The arguments for this function are:

x: calculate the number of successes - k in the equation,
size: number of trials, n in the equation, in our case 150 attempts per squirrel
prob: probability of success in each trial - p in the equation, the probability of squirrel success, 0.3, in our case.

Let’s estimate the probability that a squirrel succeeds 48 times.

n <- 150
k <- 48
p <- 0.3

prob_X_equals_k <- dbinom(k, n, p)
print(prob_X_equals_k)

[1] 0.06051733


We would expect this result around 6% of the time.
Let’s compare this with the result from our simulation. Using the sum() function, we can count how many squirrels succeeded 48 times.

n_successes <- pull(df_squirrels, N_Successful_Heists)
n_48 <- sum(n_successes == 48)
print(n_48)

[1] 64


In my version of the simulation, 64 out of 1000 squirrels succeeded 48/150 times, your results might vary.

print(n_48 / 1000)

[1] 0.064


This is around 6% of the squirrels - not far off the estimate using the PMF.

Plotting the theoretical distribution
Extension






ExerciseExercise 3 - Plotting a theoretical binomial distribution






Extension

As above, convert your results into a data frame. Include a column for the value of k.
Make a bar plot of the calculated probabilities.

This time, instead of using geom_bar(), which calculates the number of occurrences of each value in a column, we already have already calculated the heights we want for the bars in our bar chart - the probability of each number of successes. Therefore, we can use the function geom_col() which draws a bar chart based directly on the values in a data frame column.
geom_col() just needs the x and y axes to be specified - in this case N_Successful_Heists on the x axis and Probability on the y axis.

Inbuilt functions
Core
↑ top
R is often used for simulation, so there are inbuilt functions to help us.
Up to this point, we have simulated each individual attempt and then counted the number of successes. Because this type of experiment is so common, R provides a function that generates the number of successes directly.
With this binomially distributed data, we could have avoided most of the above (sorry) by using the function rbinom(), which automatically draws samples from a binomial distribution.
This function takes three arguments:

n: number of observations, in our case e.g. 1000 squirrels
size: number of trials, in our case 150 attempts per squirrel
prob: probability of success, in our case 0.3 (30% chance of stealing seeds successfully)


count_squirrels <- rbinom(n = 1000, size = 150, prob = 0.3)
print(count_squirrels)

  ylab("Number of squirrels") +

We have already used the function dbinom(), which gives us the probability of a specific number of successes, given specified values of k, n and p.
Another function, pbinom() calculates the probability that there will be no more than a specific number of successes. This is known as the cumulative probability. The arguments are similar to dbinom:

q: calculate the probability of no more than this number of successes.
size: number of trials - n in the equation, the number of attempts per squirrel, 150, in our case.
prob: probability of success in each trial - p in the equation, the probability of squirrel success, 0.3, in our case.

For example, to calculate the probability that a squirrel will succeed no more than 48 times:

prob_up_to_48 <- pbinom(48, 150, 0.3)
print(prob_up_to_48)

[1] 0.7358792


We can verify this with our count_squirrels vector generated with rbinom.
The function length() returns the number of elements in a vector.

print(sum(count_squirrels <= 48) / length(count_squirrels))

[1] 0.718








ExerciseExercise 4 - Using binomial functions






Recommended
↑ top
A botanist studies a plant species in which each flower has a 60% probability of having been pollinated. She needs 125 pollinated flowers for her experiment, but she can’t tell which flowers are pollinated until she gets back to the lab. She picks 200 flowers.
Using simulation, estimate the probability that she has collected enough pollinated flowers for her experiment.
Please solve this problem using the rbinom() function in your prac3_exercises.qmd Quarto file.






Note



To count how many numbers in a numeric vector, vec, are less than or equal to a certain value, val you can use sum(vec <= val). This syntax also works with other operators (Filtering data frames), e.g. <, >, >=, ==, !=.








AnswerAnswer







n_sims <- 1000
n_flowers_per_sim <- 200

# Simulate 1000 datasets of 200 flowers with
# a 60% chance of being pollinated
flowers <- rbinom(
  n = n_sims,
  size = n_flowers_per_sim,
  prob = 0.6
)

# How many times were at least 125 flowers
# pollinated?
times_successful <- sum(flowers >= 125)

# What proportion of the attempts is this?
prop_successful <- times_successful / n_sims
print(prop_successful)

[1] 0.264


Based on this simulation, there is an estimated 26% probability she has 125 pollinated flowers.
We can check this using pbinom().

# Probability that less than 125 flowers are
# pollinated
prob_under_125 <- pbinom(124, 200, 0.6)

# Probability that at least 125 flowers are
# pollinated
prob_125_or_over <- 1 - prob_under_125

print(prob_125_or_over)

[1] 0.2589559


26% - similar to the simulated value. Running more simulations would make the estimate more accurate.














ExerciseExercise 5 - How many flowers should she collect?






Extension
In your prac3_exercises.qmd Quarto file, estimate the smallest number of flowers the botanist would need to collect to have at least a 95% probability of obtaining 125 pollinated flowers.

props <- c()
# We know it's more than 200 - let's try to up to 250
# Run the simulation for each of these numbers of
# flowers
for (i in seq(200, 250, 1)) {
  flowers <- rbinom(
    n = n_sims,
    size = i,
    prob = 0.6
  )
  # Calculate the number and proportion of times
  # she was successful
  # Store only this value, not the whole vector
  times_successful <- sum(flowers >= 125)
  prop_successful <- times_successful / n_sims
  props <- c(props, prop_successful)
}

# Convert these into a data frame
prop_df <- tibble(
  npicked = seq(200, 250, 1),
  psuccess = props
)

# Find the rows where she succeeded at least
# 95% of the time
prop_df_filt <- prop_df |>
  filter(psuccess >= 0.95)

Review
↑ top






NoteSummary




Concepts

Simulation can be used to approximate stochastic processes by generating random data.
Random events can be simulated with equal or unequal probabilities.
Repeating a simulation many times produces an empirical distribution of its possible outcomes.
Increasing the number of simulations generally reduces random variation in an estimate, allowing the empirical distribution to more closely approximate the theoretical distribution.
R provides functions both for calculating probabilities from theoretical distributions and for generating random values from them.



Functions








Function
What it does
Level




geom_bar()
Creates a bar chart by counting the number of observations with each value and using this to calculate the height of the bars.
Core


dbinom()
Calculates the probability of a specified number of successes from a binomial distribution.
Core


rbinom()
Generates random values from a binomial distribution.
Core


pbinom()
Calculates the cumulative probability of a binomial distribution up to a specified number of successes.
Core


length()
Returns the number of elements in an object.
Core


geom_col()
Creates a bar chart using the values specified in the data to determine the heights of the bars.

title: Part 3: Using simulation to understand data
section: Comparing real, simulated and expected data - discrete distributions
text:
Comparing real, simulated and expected data - discrete distributions
Core
↑ top
We can use these functions to help establish the distribution of real datasets.
First, let’s look at some real data which is described as Poisson distributed. This data comes from a paper by Assaf et al. published in Genome Research in 2017.
In this paper, the authors performed a mutation accumulation experiment in the fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster. They allowed 17 populations of Drosophila to accumulate mutations for 36-53 generations, then sequenced them and counted novel mutations per population.
The authors describe the mutation counts on each chromosome arm per population as Poisson distributed (shown in Figure 1B in the paper).
This seems reasonable:

We are counting how many times an event - a mutation - occurs.
Counts are made over a known interval - in this case a defined number of generations.
Events occur independently (we assume).
Events occur at a constant average rate throughout the interval (again, we assume).
The chance of multiple events in a very small interval is negligible.
There is no fixed upper limit to the count - in theory any number of mutations could occur.

In this practical, we will just look at data from one chromosome arm, the right arm of chromosome 2.

Examining the data
This data is provided in a CSV file extracted from the supplementary data associated with the publication - data/drosophila_counts.csv. Let’s read it.

dcounts <- read_csv("data/drosophila_counts.csv")
gt(dcounts)







Population_ID
Novel_Mutation_Count




MA_35
6


MA_24
2

7

The Population_ID column is the ID of the Drosophila population in which the mutations were counted.
The Novel_Mutation_Count column is the number of mutations accumulated on chromosome arm 2R in that population.







ExerciseExercise 1 - Summarise data






Core
If you haven’t already, create a new Quarto file, drosophila.qmd.






NoteInclude this code




library(tidyverse)
library(gt)
set.seed(42)



In your drosophila.qmd Quarto file, read the csv file and create a data frame using the function summarise() which shows:

Total novel mutation count (function sum()), in the column total_nm.
Maximum novel mutation count (function max() in the column max_nm)
Mean novel mutation count (function mean()), in the column mean_nm.
Variance in novel mutation count (function var()), in the column variance_nm.

Store your data frame in a variable, dros_summary and look at it with gt().
Looking at the mean and variance, do you think that these data are Poisson distributed?






AnswerAnswer







dcounts <- read_csv("data/drosophila_counts.csv")

dros_summary <- dcounts |>
  summarise(
    total_nm = sum(Novel_Mutation_Count),
    max_nm = max(Novel_Mutation_Count),
    mean_nm = mean(Novel_Mutation_Count),
    variance_nm = var(Novel_Mutation_Count)
  )

gt(dros_summary)







total_nm
max_nm
mean_nm
variance_nm




97
11
5.705882
7.720588







The variance is a bit higher than the mean - maybe the data is not Poisson distributed? We can do some more analysis to find out.










Plotting the data
Let’s plot a bar chart of our mutation counts and have a look at its distribution.
We can plot the number of occurrences of each value of a discrete variable in R by adding a geom_bar() layer to our ggplot. The mapping function aes() for geom_bar only needs one argument, the column to map to the x axis. The y axis will be generated automatically by counting the number of times each value of x occurs.






ExerciseExercise 2 - Plot a bar chart






Core
In your drosophila.qmd Quarto file, plot a bar chart of the number of populations in which each number of mutations was observed, using ggplot() and geom_bar().






AnswerAnswer







ggplot(dcounts, aes(x = Novel_Mutation_Count)) +
  geom_bar() +
  ggtitle("Number of Populations with Each Mutation Count - Observed") +
  xlab("Novel mutation count") +
  ylab("Number of populations") +
  theme_minimal()
















Again, this kind of looks Poisson distributed, but it’s hard to be sure.


Adding a theoretical distribution
Extension
It might help to compare this data to a theoretical, perfect, Poisson distribution.
You have seen the probability mass function for the Poisson distribution in the lectures.
\[
P(X = k) = \frac{\lambda^k e^{-\lambda}}{k!}
\]
So, to calculate the probability of observing exactly k mutations under a Poisson distribution, we have one parameter:

λ (lambda) - in our case, the mean number of mutations on chromosome arm 2R per population.

k is the particular mutation count for which we want to calculate the probability.
We can calculate this using the R function dpois().
Let’s look at our summary data frame again:

gt(dros_summary)







total_nm
max_nm
mean_nm
variance_nm




97
11
5.705882
7.720588







We have a mean of 5.71 mutations per population. As an example, let’s calculate the probability of observing 4 mutations. In this case, lambda = 5.71 and k = 4.

sample_mean <- dros_summary |> pull(mean_nm)
k <- 4
prob <- dpois(x = k, lambda = sample_mean)
print(prob)

[1] 0.1469085


The probability is around 0.15. We can multiply this by the number of populations, 17, to get the expected number of populations which will have 4 mutations.
The function nrow() returns the number of rows in a data frame.

n_populations <- nrow(dcounts)
expected_count <- prob * n_populations
print(expected_count)

[1] 2.497444


So, on chromosome 2R, if the data were perfectly Poisson distributed, we would expect to see 4 mutations in 2.5 populations (The expected count does not need to be a whole number. It represents the average number of populations we would expect across many repetitions of the experiment).
Now let’s calculate the probability of all possible mutation counts - all possible values of k. The least possible mutations is 0, let’s use the maximum observed number of mutations as our maximum, so our theoretical distribution covers our observed range. We have this in our summary table above - the highest novel mutation count in any population is 11.
Helpfully, we can apply dpois to multiple values of k at once, e.g. to calculate the theoretical number of populations with each mutation count - each value of k - from 0 to 11, we can do the following.

max_k <- dros_summary |> pull(max_nm)
possible_ks <- seq(0, max_k)

all_theor_probs <- dpois(possible_ks,
  lambda = sample_mean
)

print(all_theor_probs)

 [1] 0.003326341 0.018979711 0.054147999 0.102987370 0.146908454 0.167648471
 [7] 0.159430409 0.129955880 0.092689120 0.058763691 0.033529870 0.017392500


We can then multiply all of them simultaneously by the number of populations.

all_theor_counts <- all_theor_probs * n_populations
print(all_theor_counts)

 [1] 0.0565478 0.3226551 0.9205160 1.7507853 2.4974437 2.8500240 2.7103170
 [8] 2.2092500 1.5757150 0.9989827 0.5700078 0.2956725


This is our theoretical Poisson distribution over the range of mutation counts observed in our data.
We can add it to our plot. To do so, it needs to be in its own data frame.

theor_df <- tibble(
  k = possible_ks,
  Theoretical_Mutation_Count = all_theor_counts
)







NoteInclude this code (Extension only)



Include this code in your drosophila.qmd Quarto file.
Combining the steps above, the full code block to generate the theoretical data frame is as follows:

# Find the maximum observed value of k
max_k <- dros_summary |> pull(max_nm)

# Make a sequence of numbers from 0
# to the observed maximum k
possible_ks <- seq(0, max_k)

# Extract the sample mean from the summary data frame
sample_mean <- dros_summary |> pull(mean_nm)

# Calculate the theoretical distribution
all_theor_probs <- dpois(possible_ks,
  lambda = sample_mean
)
all_theor_counts <- all_theor_probs * n_populations

# Put the results in a data frame
theor_df <- tibble(
  k = possible_ks,
  Theoretical_Mutation_Count = all_theor_counts
)



We can now add the theoretical points to our plot using geom_point(). We can give this function the new data frame to use instead of dcounts.






NoteInclude this code (Extension only)



Include this code in your drosophila.qmd Quarto file.

ggplot(data = dcounts, mapping = aes(x = Novel_Mutation_Count)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "skyblue") +
  geom_point(data = theor_df, mapping = aes(
    x = k,
    y = Theoretical_Mutation_Count
  ), size = 3) +
  ggtitle("Number of Populations with Each Mutation Count -\nObserved and Theoretical") +
  xlab("Novel mutation count") +
  ylab("Number of populations") +
  theme_minimal()














Note



If you want to include a line break e.g. in a plot title, you can insert \n at the point where the break should be.


Again, the data looks kind of Poisson distributed, but it is not particularly definitive.




Simulation
Core
↑ top
One explanation for the difference between the sample mean and variance is the small sample size. This would also explain why our data don’t look like an ideal Poisson distribution.
We only have 17 populations, so the values we calculate from our sample will not exactly match the true properties of the underlying distribution. Even if the mutations really do follow a Poisson distribution, different random samples of only 17 populations will likely give slightly different means and variances simply due to chance.
This is another case where simulating data is really helpful. Let’s simulate some data sets which are definitely drawn from a Poisson distribution and have a sample size of 17, and see how often the difference between the mean and the variance is as big or bigger than for our data.
We can use the rpois function for this.
First, let’s generate simulated mutation counts drawn from a Poisson distribution for 17 populations, with lambda corresponding to our sample mean.

sample_mean <- dros_summary |> pull(mean_nm)
n_populations <- nrow(dcounts)

simulated_counts <- rpois(
  n = n_populations,
  lambda = sample_mean
)
print(simulated_counts)

 [1]  3 12 10  3  6  5  9  5  8  7  8  5  7  1  8  1  4


This vector has a mean and a variance, just like our real counts.

print(mean(simulated_counts))

[1] 6

print(var(simulated_counts))

[1] 9.375


By simulating lots of similar datasets, we can establish if the difference between the mean and variance we saw with our real data is consistent with this data, which we know is Poisson distributed.
The difference we saw in our real data is easy to calculate.

sample_mean <- dros_summary |>
  pull(mean_nm)
sample_variance <- dros_summary |>
  pull(variance_nm)

sample_diff <- abs(sample_mean - sample_variance)

We saw a difference of 2.01 between the two values.






ExerciseExercise 3 - Simulate Poisson data






Core
In your drosophila.qmd Quarto file, simulate the mutation counts on chromosome 2R for 17 populations 1000 times.
You will need to combine the simulation above with the for loops you learned in Part 1.
Before starting your loop:

Create an empty vector called mean_sim.
Create an empty vector called var_sim.

Then, on each iteration of your loop:

Use rpois() to simulate mutation counts for 17 populations, as demonstrated above.
Calculate the mean (mean()) of the simulated counts.
Calculate the variance (var()) of the simulated counts.
Append these values to the mean_sim and var_sim vectors.

After the loop has finished:

Create df_sim, containing the two vectors as columns called mean and var.
Add a third column, diff, containing the absolute difference between the mean and variance.







AnswerAnswer






Create an empty vector called mean_sim. Create an empty vector called var_sim.

mean_sim <- c()
var_sim <- c()

Then, on each iteration of your loop:

Use rpois() to simulate mutation counts for 17 populations, as demonstrated above.
Calculate the mean (mean()) of the simulated counts.
Calculate the variance (var()) of the simulated counts.
Append these values to the mean_sim and var_sim vectors.


for (i in seq_len(1000)) {
  # Use `rpois()` to simulate mutation counts for
  # 17 populations
  simulated_counts <- rpois(
    n = n_populations,
    lambda = sample_mean
  )

  # Take the mean and variance of the simulated counts
  current_mean <- mean(simulated_counts)
  current_var <- var(simulated_counts)

  # Append these values to the `mean_sim` and `var_sim` vectors.
  mean_sim <- c(mean_sim, current_mean)
  var_sim <- c(var_sim, current_var)
}

Create df_sim, containing the two vectors as columns called mean and var.
Add a third column, diff, containing the absolute difference between the mean and variance.

df_sim <- tibble(
  mean = mean_sim,
  var = var_sim,
  diff = abs(mean_sim - var_sim)
)









Now, let’s plot histograms of the 1000 differences between the mean and variance we calculated and see how they compare to our value of 2.01.






ExerciseExercise 4 - Plot differences between mean and variance






Core

In your drosophila.qmd Quarto file, using ggplot, plot a histogram (geom_histogram()) showing the difference between the mean and variance values in your simulated data.







Note



You can add a histogram in ggplot using the function geom_histogram(). Like geom_bar() it only requires one mapping, the x axis variable, in this case the difference between the mean and variance. The y axis frequencies are calculated from the data.
You can change the number of bins in the histogram using the argument bins = n, where n is the number of bins.



Look at your histogram - does our observed value of 2.01 fit within the values observed for small samples pulled from a Poisson distribution?
Calculate the percentage of your simulated samples in which the difference between the sample mean and sample variance is greater than the difference observed in the study.







AnswerAnswer






In your drosophila.qmd Quarto file, using ggplot, plot a histogram (geom_histogram()) showing the difference between the mean and variance values in your simulated data.
Look at your histogram - does our observed value of 2.01 fit within the values observed for small samples pulled from a Poisson distribution?

ggplot(df_sim, aes(x = diff)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  ggtitle("Difference between mean and variance across samples - Simulated") +
  xlab("Difference between mean and variance") +
  ylab("Number of simulations") +
  theme_minimal()








The difference between the mean and variance seen in the study is consistent with what we could observe in a sample of 17 populations drawn from a Poisson distribution.
Calculate the percentage of your simulated samples in which the difference between the sample mean and sample variance is greater than the difference observed in the study.

greater <- df_sim |> filter(diff > sample_diff)
prop <- nrow(greater) / nrow(df_sim)
print(prop)

[1] 0.308


In my simulation, 31% of simulated samples had a difference between the mean and variance which is greater than the value of 2.01 observed in the study.








You can add a vertical line to the plot using the function geom_vline() with the mapping x_intercept. ggplot will add a vertical line at the position you give to x_intercept.

ggplot(df_sim, aes(x = diff)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = sample_diff, color = "red") +
  ggtitle("Difference between Mean and Variance across Samples -\nSimulated and Observed") +
  xlab("Difference between mean and variance") +
  ylab("Number of simulations") +
  theme_minimal()

section: Comparing real, simulated and expected data - continuous distributions
text:
Comparing real, simulated and expected data - continuous distributions
Core
↑ top
Whatever type of distribution our data is from, this process is very similar.
There are some very minor differences when looking at a continuous variable instead of a discrete variable.
For example, in this paper published in Diversity in 2023, Engelman estimated the body size of an extinct fish, Dunkleosteus terrelli, by looking at fossils and at the correlations between various measurements in other fish.
We will look at the data set they generated by taking various measurements of other fish, in particular, the lamprey Geotria macrostoma and determine if the total length of these fish is normally distributed.
The data, which are identical to Supplementary File S1 from the paper, are saved as data/fish.csv.






Figure 17.1: Dunkleosteus terrelli. Source









Figure 17.2: Geotria macrostoma. Source









ExerciseExercise 5 - Visualise fish length






Core
If you haven’t already, create a new Quarto file, distributions.qmd.






NoteInclude this code




library(tidyverse)
library(gt)
library(janitor)
set.seed(42)



In your distributions.qmd Quarto file:

Read the file fish.csv into a data frame variable. Use the clean_names() function to clean the column names.
Filter the data to keep only rows where the genus column is equal to Geotria, store the result as a variable named geo.
Plot the column total_length_cm as a histogram

Do you think this data is normally distributed?






AnswerAnswer







# Read the data
fish <- read_csv("data/fish.csv") |> clean_names()

# Filter to keep only the genus Geotria
geo <- fish |> filter(genus == "Geotria")

# Plot a histogram
ggplot(geo, aes(x = total_length_cm)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  ggtitle("Distribution of total length in Geotria fish - Observed") +
  xlab("Total length (cm)") +
  ylab("Number of fish") +
  theme_minimal()








The data looks basically normally distributed.









Converting probability to density
With continuous data, the probability distribution is described by a probability density function (PDF) rather than a PMF. The theoretical distribution is therefore represented by a continuous curve rather than probabilities at a series of discrete values.
So that our data is comparable with the PDF, we can easily transform our data to show density, rather than counts, using the function after_stat() with the argument density, which we use as a mapping to the geom_histogram() function. after_stat(density) rescales the histogram so that its total area is 1, allowing it to be compared directly with a probability density function.

ggplot(geo, aes(
  x = total_length_cm
)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 30
  ) +
  ggtitle("Distribution of total length in Geotria fish  - Observed") +
  xlab("Total length (cm)") +
  ylab("Density") +
  theme_minimal()










Adding a theoretical normal distribution
It might be helpful to compare our data to a perfect, theoretical normal distribution. For a continuous distribution, it’s very easy to add a theoretical distribution to our plot.
The function stat_function() is used to add a continuous curve, based on a function, onto a plot.
The arguments are:

fun - the name of a function
args - a list of the arguments to that function

In our case, the function is dnorm() - the PDF for the normal distribution. The arguments are the two parameters of the normal distribution dnorm() - mean and standard deviation.
So, we would call this function as:
stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = mean_obs, sd = sd_obs))
Where mean_obs is the mean observed total fish length from our data and sd_obs is the standard deviation of the same data.
We can add this directly to the plot using the same plotting code as before, but with this function as an extra layer.
The function sd() calculates the standard deviation of a vector or column.

# Calculate the observed mean and standard deviation
mean_obs <- mean(pull(geo, total_length_cm))
sd_obs <- sd(pull(geo, total_length_cm))

# Draw the plot
ggplot(geo, aes(
  x = total_length_cm
)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 50
  ) +
  stat_function(
    fun = dnorm,
    args = list(mean = mean_obs, sd = sd_obs)
  ) +
  ggtitle("Distribution of total length in Geotria fish  -\nObserved and Theoretical") +
  xlab("Total length (cm)") +
  ylab("Density") +
  theme_minimal()










Comparing skewness between our observed data and a theoretical distribution
Extension
One property that can help us describe how the shape of a distribution differs from a normal distribution is skewness - a measure of the asymmetry of the distribution. We can use simulation to establish if the skewness of our observed sample is within the range of skewness values for samples of the same size pulled from a normal distribution.






Figure 17.3: Skewness. Source



We can calculate skewness using the R function skewness() from the package moments.
The theoretical normal distribution has a skewness of 0. However, a finite sample drawn from a normal distribution will not usually have a skewness of exactly 0.
The only argument to this function is a vector. For example, for our observed data:

# Calculate the skewness
skew <- skewness(pull(geo, total_length_cm))
print(skew)

[1] -0.148105


Our observed value is -0.15 — reasonably close to 0. But how close should we expect it to be for a sample of this size? Let’s simulate normally distributed data for comparison.






ExerciseExercise 6 - Skewness in simulated data






Extension






NoteInclude this code



Include the following as an R code chunk in your distributions.qmd Quarto file.

library(moments)



In your distributions.qmd Quarto file:

For 10,000 repeats, using the rnorm() function, generate the same number of data points (you can count how many rows are in the data frame with the function nrow()) as in the geo table with the same mean (function mean()) and standard deviation (function sd()) as Geotria.
Store the skewness for each simulation as a vector.
Calculate the proportion of simulated datasets which were more skewed than the observed data.

Because skewness can be positive or negative, use the absolute values of the observed and simulated skewness when comparing how far they are from zero (function abs())






AnswerAnswer






For 10,000 repeats, using the rnorm() function, generate the same number of data points as in the geo table with the same mean and standard deviation as Geotria.
Store the skewness for each simulation as a vector.

nrow_obs <- nrow(geo)
mean_obs <- mean(pull(geo, total_length_cm))
sd_obs <- sd(pull(geo, total_length_cm))

skews <- c()

for (i in seq_len(10000)) {
  points <- rnorm(nrow_obs, mean = mean_obs, sd = sd_obs)
  skew <- skewness(points)
  skews <- c(skews, skew)
}

skew_df <- tibble(Skewness = skews)

Calculate the proportion of simulated datasets which were more skewed than the observed data.

# Retrieve the observed skewness
body_length <- geo |> pull(total_length_cm)
skew_obs <- skewness(body_length)

# Calculate the absolute value of the observed skewness
abs_skew_obs <- abs(skew_obs)

# Calculate the absolute value of the simulated skewness
abs_skew_sim <- abs(skews)

# Count how many times this is more than our observed skewness
more_than_obs <- sum(abs_skew_sim > abs_skew_obs)

# Count the proportion of times this is more than our observed skewness
skew_prop_more_than_obs <- more_than_obs / 10000

print(skew_prop_more_than_obs)

[1] 0.2582


25.82% of our simulated normal distributions are more skewed than our observed data.
The observed skewness is therefore consistent with what we might expect from a sample of this size drawn from a normal distribution - i.e. if the body length of the whole population of Geotria is normally distributed.

Review
↑ top






NoteSummary




Concepts

R uses a consistent naming convention for functions associated with probability distributions: r...() generates random values, d...() gives probabilities or densities, p...() gives cumulative probabilities and q...() gives quantiles.
Observed data can be compared with a theoretical probability distribution to investigate whether the proposed distribution is appropriate.
Simulation can be used to investigate whether properties of an observed sample are consistent with samples drawn from a particular theoretical distribution.
Skewness (skewness()) measures the asymmetry of a distribution. (Extension)

What it does
Level

Calculates quantiles of a binomial distribution.
Core

Calculates the variance of a set of values.
Core

Generates random values from a Poisson distribution.
Core

Adds a histogram to a ggplot, calculating the bar heights from the data provided.
Core

Adds a vertical line to a ggplot.
Core

Converts column names into a consistent format that is easier to use in R.
Core

Maps a value calculated by a ggplot statistical transformation, such as density.
Core

Adds a curve calculated from a function to a ggplot.
Core

Calculates probability densities from a normal distribution.
Core

Calculates the standard deviation of a set of values.
Core

Calculates probabilities from a Poisson distribution.

Returns the number of rows in a data frame.

title: Part 4: Simulation exercises
text:
Neuronal firing intervals
Using the skills we’ve built so far, we can now simulate data from any probability distribution implemented in R, whether to compare with observed data, test a hypothesis or model a process.
Extension
↑ top
The data in data/neurons.csv is from this paper, published by Koepcke et al. in Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience in 2019.
These authors investigated whether a single neuron can rapidly detect changes in a sensory stimulus by analysing the time between successive action potentials (inter-spike intervals). The analysis was performed using multiple neurons.
The data in data/neurons.csv come from a single neuron and contain a series of waiting times between successive spikes, measured in seconds.

title: Part 4: Simulation exercises
text:
ExerciseExercise 1 - Investigate neuronal firing






Extension
Imagine that you are a researcher and you notice that this neuron seems to fire very regularly. In particular, it never seems to pause for very long between spikes. By estimating the probability distribution of the waiting times and using simulation, investigate whether the longest observed wait is unusually short.
In your distributions.qmd Quarto file:

Read the CSV file containing the data.
Plot a histogram with an appropriate number of bins showing how the waiting times are distributed.
Based on the shape of the histogram and the biological process being measured, decide which probability distribution might provide an appropriate model for the waiting times.
Find the longest wait time in the observed data.
Using the appropriate function from the table in Other distributions, generate 1000 random datasets with the same number of measurements from the distribution you have selected, generating parameters from your data as needed. Record the longest wait time.
Assuming the observed data follows the same distribution as the simulated data, plot a histogram of your simulated maxima and estimate if the maximum observed wait time is unexpectedly short.
Calculate the percentage of your simulated samples in which the maximum wait time is less than or equal to the maximum observed in the study.
Using the appropriate cumulative probability function, calculate the theoretical probability that a single wait time will be less than or equal to your observed maximum.
Use this probability to calculate the theoretical probability that all observed waiting times would be less than or equal to the observed maximum.







AnswerAnswer






Read the file containing the data.

neuron_df <- read_csv("data/neurons.csv")

Plot a histogram with an appropriate number of bins showing how the data is distributed.

ggplot(
  neuron_df,
  aes(x = Inter_Spike_Interval)
) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  ggtitle("Distribution of waiting times for single neurons - Observed") +
  xlab("Waiting time (s)") +
  ylab("Number of observations") +
  theme_minimal()








Based on the shape of the histogram and the biological process being measured, decide which probability distribution might provide an appropriate model for the waiting times.
The distribution of waiting times between spikes looks approximately exponential.
If instead we were to count the number of spikes in a fixed interval, the simplest model would be to assume they are Poisson distributed.

We are counting how many times an event - a spike - occurs.
Counts are made over a known interval.
Spikes occur independently (we assume).
Spikes occur at a constant average rate throughout the interval (again, we assume).
The chance of multiple spikes in a very small interval is negligible.
There is no fixed upper limit to the count - in theory any number of spikes could occur.

If spike occurrences can be modelled as a Poisson process, the waiting times between successive spikes follow an exponential distribution.
Find the longest wait time in the observed data.

max_observed <- max(pull(neuron_df, Inter_Spike_Interval))
print(max_observed)

[1] 0.1273


Using the appropriate function from the table in Other distributions, generate 1000 random datasets with the same number of measurements from the distribution you have selected, generating parameters from your data as needed. Record the longest wait time.

sample_mean_wait_time <- mean(pull(neuron_df, Inter_Spike_Interval))
n_observations <- nrow(neuron_df)
lambda <- 1 / sample_mean_wait_time

The mean wait time in our dataset is 0.0296, so the rate for our exponential distribution is 1/0.0296.

maxis <- c()
for (i in seq_len(1000)) {
  expo <- rexp(
    n = n_observations,
    rate = lambda
  )
  maxi <- max(expo)
  maxis <- c(maxis, maxi)
}
maxi_df <- tibble(Maximum_Wait_Time = maxis)

Assuming the observed data follows the same distribution as the simulated data, plot a histogram of your simulated maxima and estimate if the maximum observed wait time is unexpectedly long or short.

ggplot(
  maxi_df,
  aes(x = Maximum_Wait_Time)
) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = max_observed, color = "red") +
  ggtitle("Distribution of maximum waiting times for single neurons - Simulated and Observed") +
  xlab("Maximum waiting time (s)") +
  ylab("Number of simulations") +
  theme_minimal()








The observed maximum waiting time is towards the lower end of the simulated maxima, but still falls within the range expected under the fitted exponential model.
Calculate the percentage of your simulated samples in which the maximum wait time is less than or equal to the maximum observed in the study.

filt_maxi <- maxi_df |>
  filter(Maximum_Wait_Time <= max_observed)

prop <- nrow(filt_maxi) / nrow(maxi_df)
print(prop)

[1] 0.163


Using the appropriate cumulative probability function, calculate the theoretical probability that a single wait time will be less than or equal to your observed maximum.

prob_one_wt <- pexp(max_observed, rate = lambda)
print(prob_one_wt)

[1] 0.9864358


Calculate the theoretical probability that all 144 of your observations would be less than this value.

prob_all_wt <- prob_one_wt^n_observations
print(prob_all_wt)

[1] 0.1399304


Based on these results, the observed maximum waiting time is shorter than many of the simulated maxima. However, it is still well within the range expected from an exponential distribution, so there is no strong evidence that its behaviour is unusual, assuming our wait times are exponentially distributed.

title: Part 4: Simulation exercises
text:
Pancreatic islet sizes
Bonus
Pancreatic islets of Langerhans are clusters of endocrine cells in the pancreas. Individual pancreatic islets vary in size - measurements from human pancreatic islet isolations show a distribution of islet diameters.
In this paper, published in Cell Transplantation in 2009, Buchwald et al. analysed the size composition of human pancreatic islet isolations. The authors had data from more than 200 human islet isolations and looked at the distribution of islet diameters. They found lots of relatively small islets and progressively fewer large ones.
They found that the distribution of individual islet diameters could be described by a Weibull probability distribution with shape parameter κ=1.5 and scale parameter λ=105.
The Weibull probability distribution is available in R using the functions rweibull(), dweibull(), pweibull() and qweibull().
The main arguments for rweibull are: * n - number of points to simulate * shape - the shape parameter of the distribution * scale - the scale parameter of the distribution






ExerciseExercise 2 - The Weibull distribution






Bonus
In your distributions.qmd Quarto file: * Plot a density-scaled histogram of the diameters of 10,000 simulated islets. * Overlay a theoretical Weibull distribution. * During manual assessment, only islets with a diameter of at least 50 μm are included in the standard counting procedure. Given that an islet is included in the count, estimate the probability that its diameter is between 100 and 150 μm.






AnswerAnswer






Plot a density-scaled histogram of the diameters of 10,000 simulated islets.
Overlay a theoretical Weibull distribution.

# Simulate the islets
islet_diams <- rweibull(
  n = 10000,
  shape = 1.5,
  scale = 105
)
# Put them in a data frame
islet_diams_df <- tibble(Islet_Diameter = islet_diams)

# Plot the results as a histogram with an overlaid
# Weibull distribution
ggplot(islet_diams_df, aes(x = Islet_Diameter)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 50,
    fill = "hotpink"
  ) +
  stat_function(
    fun = dweibull,
    args = list(
      shape = 1.5,
      scale = 105
    )
  ) +
  ggtitle("Distribution of diameter of islets - Simulated and Theoretical") +
  xlab("Diameter (μm)") +
  ylab("Density") +
  theme_minimal()








During manual assessment, only islets with a diameter of at least 50 μm are included in the standard counting procedure. Given that an islet is included in the count, estimate the probability that its diameter is between 100 and 150 μm.

# Filter the data frame to keep only islets >= 50 um
islets_over_50 <- islet_diams_df |> filter(Islet_Diameter >= 50)

# Count how many of these there are
n_islets_over_50 <- nrow(islets_over_50)

# Filter the data frame to keep only islets 100-150 um
islets_100_150 <- islet_diams_df |> filter(
  Islet_Diameter >= 100,
  Islet_Diameter <= 150
)
# Count how many of these there are
n_islets_100_150 <- nrow(islets_100_150)

# Calculate the proportion of islets >= 50 um which are 100 to 150 um
prop_counted_islets_100_150 <- n_islets_100_150 / n_islets_over_50
print(prop_counted_islets_100_150)

[1] 0.2982481

title: Part 5: Conditional Probability
text:
UK cervical screening data
Core
↑ top
In the UK, cervical screening is routinely offered regularly to any individual with a cervix aged 25 to 64. This screening tests for high-risk strains of human papillomavirus (HPV). Members of this group of viruses can damage cells in the cervix and cause cervical cancer. Where tests are positive for high-risk HPV (hrHPV), the samples are further tested for abnormal cells and, if abnormal cells are found, additional tests for pre-cancerous cells and cervical cancer are performed.
For the purposes of this practical, we will treat hrHPV status as a marker associated with abnormal cervical cytology, and later explore how this relates to the probability of cervical cancer.
The following data are from this publication, published in 2006 in the British Journal of Cancer (note that this is before routine vaccination against HPV was introduced in the UK).
In this study 24,510 people in the UK were screened for hrHPV and cytology was performed in all cases to detect abnormal cells. In this practical we will consider 21,843 of these people - by excluding people who had borderline or mild abnormal cytology.

title: Part 5: Conditional Probability
text:
HPV data analysis
Core
↑ top
Of these 21,843, 12.1% of people tested positive for hrHPV. 2.1% of people had moderately or severely abnormal cytology, the remainder were normal.
The number of people with and without hrHPV and with and without abnormal cytology are provided in CSV format in data/cm_all_ages.csv.






ExerciseExercise 1 - Calculate conditional probabilities






Core
If you haven’t already, create a new Quarto file, hpv.qmd.






NoteInclude this code




library(tidyverse)
library(gt)
set.seed(42)



In your hpv.qmd Quarto file, read data/cm_all_ages.csv into a data frame and view the contents with gt().
For this first part of the exercise you do not need to use simulation, you can directly calculate the values from the data frame.
Calculate:

The proportion of people with hrHPV who have abnormal cells. Store this as prop_abnormal_given_hpv
The proportion without hrHPV who have abnormal cells. Store this as prop_abnormal_given_no_hpv
The proportion of people with abnormal cells who have hrHPV - the sensitivity of hrHPV as a marker. Store this as prop_hpv_given_abnormal.
The proportion of people who have normal cells and don’t have hrHPV - the specificity of hrHPV as a marker. Store this as prop_no_hpv_given_normal.







Note



Remember that you can use the pull() function to extract a column from a data frame and the filter() function to filter rows based on specific criteria.








AnswerAnswer






In your hpv.qmd Quarto file, read data/cm_all_ages.csv into a data frame and view the contents with gt().

hpv_df <- read_csv("data/cm_all_ages.csv")
gt(hpv_df)

Extract the true positives, true negatives, false positives, false negatives:

True positives - have HPV and have abnormal cells
True negatives - don’t have HPV and have normal cells
False positives - have HPV and have normal cells
False negatives - don’t have HPV and have abnormal cells


tp <- hpv_df |>
  filter(
    HPV_Status == "HPV+",
    Cytology == "Abnormal"
  ) |>
  pull(N_individuals)
tn <- hpv_df |>
  filter(
    HPV_Status == "HPV-",
    Cytology == "Normal"
  ) |>
  pull(N_individuals)
fp <- hpv_df |>
  filter(
    HPV_Status == "HPV+",
    Cytology == "Normal"
  ) |>
  pull(N_individuals)
fn <- hpv_df |>
  filter(
    HPV_Status == "HPV-",
    Cytology == "Abnormal"
  ) |>
  pull(N_individuals)

Calculate the proportion of people with hrHPV who have abnormal cells.

# Count how many people have hrHPV - positives
hpv_count <- tp + fp

# Calculate the proportion of people with hrHPV who
# also have abnormal cells - true positives / positives
prop_abnormal_given_hpv <- tp / hpv_count
print(prop_abnormal_given_hpv)

[1] 0.1577753


15.78% of people with hrHPV have abnormal cells.
Calculate the proportion of people without hrHPV who have abnormal cells.

# Count how many people don't have hrHPV - negatives
hpv_m_count <- tn + fn

# Calculate the proportion of people who don't have hrHPV who
# do have abnormal cells - false_negatives / negatives
prop_abnormal_given_no_hpv <- fn / hpv_m_count
print(prop_abnormal_given_no_hpv)

[1] 0.002395833


0.24% of people without hrHPV have abnormal cells.
Calculate the proportion of people with abnormal cells who have hrHPV - the sensitivity of the hrHPV as a marker.
\[
\text{Sensitivity} =
\frac{\text{True positives}}
{\text{True positives} + \text{False negatives}}
\]

# Count how many people have abnormal cells -
# true positives and false negatives
ab_count <- tp + fn

# Calculate the proportion of people who have
# abnormal cells who also have hpv
prop_hpv_given_abnormal <- tp / ab_count
print(prop_hpv_given_abnormal)

[1] 0.9006479


The sensitivity of HPV status as a test for abnormal cells is 90.06%.
Calculate the proportion of people who have normal cells and don’t have hrHPV - the specificity of hrHPV as a marker.
\[
\text{Specificity} =
\frac{\text{True negatives}}
{\text{True negatives} + \text{False positives}}
\]

# Count how many people have normal cells -
# true negatives and false positives
n_count <- tn + fp

# Calculate the proportion of people who have
# normal cells who don't have hpv
prop_no_hpv_given_normal <- tn / n_count
print(prop_no_hpv_given_normal)

[1] 0.895884


The specificity of HPV status as a test for abnormal cells is 89.59%.

title: Part 5: Conditional Probability
text:
Variation with age
Recommended
↑ top
So far, we’ve calculated proportions using the whole sample of 21,843 individuals. However, the prevalence of moderate/severe abnormal cytology varies considerably with age.
In this sample the authors described:

5.08% prevalence of moderate/severe abnormal cytology in individuals aged 20-29
1.81% prevalence of moderate/severe abnormal cytology in individuals aged 30-49
0.47% prevalence of moderate/severe abnormal cytology individuals aged 50-64

In the following series of exercises, we will use simulation to deduce the probability that someone with hrHPV has moderate/severe abnormal cytology.






ExerciseExercise 2 - Simulate different age groups






Recommended
In your hpv.qmd Quarto file:

For each of these age groups, simulate a sample of 10,000 individuals with the appropriate prevalence of moderate/severe cytology. You can use a binomial distribution with the function rbinom() where n_sim is 10000, size is 1 and prob is the proportion of people with moderate/severe morphology from the table above.
For each age range, count how many samples in the simulation have moderate/severe cytology and how many do not.

You can answer this question with or without using a for loop - either is fine.






AnswerAnswer






For each of these age groups, simulate a sample of 10,000 individuals with the appropriate prevalence of moderate/severe cytology. You can use a binomial distribution with the function rbinom() where n_sim is 10000, size is 1 and prob is the proportion of people with moderate/severe morphology from the table above.

cyt_statuses_20_29 <- rbinom(10000, size = 1, prob = 0.0508)
cyt_statuses_30_49 <- rbinom(10000, size = 1, prob = 0.0181)
cyt_statuses_50_64 <- rbinom(10000, size = 1, prob = 0.0047)

For each age range, count how many samples in the simulation have moderate/severe cytology and how many do not.

n_mod_sev_20_29 <- sum(cyt_statuses_20_29)
n_ok_20_29 <- 10000 - n_mod_sev_20_29
n_mod_sev_30_49 <- sum(cyt_statuses_30_49)
n_ok_30_49 <- 10000 - n_mod_sev_30_49
n_mod_sev_50_64 <- sum(cyt_statuses_50_64)
n_ok_50_64 <- 10000 - n_mod_sev_50_64

Or alternatively, using a for loop:

ages <- c("20-29", "30-49", "50-64")
probs <- c(0.0508, 0.0181, 0.0047)

results <- tibble()
for (i in 1:length(ages)) {
  simulation <- rbinom(10000, 1, prob = probs[i])
  row <- tibble(
    age = ages[i],
    perc = probs[i],
    nModerateSevere = sum(simulation == 1),
    nNot = sum(simulation == 0)
  )
  results <- results |>
    bind_rows(row)
}

Now we know how many people have normal and abnormal cells. The next step is to simulate which of the people with and without abnormal cells are hrHPV positive.
In Exercise 1 we already calculated the probability of an individual having hrHPV, given that they have abnormal cells, and stored this in the variable prop_hpv_given_abnormal.
We didn’t calculate the probability of an individual having hrHPV given that they have normal cells, but we did calculate the probability of not having hrHPV given that they have normal cells - this is stored as prop_no_hpv_given_normal. We can therefore subtract this from 1 to get the probability of having HPV given that they have normal cells.






NoteInclude this code



Include this code in your hpv.qmd Quarto file.

prop_hpv_given_normal <- 1 - prop_no_hpv_given_normal









ExerciseExercise 3 - Investigate the effect of prevalence






Recommended
In your hpv.qmd Quarto file:

For each age range, for the number of individuals in the simulation with moderate / severe cytology, calculate the number with HPV, again using rbinom() but this time with size as the number of individuals with moderate/severe cytology and prob as prop_hpv_given_abnormal.
For each age range, for the number of individuals in the simulation without moderate / severe cytology, calculate the number with HPV, again using rbinom() but this time with size as the number of individuals without moderate/severe cytology and prob as prop_hpv_given_normal.
For each age range, find the total number of people with HPV by adding together the number of people with HPV and moderate / severe cytology and the number of people with HPV and not moderate / severe cytology.
Store the number of people with HPV, the number of people with abnormal cells and the number of people with abnormal cells and HPV in a data frame, with one row for each age range. You may find it easiest to create a one-row data frame for each age range and combine them using bind_rows().

You can answer this question with or without using a for loop - either is fine.






AnswerAnswer






For each age range, for the number of individuals in the simulation with moderate / severe cytology, calculate the number with HPV, again using rbinom() but this time with size as the number of individuals with moderate/severe cytology and prob as prop_hpv_given_abnormal.

hpv_count_ab_20_29 <- sum(rbinom(n_mod_sev_20_29, size = 1, prob = prop_hpv_given_abnormal))
hpv_count_ab_30_49 <- sum(rbinom(n_mod_sev_30_49, size = 1, prob = prop_hpv_given_abnormal))
hpv_count_ab_50_64 <- sum(rbinom(n_mod_sev_50_64, size = 1, prob = prop_hpv_given_abnormal))

For each age range, for the number of individuals in the simulation without moderate / severe cytology, calculate the number with HPV, again using rbinom() but this time with size as the number of individuals without moderate/severe cytology and prob as prop_hpv_given_normal.

hpv_count_norm_20_29 <- sum(rbinom(n_ok_20_29, size = 1, prob = prop_hpv_given_normal))
hpv_count_norm_30_49 <- sum(rbinom(n_ok_30_49, size = 1, prob = prop_hpv_given_normal))
hpv_count_norm_50_64 <- sum(rbinom(n_ok_50_64, size = 1, prob = prop_hpv_given_normal))

For each age range, find the total number of people HPV by adding together the number of people with HPV and moderate / severe cytology and the number of people with HPV and not moderate / severe cytology.

n_hpv_20_29 <- hpv_count_ab_20_29 + hpv_count_norm_20_29
n_hpv_30_49 <- hpv_count_ab_30_49 + hpv_count_norm_30_49
n_hpv_50_64 <- hpv_count_ab_50_64 + hpv_count_norm_50_64

32.5% of people aged 20-29 with HPV have abnormal cells.
15.4% of people aged 30-49 with HPV have abnormal cells.
3.73% of people aged 50-64 with HPV have abnormal cells.

Why does the probability that an individual in each group with hrHPV has moderate-or-worse abnormal cytology differ so much, even though the sensitivity and specificity of hrHPV as a marker were kept constant?
Because the prevalence of abnormal cells changes so much between the groups. The sensitivity of the test tells us the probability the person will test positive if they have the disease and the specificity tells us the probability they will test negative if they don’t have the disease. The ratio of people who do and don’t have the disease differs between the three samples.

title: Part 5: Conditional Probability
text:
Cervical cancer as an outcome
Bonus
We can extend this simulation to consider cervical cancer as an outcome, rather than just abnormal cells.
Based on this paper published in Cytopathology in 2016 and also based on UK individuals, the positive predictive value of moderate or severely abnormal cells for cervical cancer is:

1.5% for people aged 20-29
3.4% for people aged 30-49
5.1% for people aged 50-64

(Note that these are estimates, as this paper uses slightly different age ranges)
This means that, based on this sample, for example, 1.5% of people aged 20-29 with at least moderately abnormal cells will then be diagnosed with cervical cancer. In this study no-one of any age with normal cells was diagnosed with cervical cancer.






ExerciseExercise 5 - Cervical cancer as an outcome






Bonus
In your hpv.qmd Quarto file, extend your simulation to calculate the probability that a 24 year old who is HPV positive and has a cervix would be diagnosed with cervical cancer on further testing (assuming prevalence is constant across the 20-29 age group).






Note



The & operator means AND and returns TRUE only when both conditions are TRUE and might be useful here.








AnswerAnswer







results_cc <- tibble()
prop_cc_given_abnormal <- 0.015
prop_abnormal <- 0.0508
n_sim <- 10000

# Simulate a population of people with normal and
# abnormal cells at the population rate for age 20-29
# 1 = abnormal
# 0 = normal
cyt_statuses <- rbinom(n_sim, 1, prop_abnormal)

# Count how many people have abnormal cells
n_abnormal <- sum(cyt_statuses == 1)
n_normal <- sum(cyt_statuses == 0)

# For the people with abnormal cells, simulate HPV
# presence based on the proportion of people with HPV
# given abnormal cells calculated in ex1.
hpv_statuses_abnormal <- rbinom(
  n_abnormal, 1,
  prop_hpv_given_abnormal
)
# For the people with normal cells, simulate HPV
# presence based on the probability of HPV
# given normal cells calculated above.
hpv_statuses_normal <- rbinom(
  n_normal, 1,
  prop_hpv_given_normal
)

# For the people with abnormal cells, simulate cervical
# cancer with a prevalence of 0.015
cc_statuses_abnormal <- rbinom(
  n_abnormal, 1,
  prop_cc_given_abnormal
)
# How many people have HPV
n_hpv <- sum(hpv_statuses_abnormal == 1) + sum(hpv_statuses_normal == 1)

# How many people have HPV and cervical cancer
n_hpv_cc <- sum(cc_statuses_abnormal == 1 & hpv_statuses_abnormal == 1)

# What proportion of people with HPV have cervical cancer
prop_cc <- n_hpv_cc / n_hpv

print(prop_cc)

[1] 0.005536332


Under this simplified model, we estimate that 0.55% of HPV-positive individuals aged 20–29 would be diagnosed with cervical cancer.






Note



This is a simplified model designed to explore conditional probability and should not be interpreted as a model of an individual’s clinical risk.

title: Part 6 - Sampling from a user-defined probability distribution
text:
Sampling from a user-defined probability distribution
Bonus
↑ top
Earlier, we used functions such as rbinom(), rpois() and rnorm() to simulate data from named probability distributions. However, sometimes we may want to simulate from a probability distribution for which R does not provide a built-in random-sampling function, or from a PDF that we have defined ourselves.
In R, it is possible to simulate data from a user-defined probability distribution using the package Runuran.
library(Runuran)
For example, cats like to sit on keyboards, particularly if they are currently being used. Let’s say a researcher has developed a probability density function describing the position at which a cat’s centre of mass occurs along a 40-cm keyboard, measured as distance in cm from the left edge.
\[
f(x) =
\begin{cases}
\frac{3x(40-x)}{32000}, & 0 \leq x \leq 40 \\
0, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]
Let’s plot just the function.
Here, instead of giving the argument fun our function name, we directly give it our cat PDF.
ggplot() +
  stat_function(
    fun = function(x) {
      3 * x * (40 - x) / 32000
    },
    xlim = c(0, 40)
  ) +
  ggtitle("Distribution of Cat Locations on Keyboards - Theoretical") +
  xlab("Distance from left edge (cm)") +
  ylab("Density") +
  theme_minimal()
As expected, cats like to sit in the middle where they can obscure the most keys and, ideally, block the view of the screen.
For a function to be a valid PDF, it must be non-negative over its range and its total area must equal 1. We can check the area in R using integrate(). Here, we will use integrate() with 3 arguments - the PDF, lower - the lower bound - and upper - the upper bound.
cat_int <- integrate(function(x) {
  3 * x * (40 - x) / 32000
}, lower = 0, upper = 40)
print(cat_int)

1 with absolute error < 1.1e-14
The total area under this curve is 1 - so the function is valid.
Using our probability density function, let’s simulate the positions of 10,000 cats, then estimate the probability that the centre of the cat is within the central 10 cm of the keyboard.
First, we use the function pinv.new() to create a random number generator which can sample values from a continuous distribution described by a user-defined PDF.
The arguments we will use are:
cat_gen <- pinv.new(
  pdf = function(x) {
    3 * x * (40 - x) / 32000
  },
  lb = 0,
  ub = 40
)
Now, to simulate data from this distribution, we use the function ur().
cat_positions <- ur(cat_gen,
  n = 10000
)
Let’s plot our cats. First, we need to put the data in a data frame.
cat_df <- tibble(Position = cat_positions)
ggplot(cat_df, aes(x = Position)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 50) +
  stat_function(
    fun = function(x) {
      3 * x * (40 - x) / 32000
    }
  ) +
  ggtitle("Distribution of Cat Locations on Keyboards - Simulated and Theoretical") +
  xlab("Distance from left edge (cm)") +
  ylab("Density") +
  theme_minimal()
Finally, let’s estimate the probability that a cat will sit within the central 10 cm of the keyboard. The middle 10 cm lies between 15 cm and 25 cm from the left edge.
middle_only <- cat_df |> filter(
  Position >= 15,
  Position <= 25
)
prop_middle <- nrow(middle_only) / nrow(cat_df)
print(prop_middle)

[1] 0.3628
Based on our simulation, cats will sit in the middle 10 cm of the keyboard approximately 36.28% of the time.

title: Part 6 - Sampling from a user-defined probability distribution
text:
User-defined PDF Exercise
Bonus
↑ top
Some cat parents like to, for their own amusement, pile objects onto their sleeping cat, a game known as cat buckaroo.






Figure 20.2: Example data point. Source: LPW



Cats will tolerate this to a certain extent but, at some point, will get up and shake the objects off. The weight of objects the cat will tolerate varies considerably between cats.
Cats appear to fall into two broad groups: those that almost immediately object to this game, and those that will tolerate a substantial pile before taking action. A researcher proposes the following probability density function for the total weight of objects a sleeping cat will tolerate before shaking them off.
\[
f(x) =
\begin{cases}
\frac{1-\cos\left(\frac{4\pi x}{1000}\right)}{1000},
& 0 \leq x \leq 1000 \\
0, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]






Note



The value of \(\pi\) is available in R as pi

print(pi)

[1] 3.141593


To calculate a cosine you can use the function cos() with one argument, the number for which you want to calculate the cosine.








ExerciseExercise 1












NoteInclude this code



Include this code at the start of your distributions.qmd file.

library(Runuran)



In your distributions.qmd Quarto file:

Plot this function.
Check it is a valid PDF.
Create a random number generator which can sample values from the distribution described by this PDF.
Simulate 10,000 values.
A cat has already tolerated 500 g of objects. Estimate the probability that it will tolerate the addition of a 75 g Yoda figurine without shaking everything off.







Figure 20.3: Example data point. Source: LPW









AnswerAnswer






Plot this function.

ggplot() +
  stat_function(
    fun = function(x) {
      (1 - cos(4 * pi * x / 1000)) / 1000
    },
    xlim = c(0, 1000)
  ) +
  ggtitle("Distribution of Cat Tolerance - Theoretical") +
  xlab("Total weight of objects (g)") +
  ylab("Density") +
  theme_minimal()








Check it is a valid PDF.

cataroo_int <- integrate(
  function(x) {
    (1 - cos(4 * pi * x / 1000)) / 1000
  },
  lower = 0,
  upper = 1000
)
print(cataroo_int)

1 with absolute error < 7.3e-10


The area under the curve is 1 so this is a valid PDF.
Create a random number generator which can sample values from the distribution described by this PDF.

cataroo_gen <- pinv.new(
  pdf = function(x) {
    (1 - cos(4 * pi * x / 1000)) / 1000
  },
  lb = 0,
  ub = 1000
)

[UNU.RAN - warning] NaN occured: tail probability gives NaN --> assume 0.
[UNU.RAN - warning] NaN occured: tail probability gives NaN --> assume 0.


Simulate 10,000 values.

cat_tolerance <- ur(cataroo_gen,
  n = 10000
)

A cat has already tolerated 500 g of objects. Estimate the probability that it will tolerate the addition of a 75 g Yoda figurine without shaking everything off.

cat_tolerance_df <- tibble(Tolerance = cat_tolerance)

# Find all the cats who tolerated at least 500g
over_500 <- cat_tolerance_df |> filter(Tolerance >= 500)

# Find all the cats who tolerated at least 575g
over_575 <- cat_tolerance_df |> filter(Tolerance >= 575)

# Calculate the proportion of cats who tolerated at least 500g who will tolerate at least 575g.
prop <- nrow(over_575) / nrow(over_500)

print(prop)

[1] 0.9782








Figure 20.4: Example data point. Source: LPW



If a cat has tolerated the addition of 500g of objects, there is an estimated 97.82% probability they will tolerate an additional 75g Yoda figurine.






Figure 20.5: Example data point. Source: LPW
