title: Probability Problem Sheets
text:
Problem Sheet 1
These are the solutions to the Probability problem sheets you completed earlier in the course, solved using simulation alone.
You are not expected to work through all of these problems, and they have not been assigned to different levels. They are provided as a reference to demonstrate how useful simulation can be for solving probability problems.
We will use 10,000 simulations, unless otherwise specified.
n_sim <- 10000

title: Probability Problem Sheets
text:
Question 1
In a natural habitat, grey wolves, foxes and coyotes co-exist. The current population is estimated to be 60 foxes, 30 coyotes and 10 wolves. If each animal is equally likely to be sighted first, find the probability of: a. a coyote being sighted first b. a wolf being sighted first c. a fox being sighted second after either a coyote or a wolf has been sighted and then removed from the habitat, so they can be fitted with a tracking device (Consider: what is the impact of the first sighting on what you see next?)






AnswerAnswer







# Make a population with 60 foxes, 30 coyotes and 10 wolves
animals <- c(
  rep("fox", 60),
  rep("coyote", 30),
  rep("wolf", 10)
)

# Sample 10000 animals, with replacement
samps <- sample(
  x = animals,
  size = n_sim,
  replace = TRUE
)


a
Probability that a coyote is sighted first.

# Count how many samples are coyotes
n_coy <- sum(samps == "coyote")

# What proportion of the total samples is this?
ans <- n_coy / length(samps)

print(ans)

[1] 0.3024


The probability a coyote is sighted first is 0.3024


b
Probability that a wolf is sighted first.

# Count how many samples are wolves
n_wolves <- sum(samps == "wolf")

# What proportion of the total samples is this?
ans <- n_wolves / length(samps)
print(ans)

[1] 0.1006


The probability a wolf is sighted first is 0.1006


c
Probability of a fox being sighted second after either a coyote or a wolf has been sighted and then removed from the habitat, so they can be fitted with a tracking device.

times_w_c_first <- 0
times_f_second <- 0

first_animal <- c()
second_animal <- c()
for (i in seq_len(n_sim)) {
  # Sample 2 animals from the habitat
  # and remove each after sampling
  samps <- sample(
    x = animals,
    size = 2,
    replace = FALSE
  )
  # Track who was caught first
  first_animal <- c(first_animal, samps[1])

  # Track who was caught second
  second_animal <- c(second_animal, samps[2])
}

# Vector of all the times wolf or coyote was
# first
w_c_first <- first_animal %in% c("wolf", "coyote")

# Vector of all the times fox was second
fox_second <- second_animal == "fox"

# Count how many times a wolf or coyote was
# first
w_c_first_count <- sum(w_c_first)

# Count how many times a wolf or coyote was
# first and a fox was second
w_c_first_and_fox_second_count <- sum(w_c_first & fox_second)

# Calculate the proportion of the times that
# a wolf or coyote was first that a fox was
# also second
ans <- w_c_first_and_fox_second_count / w_c_first_count
print(ans)

[1] 0.6134601


The probability of a fox being sighted second after either a coyote or a wolf has been sighted and then removed from the habitat 0.6135







Question 2
A transmitter emits the signals “0” or “1” in the ratio 1:2. Two independent receivers, labelled R1 and R2 are set up. If, unknown to the users, receiver R1 is incorrect in 2% of the cases and receiver R2 is incorrect in 3% of the cases, find

the probability that R1 reports that the transmitted signal is “0”
the probability that R2 reports that the transmitted signal is “1”
following an incoming signal there is some confusion, because R1 reports signal “0” and R2 reports signal “1”. Which of the two receivers is most likely to be correct?







AnswerAnswer







# Run the transmitter 10,000 times, with a 2/3 probability of success
# where success == 1
transmitter <- rbinom(n = n_sim, size = 1, prob = 2 / 3)

# Run R1 10,000 times, with a 98% probability of success
# 1 - correct
# 0 - incorrect
R1_correct <- rbinom(n = n_sim, size = 1, prob = 0.98)

# Run R2 10,000 times, with a 97% probability of success
# 1 - correct
# 0 - incorrect
R2_correct <- rbinom(n = n_sim, size = 1, prob = 0.97)


a
The probability that R1 reports that the transmitted signal is “0”






Note



The | operator means OR and returns TRUE when either condition is TRUE.



# R1 reports 0 when either the signal is 0
# and it is correct or the signal is 1
# and it is incorrect
zero_and_correct <- transmitter == 0 & R1_correct == 1
one_and_incorrect <- transmitter == 1 & R1_correct == 0

# Find times when either of these are true
# | = OR
R1_output_of_zero <- zero_and_correct | one_and_incorrect

# Count how many times either were true
count_R1_output_of_zero <- sum(R1_output_of_zero)

# Convert to a proportion
ans_a <- count_R1_output_of_zero / n_sim
print(ans_a)

[1] 0.3382


The probability that R1 reports that the transmitted signal is “0” is 0.3382


b
The probability that R2 reports that the transmitted signal is “1”

# R2 reports 1 when either the signal is 1
# and it is correct or the signal is 0
# and it is incorrect
one_and_correct <- transmitter == 1 & R2_correct == 1
zero_and_incorrect <- transmitter == 0 & R2_correct == 0

# Find times when either of these are true
R2_output_of_one <- one_and_correct | zero_and_incorrect

# Count how many times either were true
count_R2_output_of_one <- sum(R2_output_of_one)
ans_b <- count_R2_output_of_one / n_sim

print(ans_b)

[1] 0.6559


The probability that R2 reports that the transmitted signal is “1” is 0.6559


c

following an incoming signal there is some confusion, because R1 reports signal “0” and R2 reports signal “1”. Which of the two receivers is most likely to be correct?


# Find when R1 reports 0 and R2 reports 1
R1_0_R2_1 <- (R1_output_of_zero == 1) & (R2_output_of_one == 1)

# Count how many of these times R1 reports 0 and is correct
R1_reports_zero_correctly <- sum(R1_correct == 1 & R1_0_R2_1 == 1)

# Count how many of these times R1 reports 0 and is correct
R2_reports_one_correctly <- sum(R2_correct == 1 & R1_0_R2_1 == 1)

# Calculate the proportion of times R1 is correct
R1_correct_prop <- R1_reports_zero_correctly / sum(R1_0_R2_1 == 1)
R2_correct_prop <- R2_reports_one_correctly / sum(R1_0_R2_1 == 1)


print(paste("R1 = ", R1_correct_prop))

[1] "R1 =  0.435897435897436"

print(paste("R2 = ", R2_correct_prop))

[1] "R2 =  0.564102564102564"


Given that R1 has reported 0 and R2 has reported 1, R2 is more likely to be correct, with a probability of 0.5641, compared to 0.4359 for R1.







Question 3






Important



Parts 3a and 3c here cannot be reliably answered using simulation, so they are omitted here.


Of a batch of 22 imported oak saplings, 12 are healthy and 10 have hidden oak processionary moth eggs. A tree health officer is aware that there may be an issue and chooses 5 trees at random to inspect in detail.

What is the probability that a sample of five trees, chosen at random from the batch of 22 imported trees, consists of three healthy and two infested trees?
What is the probability that a sample of five, chosen at random from the batch consists only of healthy trees?







AnswerAnswer







b
What is the probability that a sample of five trees, chosen at random from the batch of 22 imported trees, consists of three healthy and two infested trees?

# Make a batch of 12 healthy and 10 infested trees
healthy <- rep("healthy", 12)
eggs <- rep("eggs", 10)
combined <- c(healthy, eggs)

# Sample 5 trees 10,000 times and track how many are
# healthy each time.
healthy_counts <- c()
for (i in seq_len(n_sim)) {
  samp <- sample(x = combined, size = 5, replace = FALSE)
  n_healthy <- sum(samp == "healthy")
  healthy_counts <- c(healthy_counts, n_healthy)
}
# Count how many times 3 were healthy
total_three_healthy <- sum(healthy_counts == 3)

# Divide by the number of simulations
prop <- total_three_healthy / n_sim
print(prop)

[1] 0.3757


There is a probability of 0.3757 that 3 trees are healthy and two are infested.


d
What is the probability the sample of five, chosen at random from the batch consists only of healthy trees?

# Use the sample from part b - 5 trees sampled 10,000
# times, tracked how many are healthy each time.

# Count how many times 5 were healthy
total_five_healthy <- sum(healthy_counts == 5)

# Divide by the number of simulations
prop <- total_five_healthy / n_sim
print(prop)

[1] 0.0315


There is a probability of 0.0315 that all 5 trees are healthy.







Question 4
A spam filter on a mail server scrutinises messages for the appearance of key words that make it likely that the message is spam.
The filter works as follows: • it is assumed that evidence for spam is that the subject message of the email contains the sentence “check this out”.
According to some historical data we know that: • 40% of emails are spam • 1% of spam emails have “check this out” in the subject line • 0.4% of non-spam emails have “check this out” in the subject line. Find the probability that an email is spam given that it has the phrase “check this out” in the subject






AnswerAnswer







# Simulate 100,000 emails with a 40% chance of being spam
# 1 = spam
# 0 = not spam
is_spam <- rbinom(100000, size = 1, prob = 0.4)

# Count how many of these are and are not spam
n_spam <- sum(is_spam == 1)
n_not_spam <- 100000 - n_spam

# For the results which are spam, simulate a 1% chance
# of saying CTO
is_cto_spam <- rbinom(n_spam, size = 1, prob = 0.01)

# For the results which are not spam, simulate a 0.4% chance
# of saying CTO
is_cto_not_spam <- rbinom(n_not_spam, size = 1, prob = 0.004)

# Calculate the total number of simulations that are CTO
cto <- sum(is_cto_spam, is_cto_not_spam)

# Calculate the proportion of CTO simulations which are spam
prob_spam_cto <- sum(is_cto_spam) / cto

print(prob_spam_cto)

[1] 0.6054217


The probability that an email is spam given that it has the phrase “check this out” in the subject is 0.6054
Note that I used a higher number of simulations here because so few emails have “check this out” overall.






Question 5
The number of particles emitted from a radioactive substance follows a Poisson distribution with parameter λ=4 particles per minute. Find the probability that:

three particles are emitted in one minute
at least one particle is emitted in a minute
three particles are emitted in 2 minutes







AnswerAnswer







# Simulate a Poisson distributed data set with a lambda of 4
particles_per_min <- rpois(n_sim, 4)


a
Find the probability that three particles are emitted in one minute

# How many of the simulated data points have a count of exactly 3
ans_a <- sum(particles_per_min == 3) / n_sim
print(ans_a)

[1] 0.1908


The probability that 3 particles are emitted in one minute is 0.1908.


b
Find the probability that at least one particle is emitted in a minute

# How many of the simulated data points have a count of at least 1
ans_b <- sum(particles_per_min >= 1) / n_sim
print(ans_b)

[1] 0.9829


The probability that at least one particle is emitted in a minute is 0.9829.


c
Find the probability that 3 particles are emitted in 2 minutes

# Simulate a Poisson distributed data set with a lambda of 8
particles_per_2min <- rpois(n_sim, 8)
# How many of the simulated data points have a count of exactly 3
ans_c <- sum(particles_per_2min == 3) / n_sim
print(ans_c)

[1] 0.0294


The probability that 3 particles are emitted in 2 minutes is 0.0294.







Question 6

The survival rate of a specific disease is forty percent. In a certain day eight patients are admitted into hospital with that disease. What are the chances that three will survive?
A new drug is discovered that can cure the disease but can only be administered in a way that has a success rate of reaching the affected area of 0.6. There usually are four doses of the drug administered. Find the chances of:
three doses successfully administered


no doses successfully administered
at least one dose successfully administered
at most two doses successfully administered







AnswerAnswer







a
The survival rate of a specific disease is forty percent. In a certain day eight patients are admitted into hospital with that disease. What are the chances that three will survive?

# Sample 8 individuals from a binomial distribution
# 10,000 times with a 40% probability of survival
survival <- rbinom(n_sim, 8, 0.4)

# Calculate the number of simulated values which are
# equal to 3, convert to a proportion of 10,000
n_three <- sum(survival == 3)
prop_three <- n_three / n_sim

print(prop_three)

[1] 0.2832


The probability that three will survive is 0.2832.
A new drug is discovered that can cure the disease but can only be administered in a way that has a success rate of reaching the affected area of 0.6.

# Simulate giving four doses of the drug 10,000
# times with a 0.6 probability of success
success <- rbinom(n_sim, 4, 0.6)


i
Three doses successfully administered

# Number of times there were exactly 3 successes
ans_i <- sum(success == 3) / n_sim
print(ans_i)

[1] 0.3475


The probability that three doses were successfully administered is 0.3475


ii
No doses successfully administered

# Number of times there were exactly 0 successes
ans_ii <- sum(success == 0) / n_sim
print(ans_ii)

[1] 0.0275


The probability that no doses were successfully administered is 0.0275


iii
At least one dose successfully administered

# Number of times at least one success (i.e. not zero successes)
ans_iii <- sum(success != 0) / n_sim
print(ans_iii)

[1] 0.9725


The probability that at least one dose was successfully administered is 0.9725


iv
At most two doses successfully administered

# Number of times 2 or less successes
ans_iv <- sum(success <= 2) / n_sim
print(ans_iv)

[1] 0.5202


The probability that at most two doses were successfully administered is 0.5202








Question 7
A scientist randomly selects dolphins until she finds one that has been tagged with a tracking device, so that she can collect the data on the pod’s movements. The probability that she finds the dolphin with the tracking device is 0.2.

What is the probability that the scientist must select exactly 4 dolphins before she finds one with a tracking device?
What is the probability that she must select more than 6 dolphins before she finds one with a tracking device?







AnswerAnswer







# Simulate a geometric distribution with 10,000 data points, with a
# 20% probability of success in each trial.
dolphins <- rgeom(n_sim, 0.2)


a
What is the probability that the scientist must select exactly 4 dolphins before she finds one with a tracking device?

# Probability there are 3 failures before the first success
ans_a <- sum(dolphins == 3) / n_sim
print(ans_a)

[1] 0.1085


There is a 0.1085 probability that she must select exactly 4 dolphins to find one with a tracking device.


b

What is the probability that she must select more than 6 dolphins before she finds one with a tracking device?


# Probability there are at least 6 failures before the first success
ans_b <- sum(dolphins >= 6) / n_sim
print(ans_b)

[1] 0.2616


There is a 0.2616 probability that she will have to select more than 6 dolphins before finding one with a tracking device.







Question 8
The number of results we get per minute from a simple computational model is a Poisson random variable with mean 3.

Find the probability that no results come in a given 1 minute period.
Find the probability that at least two results will come in a given two minute period.







AnswerAnswer







# Simulate a Poisson distribution with lambda 3
results_per_min <- rpois(n_sim, 3)


a
Find the probability that no results come in a given 1 minute period.

# Probability of a count of exactly 0
ans_a <- sum(results_per_min == 0) / n_sim
print(ans_a)

[1] 0.0537


The probability no results come in a given 1 minute period is 0.0537.


b
The probability that at least two results will come in a given two minute period.

# Simulate a Poisson distribution with lambda 6
results_per_2min <- rpois(n_sim, 6)
# Probability of a count of at least 2
ans_b <- sum(results_per_2min >= 2) / n_sim
print(ans_b)

[1] 0.9817


The probability at least two results will come in a given 2 minute period is 0.9817.

title: Probability Problem Sheets
text:
Problem Sheet 2

Question 1
On average, a certain spectrophotometer part lasts 10 years. The length of time that the part lasts is exponentially distributed. a) What is the probability that the spectrophotometer part lasts more than 7 years? b) On the average, how long would 5 of these parts last if they were used one after another?






AnswerAnswer







# Rate per year if it lasts 10 years on average
rate <- 1 / 10

# Simulate an exponential distribution with this
# rate and 10,000 observations
distri <- rexp(n_sim, rate = rate)


a
What is the probability that the spectrophotometer part lasts more than 7 years?

# Proportion of intervals > 7
ans_a <- sum(distri > 7) / n_sim
print(ans_a)

[1] 0.496


There is an 0.496 probability the part lasts more than 7 years.


b
On the average, how long would 5 of these parts last if they were used one after another?

# Average time based on simulation
average_time <- mean(distri)

# Multiply by 5
total_time <- average_time * 5

print(total_time)

[1] 50.10592


On average, 5 parts would last 50.1059 years.







Question 2
A drug is produced in a chamber with temperature X, where X is a random variable that follows a normal distribution with μ = 21°C and σ = 5°C. If X<25°C, the production cost per unit is £20, whereas if X≥25°C the production cost per unit is £30. Find the expected production cost per unit for this drug.






AnswerAnswer







# Simulate a normal distribution where μ = 21°C and σ = 5°C
drug_dist <- rnorm(n_sim, 21, 5)

# Count how many times X is < 25
cold <- sum(drug_dist < 25)

# Count how many times X is >= 25
hot <- sum(drug_dist >= 25)

# Calculate the total cost for cold production
cold_cost <- cold * 20

# Calculate the total cost for hot production
hot_cost <- hot * 30

# Calculate the total cost for all production
total_cost <- cold_cost + hot_cost

# Convert to a proportion of the number of units
ans_2 <- total_cost / n_sim

print(ans_2)

[1] 22.123


The expected production cost per unit for this drug is £22.12 per unit.






Question 3
A box contains 3 green and 5 red balls. If we pick balls and then replace them, find: a) The probability that the third time we pick a ball, we get a red ball for the second time. b) The probability that the 4th time we pick a ball, a red ball appears for the first time c) The expected number of times we pick a ball until we get a red ball for the second time.






AnswerAnswer







a
The probability that the third time we pick a ball, we get a red ball for the second time.

# Draw two balls 10,000 times and count how many
# are red
first_two <- rbinom(n_sim, size = 2, prob = 5 / 8)

# Draw one ball 10,000 times and count how many
# are red
third <- rbinom(n_sim, size = 1, prob = 5 / 8)

# How many times is either ball 1 or ball 2 red
# but not both and ball 3 is red
count <- sum(first_two == 1 & third == 1)

# As a proportion
prop <- count / n_sim

print(prop)

[1] 0.2901


The probability that the third time we pick a ball, we get a red ball for the second time is 0.2901.


b
The probability that the 4th time we pick a ball, a red ball appears for the first time

# Draw three balls 10,000 times and count how many
# are red
first_three <- rbinom(n_sim, size = 3, prob = 5 / 8)

# Draw one ball 10,000 times and count how many
# are red
fourth <- rbinom(n_sim, size = 1, prob = 5 / 8)

# How many times are none of the first three balls
# red but ball 4 is red
count <- sum(first_three == 0 & fourth == 1)

# As a proportion
prop <- count / n_sim

print(prop)

[1] 0.0325


The probability that the 4th time we pick a ball, a red ball appears for the first time is 0.0325.


c
The expected number of times we pick a ball until we get a red ball for the second time.

# Simulate the number of green balls picked before the first red
# twice
ball_1 <- rgeom(n_sim, 5 / 8)
ball_2 <- rgeom(n_sim, 5 / 8)

# Add them together - add two for the two red balls then picked
combined_balls <- ball_1 + ball_2 + 2

# The mean of these values is the expectation
expected <- mean(combined_balls)

print(expected)

[1] 3.1955


The expected number of times we pick a ball until we get a red ball for the second time is 3.1955.







Question 4
For a group of 100 students, find: a) The expected number of days of the year that are birthdays of exactly 3 people. b) The expected number of distinct birthdays






AnswerAnswer







prob_bday <- 1 / 365

bdays_per_day <- rbinom(1000000, 100, prob_bday)


prob_3_bdays <- sum(bdays_per_day == 3) / 1000000

n_days <- 365 * prob_3_bdays

print(n_days)

[1] 0.94827



prop_distinct <- sum(bdays_per_day != 0) / 1000000
n_distinct <- 365 * prop_distinct

print(n_distinct)

[1] 87.57445








Question 5






Note



Answering this question using simulation depends on the bonus material in Part 6 - Sampling from a user-defined probability distribution.


A continuous random variable X has the following probability density function: \[
f(x) =
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{4x(9-x^2)}{81}, & \text{if } 0 \leq x \leq 3 \\[6pt]
0, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]

Verify that f(x) is a valid probability density function.
Find (a) the mean of f(x), (b) the mode of f(x) and (c) the median of f(x)







AnswerAnswer







a
Verify that f(x) is a valid probability density function.

# Calculate the area under the curve
area <- integrate(
  function(x) {
    ((4 * x) * (9 - x^2)) / 81
  },
  lower = 0,
  upper = 3
)
print(area)

1 with absolute error < 1.1e-14


The function is non-negative over its specified range and the area under the curve is 1 so the PDF is valid.


b
Find (a) the mean of f(x), (b) the mode of f(x) and (c) the median of f(x)

# Make a random number generator using this function
rand_gen <- pinv.new(
  pdf = function(x) {
    ((4 * x) * (9 - x^2)) / 81
  },
  lb = 0,
  ub = 3
)

# Generate 10,000 random points
simu <- ur(rand_gen, n_sim)

# Calculate the mean and median of the points
mean_simu <- mean(simu)
median_simu <- median(simu)

# Mean
print(mean_simu)

[1] 1.608206

# Median
print(median_simu)

[1] 1.634621


The simulated mean is 1.6082.
The simulated median is 1.6346.
The mode is trickier, as R doesn’t by default calculate the mode for continuous data. It’s easiest to do this visually based on a histogram.

# Convert to a data frame
simu_df <- tibble(simulated_data = simu)

# Plot a histogram
ggplot(simu_df, aes(x = simulated_data)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  ggtitle("Distribution of x - Simulated") +
  xlab("x") +
  ylab("Number of simulations") +
  theme_minimal()








The peak is apparent on this plot at about 1.7.







Question 6






Note



Answering this question using simulation depends on the bonus material in Part 6 - Sampling from a user-defined probability distribution.




a
Let X be a continuous random variable with probability density function:
\[
f(x) =
\begin{cases}
4x^3, & \text{if } 0 < x \leq 1 \\
0, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]
Find
\[
P\left(X \leq \frac{2}{3} \mid X > \frac{1}{3}\right).
\] ::: {.callout-answer collapse=“true” .show-code #ex-qq6_ans}

# Create a random number generator for this distribution
rand_gen <- pinv.new(
  pdf = function(x) {
    4 * x^3
  },
  lb = 0,
  ub = 1
)

# Generate 10,000 random points
simu <- ur(rand_gen, n_sim)

# Convert to a data frame
rand_df <- tibble(points = simu)

# Extract the points where x > 1/3
# within this interval
rand_df_2_3 <- rand_df |>
  filter(
    points <= (2 / 3),
    points > 1 / 3
  )

# Extract the points where x > 1/3
rand_df_1_3 <- rand_df |>
  filter(points > (1 / 3))

# Calculate the proportion of points within the interval
prop_between <-
  nrow(rand_df_2_3) / nrow(rand_df_1_3)

print(prop_between)

[1] 0.1885321




b
Let (X) be a continuous random variable with probability density function:
\[
f(x) =
\begin{cases}
x^2\left(2x+\frac{3}{2}\right), & \text{if } 0 < x \leq 1 \\
0, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]
If
\[
Y = \frac{2}{X} + 3,
\]
find
\[
\operatorname{Var}(Y).
\]

# Create a random number generator for this function
rand_gen <- pinv.new(
  pdf = function(x) {
    x^2 * (2 * x + (3 / 2))
  },
  lb = 0,
  ub = 1
)

# Generate 100,000 random points
# This one isn't very stable so use a bigger number
simu <- ur(rand_gen, 100000)

# Calculate the Y value for each point and store it.
simu_y <- c()
for (sim_x in simu) {
  y <- (2 / sim_x) + 3
  simu_y <- c(simu_y, y)
}

# Find the variance of Y
var_y <- var(simu_y)

print(var_y)

[1] 1.888409


The variance of Y is 1.8884.
The simulated estimate of the variance may differ noticeably from the exact answer of approximately 1.97, because values of X close to zero produce very large values of Y, making the sample variance relatively unstable.
:::


Question 7
A polar bear is hunting for food. From its current position, there are three different routes. The first one brings it back to the same point after 1 hours of walking. The second route brings it back to the same point after 6 hours of walking. The last route leads to the food source after 2 hours of walking. Assuming that the probability the bear chooses route 1 is 0.25, route 2 is 0.25 and route 3 is 0.5, what is the expected time it will take for the bear gets some food?






Note



This solution uses conditional statements if and else, along with a while loop - a loop which runs over and over again until something becomes true. We have not covered these programming techniques in the practicals.








AnswerAnswer







# Length of each route
route1 <- 1
route2 <- 6
route3 <- 2

# Probability of each route
prob1 <- 0.25
prob2 <- 0.25
prob3 <- 0.5

# Currently, the bear has no food
food <- FALSE

# Vector to track the time taken in each simulation
total_times <- c()

for (i in seq_len(n_sim)) {
  total_time <- 0
  food <- FALSE
  # Keep running these steps until he finds food
  while (!food) {
    # Randomly, based on the probabilities above, choose a route
    which_route <- sample(seq_len(3), 1, prob = c(prob1, prob2, prob3))

    # If it is route 1, add 1 hour to the total time
    if (which_route == 1) {
      total_time <- total_time + route1
    }
    # If it is route 2, add 6 hours to the total time
    else if (which_route == 2) {
      total_time <- total_time + route2
    }
    # If it is route 3, add 2 hours to the total time
    # then stop the loop because he has found food.
    else if (which_route == 3) {
      total_time <- total_time + route3
      food <- TRUE
    }
  }
  # Store the total time taken
  total_times <- c(total_times, total_time)
}
# Calculate the mean of the time taken over the 10,000 simulations
mean_total <- mean(total_times)
print(mean_total)

[1] 5.4814


The mean time for the polar bear to find food is 5.4814.

title: Part 1: UK Pollinator Monitoring Scheme Dataset
text:
Pollinator dataset
Core
We will use this research dataset repeatedly throughout both this practical and Practical 6 (Further Statistics) and visit others as needed.
The main dataset we will use in this practical is pan-trap survey data from the UK Pollinator Monitoring Scheme (PoMS). In this scheme, multiple pan-traps are set in each of a set of specific 1km squares across the UK. On four days each summer, volunteers will set out traps for six hours, then send the insects to be counted. Flowering plants within a 2m radius of the trap are also recorded.
The data from the scheme is provided as data per trap, for this practical we have amalgamated the data across all dates and across each 1km square.
You have been provided with three data files:

In the insect counts CSV file - data/insect_counts.csv each row represents a combination of an insect species and a sampling site, and the total number of times that insect was observed at that site. Many of the counts will be zero.
In the flower counts CSV file - data/flower_counts.csv each row represents a combination of a flower species and a sampling site, plus TRUE or FALSE depending if that flower was ever observed within 2m of the site.
In the site metadata CSV file - data/site_metadata.csv, each row represents a single 1km square sampling site. The data frame contains information about the geographical location, plus land use and climate at the sample site. Additional climate data has been added based on WorldClim data, which has detailed climate data by square averaged from 1970-2000. Various additional statistics have been calculated based on the information in the original data frame.



Data citation

UK Pollinator Monitoring Scheme (2024). 1km square pan trap data from the UK Pollinator Monitoring Scheme, 2017-2021. NERC EDS Environmental Information Data Centre. (Dataset).
The UK Pollinator Monitoring Scheme (PoMS) is a partnership funded jointly by UKCEH and JNCC (through funding from Defra, Scottish Government, Welsh Government, and DAERA). UKCEH’s contribution is funded by the Natural Environment Research Council award number NE/R016429/1 as part of the UK-SCAPE programme delivering National Capability. Between 2017 and 2021, PoMS was funded by UKCEH and Defra (England), Welsh Government, Scottish Government, DAERA (Northern Ireland), and JNCC. PoMS is indebted to the many volunteers who carry out surveys and contribute data to the scheme.







ExerciseExercise 1 - Revise data frame operations






Recommended
If you haven’t already, create a new Quarto file, pollinators.qmd.

set.seed(42)

Find the insect species which was observed most frequently and how many times it was observed. Insect species is in the column species of the insect counts data frame.

Examining data
Core
For now, let’s concentrate on a single species, the “bronze furrow bee” Halictus tumulorum. This is a relatively common bee species in the UK. It is a species of sweat bee, named because they are often attracted to sweat (although the UK ones usually aren’t).






Figure 23.1: Halictus tumulorum Source

title: Part 2: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Statistical test recap
Here is a reminder of some statistical tests and the data types they are appropriate for, and an example of a good way to visualise them. We’ll cover each of these as we progress through this practical.
As long as there are many possible values (e.g. the values aren’t limited to 1, 2 or 3), count data (such as number of insects) can be treated as continuous when used as an explanatory variable. For the tests in this table, response variables described as continuous should usually be genuinely continuous rather than counts.

title: Part 2: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Choosing a test
Looking at our box plot from the end of Part 1, it seems like perhaps these bees don’t like the cold.
Core
Now we have some hypotheses to investigate:

Null hypothesis: Mean minimum temperature is the same at sites where H. tumulorum is present and absent.
Alternative hypothesis: Mean minimum temperature is different at sites where H. tumulorum is present than at sites where it is absent.







Important



We developed our hypothesis that H. tumulorum prefers sites with a higher minimum temperature after looking at these data, and we’re about to use the same data to test that hypothesis. This is sometimes called HARKing — Hypothesizing After the Results are Known.
Ideally, we would now test our hypothesis using a new dataset. However, given the limitations of this practical, we will instead look for evidence of an association in this dataset.


We have a continuous response variable and a categorical explanatory variable - maybe we can use a t-test.









Response variable
Explanatory variable(s)
Statistical test/model
Visualisation example




Continuous
One categorical variable, 2 groups
Two-sample t-test or one-way ANOVA
Box plot



There are various assumptions which underlie a t-test - we’ll come back to these later in the practical. For the moment, assume these assumptions are met.

title: Part 2: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Running statistical tests in R
Core
In R statistical functions, ~ is used to specify a formula describing the relationship between variables.
The basic structure is response ~ explanatory, which you can read as “response as a function of explanatory variable”.
In our example above, the response variable is minimum temperature and the explanatory variable is presence or absence of H. tumulorum bees.






Note



“Explanatory” here means the variable we’re using to explain/describe variation in the response statistically, not necessarily a biological cause - we’re not claiming that the bees are affecting the temperature.


To run a t-test in R, the function is t.test().
The first argument is our formula - response ~ explanatory, or in this case, min_temp_coldest_month ~ detected. We need two additional arguments:

data = ht_temp_df - this is the data frame containing the data.
var.equal = TRUE - run an equal variance t-test, the default in R is to assume unequal variance and run a Welch’s t-test.







ExerciseExercise 1 - T-test






Core
In your pollinators.qmd Quarto file, run a t-test in R to test the hypotheses above. View the output using print().






AnswerAnswer







ttest_ht_temp <- t.test(min_temp_coldest_month ~ detected,
  data = ht_temp_df,
  var.equal = TRUE
)
print(ttest_ht_temp)


    Two Sample t-test

data:  min_temp_coldest_month by detected
t = -5.7259, df = 74, p-value = 2.073e-07
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group FALSE and group TRUE is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -1.7010818 -0.8228055
sample estimates:
mean in group FALSE  mean in group TRUE 
          0.1128519           1.3747955 










To fully describe our t-test output we need to include at least the following:

Test statistic: t
Degrees of freedom: df
p-value: p-value

In addition to the test statistic, degrees of freedom and p-value, we should describe the size and direction of the observed difference. R reports the two group means, from which we can calculate the difference between the means.
We could therefore report our results here as:

There is evidence that mean minimum temperature is higher at sites where H. tumulorum is present than at sites where it is absent (\(t\)(74) = -5.73, \(p\) = 2.07e-07, mean difference [absent − present] = -1.26°C). This means we can reject our null hypothesis.

This doesn’t mean that our alternative hypothesis is definitely true for the population, but based on this sample the evidence supports it.

title: Part 2: Hypothesis Testing
text:
The t-distribution
Extension
The p-value for a t-test is the probability of a test statistic at least as far from zero as the value calculated from our data, if we drew values from a t-distribution with the specified number of degrees of freedom.
The t-distribution is just a probability distribution, so we can simulate and visualise it in R using the same methods we learned for other probability distributions (Part 4: Simulation exercises).






ExerciseExercise 3 - Visualising the t-distribution






Extension
In your pollinators.qmd Quarto file:

Simulate a sample of 1000 observations from t-distribution with 74 degrees of freedom. You can draw a random sample from a t-distribution with the function rt with the arguments n - number of observations and df degrees of freedom.
Create a data frame where this set of observations forms a column.
Plot the results using the ggplot layer geom_density().
Calculate an approximated p-value using your simulated data - the proportion of observations which are at least 5.726 from zero in either direction. You can extract the test statistic from the t-test as ttest_ht_temp$statistic.
Calculate the exact p-value using the t-distribution cumulative probability function pt().







AnswerAnswer






Simulate a sample of 1000 observations from t-distribution with 74 degrees of freedom. You can draw a random sample from a t-distribution with the function rt with the arguments n - number of observations and df degrees of freedom.

df74 <- rt(1000, df = 74)

Create a data frame where this set of observations forms a column.

t_dist <- tibble(simulated = df74)

Plot the results using the ggplot layer geom_density().

ggplot(
  t_dist,
  aes(x = simulated)
) +
  geom_density() +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = c(
      ttest_ht_temp$statistic,
      -ttest_ht_temp$statistic
    ),
    color = "red"
  ) +
  ggtitle("Density of t-distribution - Simulated and Observed") +
  xlab("t") +
  ylab("Density") +
  theme_minimal()








Calculate an approximated p-value using your simulated data - the proportion of observations which are at least 5.726 from zero in either direction. You can extract the test statistic from the t-test as ttest_ht_temp$statistic.

p_lower_sim <- sum(t_dist$simulated <= ttest_ht_temp$statistic)
p_upper_sim <- sum(t_dist$simulated >= -ttest_ht_temp$statistic)

p_sim <- (p_lower_sim + p_upper_sim) / nrow(t_dist)

print(p_sim)

[1] 0


With 1000 simulations your value will almost certainly be zero.






ExerciseExercise 2 - Bonus question: Probability






Bonus
What is the probability of getting a value which is not zero here given the p-value calculated by R above of 2.07e-07.






AnswerAnswer







prob_no_extreme <- (1 - ttest_ht_temp$p.value)^1000
prob_at_least_one <- 1 - prob_no_extreme

print(prob_at_least_one)

[1] 0.0002073172


There is a 0.0207% probability of observing at least one simulated value this extreme when drawing 1,000 points from a t-distribution with 74 degrees of freedom.








Calculate the exact p-value using the t-distribution cumulative probability function pt().

p_lower <- pt(ttest_ht_temp$statistic, 74)
p_upper <- 1 - pt(-ttest_ht_temp$statistic, 74)

pval <- p_lower + p_upper

print(pval)

           t 
2.073387e-07 


This should be the exact p-value calculated in our t-test.

title: Part 2: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Confidence intervals
Core
In our description of the t-test output above, something is missing - it is also worth looking at our confidence interval here. This data is provided in our t-test summary above.
Lower: -1.7011
Upper: -0.8228
A 95% confidence interval means that if we repeatedly sampled from the population and calculated a 95% confidence interval in the same way each time, 95% of those intervals would contain the true population value. In this case, the true population value is the true difference between the mean minimum annual temperature at sites where H. tumulorum is present and at sites where it is absent.
For a two-sided test at the 5% significance level, if the 95% confidence interval for the difference between the means does not contain zero, we can reject the null hypothesis that the mean difference is zero. Here, our confidence interval does not contain zero, which agrees with our conclusion based on the p-value.
We should add this to our conclusion above:

There is evidence that mean minimum temperature is higher at sites where H. tumulorum is present than at sites where it is absent (\(t\)(74) = -5.73, \(p\) = 2.07e-07, mean difference [absent − present] = -1.26°C, 95% CI [-1.7, -0.82]°C). This means we can reject our null hypothesis.


The t-distribution and confidence intervals
Extension
“A 95% confidence interval means that if we repeatedly sampled from the population and calculated a 95% confidence interval in the same way each time, 95% of those intervals would contain the true population value. In this case, the true population value is the true difference between the mean minimum annual temperature at sites where H. tumulorum is present and at sites where it is absent.”
Let’s check using simulation. If we simulate samples from populations with known means, we know the “true” difference between means of the source populations.
To simplify this process, let’s first calculate the mean, standard deviation and sample size for sites with and without H. tumulorum. This is straightforward using the group_by() and summarise() functions.
The function n() returns the number of observations in each group in a data frame (or the total number of observations in an ungrouped data frame).

1,000 times:

Simulate two samples drawn from a normal distribution:

one with the same mean, standard deviation and sample size as the sites with H. tumulorum
one with the same mean, standard deviation and sample size as the sites without H. tumulorum.

Put the data for the two samples into a data frame in long format.
For each pair of simulated samples, use a t-test to calculate the difference between the sample means and its 95% confidence interval.

Determine whether the confidence interval contains the true difference between the two population means.

# Find the real difference for comparison
true_diff <- pull(present, mean) - pull(absent, mean)

# Vector to store the results
res_vec <- c()

for (i in seq_len(1000)) {
  # Simulate the two samples
  sample_present <- rnorm(pull(present, count), mean = pull(present, mean), sd = pull(present, sd))
  sample_absent <- rnorm(pull(absent, count), mean = pull(absent, mean), sd = pull(absent, sd))

  # Put the results into a data frame
  df <- tibble(
    sample = c(
      rep("sample_1", length(sample_present)),
      rep("sample_2", length(sample_absent))
    ),
    min_temp_coldest_month = c(sample_present, sample_absent)
  )

  # Run the t-test
  ttest_res <- t.test(min_temp_coldest_month ~ sample,
    data = df,
    var.equal = TRUE
  )

  # Extract the confidence interval
  ci_lower <- ttest_res$conf.int[1]
  ci_upper <- ttest_res$conf.int[2]

  # Check if the result is in the confidence interval or not
  res_in_ci <- between(true_diff, ci_lower, ci_upper)

  # Store the result
  res_vec <- c(res_vec, res_in_ci)
}

Calculate the percentage of the 1,000 confidence intervals that contain the true difference.

perc <- (sum(res_vec) / length(res_vec)) * 100
print(perc)

[1] 94.4


Write a conclusion.
In this simulation, the 95% confidence interval contained the true difference between the population means 94.4% of the time. This is close to the expected 95%, illustrating that when we repeatedly sample from a population and calculate a 95% confidence interval, approximately 95% of those intervals contain the true population value.










Calculating confidence intervals
Extension
We can revisit our simulated t-distribution above to understand how confidence intervals are calculated.
For a 95% confidence interval, we want the central 95% of the t-distribution. This leaves 2.5% of the distribution in each tail.
In our t_dist data frame there are 1,000 observations sampled from a t-distribution with 74 degrees of freedom.

ggplot(
  t_dist,
  aes(x = simulated)
) +
  geom_density() +
  ggtitle("Density of t-distribution - Simulated") +
  xlab("t") +
  ylab("Density")








To calculate our confidence interval, we want the middle 95% of values from this distribution.
With our simulated data, we can extract these using summarize() and then the quantile() function with the data column as the first argument and the quantile we want to extract as the second. The \(x\) quantile is the value below which \(x\) proportion of the observations fall.

quantile_df <- t_dist |>
  summarise(
    lower = quantile(simulated, 0.025),
    upper = quantile(simulated, 0.975)
  )
gt(quantile_df)







lower
upper




-1.884933
1.975184







Let’s add these to our density plot.

ggplot(
  t_dist,
  aes(x = simulated)
) +
  geom_density() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(pull(quantile_df, lower), pull(quantile_df, upper)), color = "blue") +
  ggtitle("Density of t-distribution -\nSimulated with simulated quantiles") +
  xlab("t") +
  ylab("Density") +
  theme_minimal()








We can also calculate the exact values using the function qt().

lower_exact <- qt(0.025, 74)
upper_exact <- qt(0.975, 74)

print(lower_exact)

[1] -1.992543

print(upper_exact)

[1] 1.992543


The absolute values of these exact values should be identical to each other.

ggplot(
  t_dist,
  aes(x = simulated)
) +
  geom_density() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(lower_exact, upper_exact), color = "orange") +
  ggtitle("Density of t-distribution -\nSimulated with theoretical quantiles") +
  xlab("t") +
  ylab("Density") +
  theme_minimal()








Because the t-distribution is symmetric, the two exact quantiles have the same absolute value. This value is called the critical t-value, often written \(t*\). These values are measured on the t-distribution. To calculate a confidence interval for our estimated difference between means, we need to convert \(t*\) into the units of our response variable.
We do this by multiplying \(t*\) by the standard error of our t-test. We can access from our t-test above using ttest_ht_temp$stderr.

tstar <- upper_exact
SE <- ttest_ht_temp$stderr

confint_rv_units <- tstar * SE

print(confint_rv_units)

[1] 0.4391381


This tells us how far we need to go above and below our estimated difference between means to obtain the 95% confidence interval.

diff_means <- pull(absent, mean) - pull(present, mean)

lower_cint <- diff_means - confint_rv_units
upper_cint <- diff_means + confint_rv_units

print(c(lower_cint, upper_cint))

[1] -1.7010818 -0.8228055


This gives us our lower value of -1.7011 and upper value of -0.8228 as above.

title: Part 2: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Linear models
Core
The comparison we have just made can also be represented using a linear model.
As you know, a simple linear model can be written as:
\[
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \epsilon
\] where:

\(y\) is the response variable - minimum temperature
\(x\) is the explanatory variable - H. tumulorum present or absent.
\(\beta_0\) is the intercept
\(\beta_1\) is the coefficient (or slope)
\(\epsilon\) represents the variation not explained by the model

In our case, the value of \(x\) (detected, the explanatory variable) - can only be TRUE or FALSE. It is usual in this case to assign FALSE a value of 0 and TRUE a value of 1.

If H. tumulorum is absent, \(x\) equals 0.
When \(x\) is zero, the line intercepts the y axis - so the intercept \(\beta_0\) is the mean minimum temperature when H. tumulorum is absent.
If H. tumulorum is present, \(x\) equals 1.
The slope is the change in \(y\) over one unit of \(x\). So, the change in mean minimum temperature between \(x\) = 0 and \(x\) = 1, or the difference in mean temperature when H. tumulorum is present, compared to when it is absent.

We know these numbers already:

gt(ht_temp_summ |> select(detected, mean))







detected
mean




FALSE
0.1128519


TRUE
1.3747955







The difference between the two means is:

diff <- pull(present, mean) - pull(absent, mean)
print(diff)

[1] 1.261944


When the bee is absent, \(x = 0\):
\[
y = 0.11 + (1.26 \times 0) + \epsilon
\]
so:
\[
y = 0.11 + \epsilon
\]
When the bee is present, \(x = 1\):
\[
y = 0.11 + (1.26 \times 1) + \epsilon
\]
so:
\[
y = 1.37 + \epsilon
\]
Our t-test tests whether there is evidence that the difference between the mean values of the two groups is different from zero.
Our linear model tests whether there is evidence that the slope of the line is different from zero.
They are therefore testing exactly the same thing.

Fitting linear models in R
Core
Let’s see if this is correct by fitting a linear model to our data in R. We do this with the function lm() and the same formula we used previously - response ~ explanatory.






ExerciseExercise 5 - Fit a linear model






Core
In your pollinators.qmd Quarto file, fit a linear model using the function lm() and the same formula as for the t-test above. As for the t-test, you’ll need to add the argument data = ht_temp_df so R can see the data frame. Store the output in the variable lm_ht.






AnswerAnswer







lm_ht <- lm(min_temp_coldest_month ~ detected,
  data = ht_temp_df
)









We can summarise the linear model using the function summary() on the fitted model.

summ_lm_ht <- summary(lm_ht)
print(summ_lm_ht)


Call:
lm(formula = min_temp_coldest_month ~ detected, data = ht_temp_df)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-2.40085 -0.61417  0.02203  0.60461  2.55090 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)    0.1129     0.1579   0.715    0.477    
detectedTRUE   1.2619     0.2204   5.726 2.07e-07 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.9603 on 74 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.307, Adjusted R-squared:  0.2977 
F-statistic: 32.79 on 1 and 74 DF,  p-value: 2.073e-07


This function gives us a lot of information, including the numbers we calculated above.

The estimated intercept is our mean minimum temperature without H. tumulorum
The estimated slope (listed as detectedTRUE) is the difference in minimum temperature with and without H. tumulorum.
The p-value for the slope is identical to the p-value we calculated earlier with our t-test.

We can extract the 95% confidence intervals from our linear model with the function confint() with one argument - the fitted model, lm_ht.






ExerciseExercise 6 - Confidence intervals






Recommended
In your pollinators.qmd Quarto file, use the function confint() to find the confidence intervals for your lm_ht fitted model.






AnswerAnswer







ci <- confint(lm_ht)
print(ci)

                  2.5 %    97.5 %
(Intercept)  -0.2017249 0.4274287
detectedTRUE  0.8228055 1.7010818










The second confidence interval here is the confidence interval of the slope of the line - and again it’s identical to our t-test values above.
As discussed above, for a linear regression, we are interested in whether the coefficient (slope) for our explanatory variable differs from zero. We still use the t-statistic, which is calculated by dividing the estimated coefficient by its standard error.
The p-value is obtained from a t-distribution specified by the residual degrees of freedom. For a simple linear regression, we estimate two parameters: the intercept and the slope. Here we have 76 observations, so the residual degrees of freedom are 76 - 2 = 74.
We therefore need to look for the following values in the linear model output:

Coefficient (slope): Estimate
Test statistic: t value
Degrees of freedom: residual degrees of freedom
p-value: Pr(>|t|)
Proportion of variation explained: Multiple R-squared

For a linear model with a categorical explanatory variable like this, we can also report the difference in means between the two conditions.
For the linear model above, we could report:

There is evidence that minimum temperature differs according to the presence or absence of H. tumulorum (\(\beta\) = 1.26°C, 95% CI [0.82, 1.7]°C, \(t\)(74) = 5.73, \(p\) = 2.07e-07, \(R^2\) = 0.307). Sites where H. tumulorum is present have a mean minimum temperature approximately 1.26°C higher than sites where it is absent. The model explains approximately 30.7% of the variation in minimum temperature.



Visualising linear models with a logical categorical variable
Extension
We can easily visualise our linear model in ggplot.
First, we plot a scatter plot with our detected variable on the x-axis and minimum temperature on the y-axis.
We need to convert our detected column to show 0 for FALSE and 1 for TRUE. To convert a column to numeric, we use the function as.numeric(). For a logical column, it will automatically do what we want - convert FALSE to 0 and TRUE to 1.
We can then use the function geom_smooth() to apply and plot a linear model to the data. This corresponds to plotting a line between 0.11 when x is 0 and 1.37 when x is 1.
Let’s also add a horizontal line using geom_hline() showing a slope of 0 and the same mean for both groups.

ht_temp_df <- ht_temp_df |>
  mutate(detected_num = as.numeric(detected))

overall_mean <- ht_temp_df |>
  pull(min_temp_coldest_month) |>
  mean()

ggplot(ht_temp_df, aes(
  x = detected_num,
  y = min_temp_coldest_month
)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = overall_mean), color = "red") +
  ggtitle("Minimum temperature vs H. tumulorum detection - Observed and Fitted") +
  xlab("H. tumulorum detected") +
  ylab("Minimum temperature (°C)") +
  theme_minimal()

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

title: Part 2: Hypothesis Testing
text:
ANOVA
Core
With exactly two groups, a classical one-way ANOVA is also mathematically equivalent to either of these tests.
A one-way ANOVA with two groups is testing:
Does allowing the two groups to have different means explain significantly more variation than assuming they have the same mean
This can be simplified to - is there evidence that these two means are not equal?
This is asking the same question we’ve already asked twice, in a different way.
Let’s try an ANOVA. We run ANOVA in R on an existing linear model - which we already created above, in the variable lm_ht, using the function anova().






ExerciseExercise 7 - ANOVA






Core
In your pollinators.qmd Quarto file, run an ANOVA on your existing linear model, lm_ht, using the function anova().






AnswerAnswer







anova_lm <- anova(lm_ht)
anova_lm

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: min_temp_coldest_month
          Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
detected   1 30.237 30.2366  32.786 2.073e-07 ***
Residuals 74 68.245  0.9222                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1










As you can see, we’ve again found an identical p-value. As it’s the same linear model, our confidence intervals are, by definition, also the same.
For an ANOVA, we report our results a little differently. The p-value here is obtained from an F distribution specified by two degrees-of-freedom values: the numerator and denominator degrees of freedom.

The numerator degrees of freedom are associated with the explanatory variable. Here there are two groups (present and absent), so this is 2 − 1 = 1.
The denominator degrees of freedom are the residual degrees of freedom. We have 76 observations and estimate two parameters (the intercept and slope), so this is 76 − 2 = 74.

As with the t-test, the p-value is calculated from a probability distribution. For ANOVA, this is the F-distribution rather than the t-distribution. The F-statistic compares the variation explained by the model with the unexplained variation; unusually large F-values provide evidence against the null hypothesis.
So, we need to look for the following values in our ANOVA output.

Test statistic: F value
Numerator degrees of freedom: Df for the explanatory variable
Denominator degrees of freedom: Df for the residuals
p-value: Pr(>F)







Figure 24.1: Interpreting ANOVA results



Additionally, we can report the proportion of variation explained by the model relative to the total variation in the response variable. We can calculate this from the sum of square values in the ANOVA output.

SS_model <- anova_lm["detected", "Sum Sq"]
SS_res <- anova_lm["Residuals", "Sum Sq"]

prop_var <- SS_model / (SS_res + SS_model)
print(prop_var)

[1] 0.3070276


Conveniently, this is the same as our \(R^2\) value in the linear model we used above.

print(summary(lm_ht))


Call:
lm(formula = min_temp_coldest_month ~ detected, data = ht_temp_df)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-2.40085 -0.61417  0.02203  0.60461  2.55090 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)    0.1129     0.1579   0.715    0.477    
detectedTRUE   1.2619     0.2204   5.726 2.07e-07 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.9603 on 74 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.307, Adjusted R-squared:  0.2977 
F-statistic: 32.79 on 1 and 74 DF,  p-value: 2.073e-07


So, we would report:

There is evidence that minimum temperature in the coldest month differs between sites where H. tumulorum is present and sites where it is absent (\(F\)(1, 74) = 32.79, \(p\) = 2.07e-07, \(R^2\) = 0.307). The model explains approximately 30.7% of the variation in minimum temperature in the coldest month.

The advantage of ANOVA is that, unlike a t-test, we can use it when our categorical explanatory variable has more than two groups - we’ll come to this in the next section.

title: Part 2: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Review
↑ top






NoteSummary




Concepts

A statistical formula in R uses ~ to describe the relationship between variables, with the response variable on the left and the explanatory variable on the right.
The output of a statistical test can be stored as an R object, allowing values such as the test statistic, confidence interval and p-value to be accessed.
A linear model (lm()) can be fitted with a categorical explanatory variable. With two groups, the intercept represents the mean of the reference group and the coefficient represents the difference between the two group means.
With two groups, an equal-variance two-sample t-test, a linear model with a categorical explanatory variable and a classical one-way ANOVA test the same underlying difference between group means.
A fitted linear model can be summarised (summary()) to obtain quantities including coefficients, test statistics, p-values and the proportion of variation explained.
Test statistic distributions can be simulated and used to calculate probabilities associated with the statistic. (Extension)
Simulation can be used to demonstrate the repeated-sampling interpretation of a confidence interval. (Extension)

title: Part 3: ANOVA with multiple groups or explanatory variables
text:
One-way ANOVA with more than two groups
In the previous section, we introduced one-way ANOVA using an explanatory variable with two levels. However, ANOVA can easily be expanded to look at multiple groups and multiple explanatory variables.
Core
ANOVA expands easily to take into account an explanatory variable with more than two levels (i.e. a categorical variable with three or more options).
We already know about using response ~ explanatory as a formula in R to investigate response as a function of explanatory variable. If you are using a data frame as the input to this function and the explanatory variable is categorical, R will automatically treat the different values in the column as different levels of that variable.
One of the measurements in our pollinator data frame is mean_insect_mass - the mean mass in grams of all pollinators collected at that site.
It seems feasible that this would be affected by the types of pollinators present - some pollinators are much bigger than others.
Hypothesis
Using our pollinator data, let’s investigate the following hypothesis using a one-way ANOVA.
Plot
A box plot is a typical way to visualise the type of data which is suitable for ANOVA analysis.
Statistical test
We can test the association between mean insect mass and dominant family with a one-way ANOVA, and we define it exactly as before.
Here, we would define the linear model as lm(mean_insect_mass ~ dominant_family, data=site_metadata).
We could then just look at our linear model directly. It would take one category - in this case Andrenidae, as it is first alphabetically, to be the reference level and compare each of the other levels - Syrphidae, Halictidae and Apidae to Andrenidae. It would not compare e.g. Halictidae to Apidae as neither is the reference.
Let’s try it:
This tells us:
But, this probably isn’t what we want to know - we still don’t know if all four means are equal.
If we perform an ANOVA on this data, it will compare a model in which sites with all four dominant pollinator families have the same mean insect mass with a model in which the sites with different dominant pollinator families are allowed to have different means.

Null hypothesis: Sites dominated by different insect families have the same mean mass.
Alternative hypothesis: At least one dominant insect family is associated with sites with a different mean mass.









ExerciseExercise 1 - Box plot






Recommended
In your pollinators.qmd Quarto document, plot a box plot showing the value of mean_insect_mass in your site_metadata data frame for the regions with each value of dominant_family.
Remember that:

The R function geom_boxplot() draws a box plot.
The aes function for this type of plot requires a categorical x variable and a continuous y variable as arguments - so you would use the arguments x = dominant_family and y = mean_insect_mass.

ggplot(
  site_metadata,
  aes(
    x = dominant_family, y = mean_insect_mass,
    fill = dominant_family
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  ggtitle("Mean insect mass at sites dominated by different insect families - Observed") +

Core
In your pollinators.qmd Quarto file, fit a linear model using the function lm() and the formula above. As for the t-test, you’ll need to add the argument data = site_metadata so R can see the data frame. Store the output in the variable lm_mass_domfam. View the results using the summary() function.

lm_mass_domfam <- lm(mean_insect_mass ~ dominant_family, data = site_metadata)
summary(lm_mass_domfam)


Call:
lm(formula = mean_insect_mass ~ dominant_family, data = site_metadata)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-17.5991  -5.3988  -0.5006   3.8201  20.9558 

Coefficients:

(Intercept)                 19.589      8.325   2.353   0.0214 *

Response: mean_insect_mass
                Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)

There is evidence that mean insect mass differs among dominant insect families (\(F\)(3, 72) = 14.72, \(p\) = 0.00000014), \(R^2\) = 0.38). Dominant insect family explains approximately 38% of the variation in mean insect mass among sites.

title: Part 3: ANOVA with multiple groups or explanatory variables
text:
The F-distribution
Extension
I stated above that “The p-value here is obtained from an F distribution specified by two degrees-of-freedom values: the numerator and denominator degrees of freedom. The numerator degrees of freedom are associated with the explanatory variable. The denominator degrees of freedom are the residual degrees of freedom.”. In this case, our numerator has three degrees of freedom and our denominator has 72.
Let’s use simulation to visualise this.






ExerciseExercise 4 - The F-distribution






Extension
In your pollinators.qmd Quarto file:

Simulate a sample of 1000 observations from an F-distribution with 3 numerator degrees of freedom and 72 denominator degrees of freedom. You can draw a random sample from an F-distribution with the function rf() with the arguments n - number of observations, df1 numerator degrees of freedom and df2 denominator degrees of freedom.
Create a data frame where this set of observations forms a column.
Plot the results using the ggplot layer geom_density().
Calculate an approximate p-value using your simulated data — the proportion of simulated F-values which are greater than or equal to the F-statistic calculated from our data (14.72). You can extract the F-statistic from the ANOVA table using anova_mass_domfam["dominant_family", "F value"], changing anova_mass_domfam to whichever variable name you used.
Calculate the exact p-value using the F-distribution cumulative probability function pf().







AnswerAnswer






Simulate a sample of 1000 observations from F-distribution with 3 numerator degrees of freedom and 72 denominator degrees of freedom. You can draw a random sample from an F-distribution with the function rf with the arguments n - number of observations, df1 numerator degrees of freedom and df2 denominator degrees of freedom.

df_3_72 <- rf(1000, df1 = 3, df2 = 72)

Create a data frame where this set of observations forms a column.

f_dist <- tibble(simulated = df_3_72)

Plot the results using the ggplot layer geom_density().

fstat <- anova_mass_domfam["dominant_family", "F value"]

ggplot(
  f_dist,
  aes(x = simulated)
) +
  geom_density() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = fstat, color = "red") +
  ggtitle("Density of F-distribution - Simulated and Observed") +
  xlab("F") +
  ylab("Density") +
  theme_minimal()








Calculate an approximate p-value using your simulated data — the proportion of simulated F-values which are greater than or equal to the F-statistic calculated from our data (14.72).

p_above_sim <- sum(f_dist$simulated >= fstat)

p_sim <- p_above_sim / nrow(f_dist)

print(p_sim)

[1] 0


As for the t-test previously, with 1000 simulations and such a low p-value, your value will almost certainly be zero.
Calculate the exact p-value using the F-distribution cumulative probability function pf().

p_below <- pf(fstat, 3, 72)
p_exact <- 1 - p_below
print(p_exact)

[1] 1.434646e-07


This should be the exact p-value calculated in our ANOVA.

title: Part 3: ANOVA with multiple groups or explanatory variables
text:
Multi-way ANOVA
Core
ANOVA can also be extended to include multiple categorical explanatory variables. This is called multi-way ANOVA (or factorial ANOVA). A model with two categorical explanatory variables is a two-way ANOVA, one with three is a three-way ANOVA, and so on.
We can add additional explanatory variables using + - response ~ explanatory1 + explanatory2 + explanatory3 etc.
The default ANOVA implementation in R tests whether each explanatory variable is associated with the response in turn. So, in the case above, explanatory1 would be tested first, followed by whether explanatory2 explains additional variation after explanatory1 has been included, and so forth.
Hypothesis
Using our pollinator data, let’s investigate the following hypotheses:
Dominant insect family:

Null hypothesis: mean insect mass is the same at sites dominated by different insect families
Alternative hypothesis: mean insect mass differs for at least one dominant insect family.

Broad habitat type:

Null hypothesis: after taking dominant insect family into account, mean insect mass is the same across different broad habitat types.
Alternative hypothesis: after taking dominant insect family into account, mean insect mass differs for at least one broad habitat type.

Plot
A box plot is again a typical visualisation to use here, this time using pivot_longer() to convert our data frame into long format and facet_wrap() to separate our different variables.
pivot_longer()
Here we have two categorical variables, dominant_family and broad_habitat, stored in separate columns. We can use pivot_longer() to combine these into two new columns:

The variable column will contain the names of the original columns (dominant_family or broad_habitat).
The value column will contain the values that were stored in those columns (for example, Apidae or Woodland).

We specify which columns we want to combine using the cols argument of pivot_longer(). We specify the name of the column we want to put the column names into with the names_to argument. We specify the column that we want to put the column values into with values_to.
So, if we had the following small data frame as variable data_wide.
Before:



x1km_square
dominant_family
broad_habitat
mean_insect_mass




TL1234
Apidae
Woodland
0.12



We could specify:

data_long <- data_wide |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(dominant_family, broad_habitat),
               names_to = "variable",
               values_to = "value")

After:



x1km_square
mean_insect_mass
variable
value




TL1234
0.12
dominant_family
Apidae


TL1234
0.12
broad_habitat
Woodland



facet_wrap()
The function facet_wrap() splits the data from a single data frame into multiple plots, based on the values in a categorical column. The first argument should be the variable you would like to facet by, preceded by a ~ symbol. The argument scales = "free_x" means that each plot can have a different scale on the x axis - by default they are the same.
To make a faceted plot of both explanatory variables, it will be useful to convert our data from wide to long format. We encountered this in Long and wide formats, when we reshaped the bird migration data.
coord_flip()
The function coord_flip() swaps the x- and y-axes of a ggplot, turning a vertical plot into a horizontal one (or vice versa). We do this here just because the category names are long and so they fit better on the page horizontally.

# Take the relevant columns from the data frame
domfam_habitat_sel <- site_metadata |>
  select(x1km_square, dominant_family, broad_habitat, mean_insect_mass)

# Pivot to long format
domfam_habitat_long <- domfam_habitat_sel |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(
      dominant_family,
      broad_habitat
    ),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "value"
  )

# Plot the boxplot
ggplot(
  domfam_habitat_long,
  aes(x = value, y = mean_insect_mass, fill = variable)
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_x") +
  coord_flip() +
  ggtitle("Insect mass by dominant family or broad habitat type - Observed") +
  xlab("Category") +
  ylab("Mean insect mass (g)") +
  theme_minimal()

AnswerAnswer






Statistical test
We define our linear model as follows:

And then run the ANOVA.

print(anova_domfam_habitat_mass)

dominant_family  3 3060.2 1020.06 14.6513 1.85e-07 ***
broad_habitat    4  255.5   63.87  0.9174    0.459    
Residuals       68 4734.3   69.62                     
---

Conclusion

There is evidence that mean insect mass differs among dominant insect families (\(F\)(3, 68) = 14.65, \(p\) = 1.85e-07). After accounting for dominant insect family, there is no evidence that broad habitat type explains additional variation in mean insect mass (\(F\)(4, 68) = 0.92, \(p\) = 0.46).

title: Part 3: ANOVA with multiple groups or explanatory variables
text:
Interactions
Recommended
When we use + to include multiple explanatory variables, we are assuming that their relationships with the response are additive. This means that the relationship between one explanatory variable and the response is the same at every level of the other explanatory variable. So for example, the dominant insect family can be associated with a difference in mean insect mass, and habitat can be associated with a difference, and these differences can be added together.
However, sometimes the relationship between one explanatory variable and the response depends on the value of another explanatory variable. This is called an interaction.
We can add interactions between variables using * - response ~ explanatory1 * explanatory2. The ANOVA will then test the association between each explanatory variable and the response, as well as whether there is an interaction between them.
For example, if we set up the model as mean_insect_mass ~ dominant_family * dominant_flower_order, we are asking:

Does mean insect mass vary between sites with different dominant insect families?
Does mean insect mass vary between sites with different dominant flower orders, once dominant insect family has been taken into account?
Does any difference in mean insect mass among dominant insect families depend on the dominant flower order?

This final question is the interaction: does the association between one explanatory variable and the response depend on the value of another explanatory variable?
Hypotheses
Dominant insect family:

Null hypothesis: There is no association between mean insect mass and dominant insect family.
Alternative hypothesis: Mean insect mass is associated with dominant insect family.

Dominant flower order:

Null hypothesis: There is no association between mean insect mass and dominant flower order, once dominant insect family has been taken into account.
Alternative hypothesis: Mean insect mass is associated with dominant flower order, once dominant insect family has been taken into account.

Interaction:

Null hypothesis: The association between dominant insect family and mean insect mass does not vary depending on dominant flower order.
Alternative hypothesis: The association between dominant insect family and mean insect mass varies depending on dominant flower order.







ExerciseExercise 6 - ANOVA with interaction






Recommended
In your pollinators.qmd Quarto file:

Run an ANOVA on this model and view the results.
Draw a conclusion based on the results, including the appropriate statistical evidence to support your conclusion.







AnswerAnswer






Statistical test
Fit a linear model to test the association between dominant family, dominant flower order and mean insect mass, including the interaction between dominant family and dominant flower order.
Run an ANOVA on this model and view the results.

# Fit the model
mass_fam_flower_lm <- lm(mean_insect_mass ~ dominant_family * dominant_flower_order,
  data = site_metadata
)
# Run the ANOVA
mass_fam_flower_anova <- anova(mass_fam_flower_lm)

print(mass_fam_flower_anova)

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: mean_insect_mass
                                      Df  Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
dominant_family                        3 3060.17 1020.06 16.4326 1.601e-07 ***
dominant_flower_order                 10 1124.69  112.47  1.8118   0.08323 .  
dominant_family:dominant_flower_order 13  823.43   63.34  1.0204   0.44778    
Residuals                             49 3041.69   62.08                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Conclusion
Draw a conclusion based on the results, including the appropriate statistical evidence to support your conclusion.

There is evidence that mean insect mass differs among dominant insect families (\(F\)(3, 49) = 16.43, \(p\) = 1.60e-07).
After accounting for dominant insect family, there is no evidence that mean insect mass differs among dominant flower orders (\(F\)(10, 49) = 1.81, \(p\) = 0.0832).
There is also no evidence of an interaction between dominant insect family and dominant flower order (\(F\)(13, 49) = 1.02, \(p\) = 0.4478). Therefore, there is no evidence that the difference in mean insect mass among dominant insect families depends on the dominant flower order.










Using simulation to visualise interactions
Extension
Let’s simulate a dataset with an interaction, to help illustrate this concept.
In this study, there are four samples of students and the response variable is the time they took to finish their lunch, in minutes. Response time is drawn from a normal distribution with a standard deviation of 3.
There are two categorical explanatory variables:

Did they use a spoon or a fork?
Did they eat soup or pasta?

Their mean finishing times are as follows:

Spoon + Pasta = 8 minutes
Fork + Pasta = 10 minutes
Spoon + Soup = 11 minutes
Fork + Soup = 25 minutes

The hypotheses here are:
Utensil:

Null hypothesis: There is no association between utensil choice and finishing time.
Alternative hypothesis: Utensil choice is associated with finishing time.

Food:

Null hypothesis: There is no association between food choice and finishing time, after taking into account the association with utensil choice.
Alternative hypothesis: Food choice is associated with finishing time, after taking into account the association with utensil choice.

Interaction:

Null hypothesis: The association between utensil choice and finishing time does not vary depending on food choice.
Alternative hypothesis: The association between utensil choice and finishing time varies depending on food choice.







ExerciseExercise 8 - Using simulation to visualise interactions






Extension
If you haven’t already, create a new Quarto file, prac4_exercises.qmd.






NoteInclude this code




library(tidyverse)
library(gt)
set.seed(42)

Fit a linear model with time as the response variable and utensil, food and their interaction as explanatory variables.
Run an ANOVA on the linear model.







AnswerAnswer






Data
Generate four simulated samples, each of 10 students, with response times normally distributed around these means and a standard deviation of 3.

spoon_pasta <- rnorm(10, 8, 3)
fork_pasta <- rnorm(10, 10, 3)
spoon_soup <- rnorm(10, 11, 3)
fork_soup <- rnorm(10, 25, 3)

Convert each of these into a data frame with the columns utensil, food and time.

df_sp <- tibble(
  utensil = "Spoon",
  food = "Pasta",
  time = spoon_pasta
)

  utensil = "Fork",
  food = "Pasta",
  time = fork_pasta

  utensil = "Spoon",
  food = "Soup",
  time = spoon_soup

  utensil = "Fork",

  time = fork_soup

Convert these to a single data frame using the function bind_rows(). You can pass any number of data frames as arguments to this function and it will return a single data frame combining all of the rows (assuming the data frames all have the same columns).

Statistical test
Fit a linear model with time as the response variable and utensil, food and their interaction as explanatory variables.

lm_lunch <- lm(time ~ utensil * food, data = df_food)

Run an ANOVA on the linear model.

anova_lunch <- anova(lm_lunch)
print(anova_lunch)

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: time
             Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
utensil       1 442.91  442.91  33.156 1.463e-06 ***
food          1 579.31  579.31  43.367 1.156e-07 ***
utensil:food  1 460.69  460.69  34.487 1.029e-06 ***
Residuals    36 480.90   13.36

Conclusion
Here, we need to report the F-statistic, degrees of freedom and p-value for both explanatory variables and for the interaction.

Review
↑ top






NoteSummary




Concepts

A linear model with a categorical explanatory variable containing more than two levels uses one level as the reference level, with coefficients describing differences relative to that reference.
Multiple explanatory variables can be included in an R formula using +, for example response ~ explanatory1 + explanatory2.
In R’s default ANOVA, explanatory variables are tested sequentially: each variable is tested after accounting for variables that appear before it in the model.
An interaction can be included in an R formula using *, for example response ~ explanatory1 * explanatory2. (Recommended)

title: Part 4: Linear regression and Chi-Squared
text:
Linear Regression
Core
We’ve now used all sorts of linear models, but how about a standard linear regression between two continuous variables? You already have the skills needed to do this - you can fit the model using lm() and then view the results using summary(), and you basically know how to interpret the results.
As we discussed in the previous section, for a linear model we should report the following:
Let’s use the pollinator data again and look at a straightforward regression question - how is total annual precipitation (column annual_total_prec) associated with mean annual temperature (column annual_mean_temp)?
Hypotheses
Plot
A scatter plot is the most common plot to compare two continuous variables. We can use geom_smooth(method = "lm") to add a linear model to the plot.
ggplot(
  site_metadata,
  aes(
    x = annual_mean_temp,
    y = annual_total_prec
  )
) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  ggtitle("Annual mean temperature vs annual total precipitation - Observed") +
  xlab("Annual mean temperature (°C)") +
  ylab("Annual total precipitation (mm)") +
  theme_minimal()

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'
