title: Part 3: Identifying Sequences with BLAST
text:
Review
↑ top
At this stage, we know quite a lot about our ERVs:

Which retroviral genes are present.
The location of the longest ORF for each gene within our source sequence.
Which retroviral genus each gene is likely to be derived from.
Which known retrovirus each gene best matches.

There are several things here which could mean your results are extra interesting:

Genes from more than one different genus in your identified ERV ORF set - this suggests that the retrovirus could be a recombinant generated by recombination between two different viruses.
Most ERVs in mammals are of the gamma, beta or spuma genus - alpha and epsilon like ERVs are rarer and delta and lenti like ERVs are very rare so any non-gamma/beta ERVs in beavers would be very interesting.

However, even if neither of these are true, you are still most likely the first scientist to find out anything about your specific ERV!
↑ top






NoteSummary




Concepts

BLASTp can be used to compare protein query sequences against a set of protein subject sequences to identify similar sequences.
When choosing the best BLAST matches, several measures can be considered together, including E value, query coverage, percentage identity and bit score.
BLAST results can be downloaded as a CSV file and read into R for further analysis.
Information contained within a single column can be split into multiple columns using a delimiter.
Data can be grouped and ranked within groups to select the best result separately for each group.
Values extracted from a data frame can be used to subset a sequence set, allowing selected sequences to be saved to a new FASTA file.



Functions








Function
What it does
Level




separate_wider_delim()
Splits a column into multiple columns using a specified delimiter.
Core


start()
Returns the start positions of ranges in an IRanges object.
Core


end()
Returns the end positions of ranges in an IRanges object.
Core


slice_max()
Selects rows containing the largest values of a variable, including separately within groups.
Core


ungroup()
Removes grouping from a grouped data frame.
Core





Files

output/Ccan_[ERV_ID]_alignment_table.csv

output/identified_orfs.csv

We can now align each gene sequence with the protein sequences of the same gene from other retroviruses in a multiple sequence alignment and then build a phylogeny to see the evolutionary relationships between our sequences and their relatives.
To build these multiple sequence alignments, we first need to build AAStringSet objects for each gene, containing the ORF we identified for that gene along with the sequences of known retrovirus proteins from the same gene and genus, which we identified earlier using BLASTp.
I will take you through this process with one of my ORFs, Ccan_ERV_1_ORF_4, which is a gag gene from the gamma genus.
First, I will create an AAStringSet with just this one sequence.
identified_current <- identified_orf_seqs["Ccan_ERV_1_ORF_4"]

print(identified_current)

Then, I will read the file output/Ccan_ERV_1_ORF_4_refs.fasta, generated earlier when I saved my BLAST output as a FASTA file, into a second AAStringSet with the readAAStringSet() function.
refs_current <- readAAStringSet("output/Ccan_ERV_1_ORF_4_refs.fasta")

combined_current <- c(identified_current, refs_current)

title: Part 4: Multiple Sequence Alignment and Phylogeny
text:
Build phylogenies
Core
↑ top
There are various ways we can create phylogenies from our sequences. We will use a distance-based, neighbour-joining approach.
First, we create a distance matrix for our sequences, then we use the function nj() from the package ape to create a tree.
A distance matrix contains an estimate of the evolutionary distance between every pair of sequences in our alignment. Smaller distances indicate more similar sequences. The neighbour-joining method uses these distances to construct a tree in which more similar sequences tend to be grouped together.
I will again demonstrate this process with one of my ORFs, Ccan_ERV_1_ORF_4, which is a gag gene from the gamma genus. These are currently aligned with the related sequences we identified with BLAST and stored in my combined_current_aligned_ss variable.
First, I will read the relevant FASTA file. We use readAAStringSet() rather than readDNAStringSet() because our sequences are in amino acid format.

fasta_current <- readAAStringSet(
  "output/gag_Ccan_ERV_1_ORF_4.fasta"
)

Next, we make a distance matrix based on our aligned sequences, using the function DistanceMatrix(), with one argument, our new fasta_current variable.

distance_matrix <- DistanceMatrix(fasta_current)

================================================================================

Time difference of 0 secs


Now, we’re ready to make our neighbour-joining tree. This is very easy in R, just using the function nj().

tree <- nj(distance_matrix)

We can save it with the function write.tree(). The standard format for saving phylogenetic trees is called Newick format and has the suffix .nwk.

write.tree(tree, file = "output/gag_Ccan_ERV_1_ORF_4.nwk")







ExerciseExercise 2 - Build phylogenetic trees






Core
In your beaver_ervs.qmd Quarto file, repeat the steps above for each of the ORF sequences in your identified_orf_df data frame, so that you have one Newick file for each gene.

Read the amino acid alignment.
Create a distance matrix.
Build a neighbour-joining tree.
Save the tree.

You can do this manually or using a for loop.
Save all of the trees in Newick format with names formatted as gene_Ccan_ERV_j_ORF_i.nwk, replacing gene with the gene you are currently analysing (gag, pol or env), ERV_j with your ERV ID and i with your ORF ID.

title: Part 4: Multiple Sequence Alignment and Phylogeny
text:
Visualise phylogenies
Core
↑ top
Once the phylogenetic analyses are complete, we can then read our trees into R using the function read.newick().
For example, for my output/gag_Ccan_ERV_1_ORF_4.nwk Newick file:

current_newick <- read.newick("output/gag_Ccan_ERV_1_ORF_4.nwk")

To visualise phylogenies in R, a good option is the ggtree() package, which works similarly to ggplot().
First, we call the ggtree() function and give our new tree object as an argument.

ggtree(current_newick)

! The tree contained negative edge lengths. If you want to ignore the edges,
you can set `options(ignore.negative.edge=TRUE)`, then re-run ggtree.









As you can see, this generates a basic tree, but the branch tips are not labelled.
To label them, we add the function geom_tiplab(). The size argument to geom_tiplab() sets the font size. As our tip labels are quite long, we also change the x axis limits to make some space.






Note



Sometimes, the Quarto figure size will be too small to display your tree nicely. You can adjust this by clicking on the “Settings” button at the top of the code chunk and changing the width and height options.






Figure 34.1: Quarto Figure Size






ggtree(current_newick) +
  geom_tiplab(size = 2) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 20))

! The tree contained negative edge lengths. If you want to ignore the edges,
you can set `options(ignore.negative.edge=TRUE)`, then re-run ggtree.









You should be able to find your ERV gene in the phylogeny. However, it would be helpful to make it clearer, for example by changing the colour.
Here, we fix the colour to depend on whether label == "Ccan_ERV_1_ORF_4" is TRUE or FALSE. We then colour labels as red if this is TRUE and black if it is FALSE.

ggtree(current_newick) +
  geom_tiplab(
    aes(color = label == "Ccan_ERV_1_ORF_4"),
    size = 2
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("TRUE" = "red", "FALSE" = "black"),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 20))

! The tree contained negative edge lengths. If you want to ignore the edges,
you can set `options(ignore.negative.edge=TRUE)`, then re-run ggtree.









It’s also good practice to add a scale bar to your tree. The scale bar represents evolutionary distance, in substitutions per site.
Change the x and y co-ordinates to move it around so it’s not displayed on top of your tree.

ggtree(current_newick) +
  geom_tiplab(
    aes(color = label == "Ccan_ERV_1_ORF_4"),
    size = 2
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("TRUE" = "red", "FALSE" = "black"),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 20)) +
  geom_treescale(x = 0, y = 0, fontsize = 3)

! The tree contained negative edge lengths. If you want to ignore the edges,
you can set `options(ignore.negative.edge=TRUE)`, then re-run ggtree.


Warning: Using `size` aesthetic for lines was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0.
ℹ Please use `linewidth` instead.
ℹ The deprecated feature was likely used in the ggtree package.
  Please report the issue at <https://github.com/YuLab-SMU/ggtree/issues>.









We can add a title with ggtitle() just like with ggplot2.

ggtree(current_newick) +
  geom_tiplab(aes(subset = label != "Ccan_ERV_1_ORF_4"),
    color = "black", size = 2
  ) +
  geom_tiplab(aes(subset = label == "Ccan_ERV_1_ORF_4"),
    color = "red", size = 3
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 20)) +
  geom_treescale(x = 0, y = 0, fontsize = 3) +
  ggtitle("Ccan ERV 1 Phylogeny")

! The tree contained negative edge lengths. If you want to ignore the edges,
you can set `options(ignore.negative.edge=TRUE)`, then re-run ggtree.









You can save your tree as a PDF using ggsave(), again you may need to adjust the width and height to fit it nicely on the page, you can do this with the width and height arguments.

tree_plot <- ggtree(current_newick) +
  geom_tiplab(
    aes(color = label == "Ccan_ERV_1_ORF_4"),
    size = 2
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("TRUE" = "red", "FALSE" = "black"),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 20)) +
  geom_treescale(x = 0, y = 0, fontsize = 3)

! The tree contained negative edge lengths. If you want to ignore the edges,
you can set `options(ignore.negative.edge=TRUE)`, then re-run ggtree.

ggsave(
  "output/gag_Ccan_ERV_1_ORF_4.pdf",
  plot = tree_plot,
  width = 10,
  height = 10
)

NoteSummary




Concepts

Amino acid sequences can be stored as an AAStringSet; individual sequences can be selected from it and multiple AAStringSet objects can be combined.
To build a multiple sequence alignment in R, combine the sequence of interest with its reference sequences, align them using (for example) msa(), and save the aligned sequences as a FASTA file.
To build a neighbour-joining phylogeny in R, you can calculate a distance matrix from the aligned sequences and use this to construct the tree.
Phylogenetic trees can be saved in Newick format and subsequently read back into R.
Phylogenetic trees can be visualised using ggtree, with tip labels, highlighting and an evolutionary distance scale added to the plot.
Phylogenetic tree plots can be saved in the same way as other ggplot-based figures.

title: Part 1: Functions
text:
Writing functions
Core
↑ top
In the practical course so far, we have used many of the different functions (see Functions) which are built into R and provided by additional packages.
However, it is also possible to write your own functions. This means you can use the same set of instructions multiple times, possibly with different inputs.
Functions have several advantages:

Using the same code again saves time.
If you want to change something in the code, you only have to change it once.
Because you are writing less code, you are less likely to make mistakes.

Here is a simple example of a function, to calculate the equivalent age of a dog if it were a human, its age in dog years. According to the BBC, for a medium dog the calculation is:
\[
d = 21 + \left(4 \times (\text{h} - 2)\right)
\]
Where d is the age in dog years and h is age in human years.
We can write a function to calculate this. We define a function using the function function(). It is best to give the function a descriptive name.
The steps of the function are then written in curly brackets ({}) on the following lines.
The return statement defines what the output of the function will be.

human_years_to_dog_years <- function(age_in_human_years) {
  age_in_dog_years <- 21 + (4 * (age_in_human_years - 2))
  return(age_in_dog_years)
}

So here we are saying:

human_years_to_dog_years <- function(age_in_human_years): I am defining a function, it is called human_years_to_dog_years and takes one argument, age_in_human_years.
{: Here are the steps.
age_in_dog_years <- 21 + (4 * (age_in_human_years - 2)): Run this equation on the variable age_in_human_years and store the result as the variable age_in_dog_years.
return (age_in_dog_years): Return the value of the variable age_in_dog_years as the output of the function
}: That’s all.

Let’s use our function to calculate the age in dog years of some dogs.
Monty is 6 in human years.






Figure 37.1: Monty Source




print(human_years_to_dog_years(6))

[1] 37


Noodle is 2 in human years:






Figure 37.2: Noodle Source




print(human_years_to_dog_years(2))

[1] 21


We can also apply our function to a column in a data frame.
Let’s say we have this data frame of dogs.

dog_data <- tibble(
  Name = c(
    "Biscuit",
    "Snowball",
    "Pickle",
    "Artemis",
    "Bert"
  ),
  Age_Human_Years = c(6, 1, 12, 4, 15)
)
gt(dog_data)







Name
Age_Human_Years




Biscuit
6


Snowball
1

12

15

title: Part 1: Functions
text:
Features of functions
Core
There are two important things to learn about functions:
1. In order to run the function, you need to call it
So, if I just run this code:

human_years_to_dog_years <- function(age_in_human_years) {
  age_in_dog_years <- 21 + (4 * (age_in_human_years - 2))
  return(age_in_dog_years)
}

R now knows this function exists, but it hasn’t been used yet.
If we want to actually run it, we need to add a function call.

human_years_to_dog_years <- function(age_in_human_years) {
  age_in_dog_years <- 21 + (4 * (age_in_human_years - 2))
  return(age_in_dog_years)
}
# function call
print(human_years_to_dog_years(10))

[1] 53


2. Variables you create inside a function only exist inside the function.
So, the following will work - inside the function, between the curly brackets, we can access the variable age_in_dog_years.

human_years_to_dog_years <- function(age_in_human_years) {
  print(paste("Age in human years:", age_in_human_years))
  age_in_dog_years <- 21 + (4 * (age_in_human_years - 2))
  return(age_in_dog_years)
}
# function call
print(paste("Age in dog years:", human_years_to_dog_years(10)))

[1] "Age in human years: 10"
[1] "Age in dog years: 53"


But this will not work, because outside of the function, the variable age_in_dog_years does not exist.

human_years_to_dog_years <- function(age_in_human_years) {
  age_in_dog_years <- 21 + (4 * (age_in_human_years - 2))
  return(age_in_dog_years)
}
result <- human_years_to_dog_years(10)
print(paste("Age in human years:", age_in_dog_years))

Error:
! object 'age_in_dog_years' not found

Returning multiple outputs from a function
So far, our functions have returned a single object. Sometimes we want a function to return several different results.
We can do this by putting the results into a list. A list can contain multiple objects, including objects of different types, and we can give each element a name.
For example, this function returns a mean, a vector of centred values, and a data frame:

calculate_stats <- function(x) {
  x_mean <- mean(x)
  centred_values <- x - x_mean

  summary_df <- tibble(
    observation = x,
    centred = centred_values
  )

  results <- list(
    mean = x_mean,
    centred_values = centred_values,
    summary_data = summary_df
  )

  return(results)
}

We can run the function and store the returned list:

Review
↑ top






NoteSummary




Concepts

A function is a reusable set of instructions that can be applied to different inputs.
Values supplied to a function are called arguments.
The code inside {} defines the operations performed by a function.
Defining a function does not run it; a function call runs the function with specified arguments.
Variables created inside a function normally only exist within that function.
Functions can be applied to individual values, vectors or columns in a data frame.
A list can contain multiple objects, including objects of different types. (Extension)
Named elements of a list can be accessed using the $ operator. (Extension)



Functions








Function
What it does
Level




function()
Defines a new function and specifies its arguments.

Specifies the output of a function.

title: Part 2: Testing Assumptions of Linear Models
text:
Independent observations
In this part of the practical, you will need one Quarto document:
As we discussed in Part 2: Hypothesis Testing, T-tests, ANOVA and linear regression are all based on the same general linear-model framework and therefore share many assumptions.
In Practical 4, we assumed the assumptions of all our models had been met, however, in reality we should always check this before carrying out a test.
Core
↑ top
Each observation should be independent of the others. For example, repeated measurements from the same site should not usually be treated as independent observations. Whether observations are independent depends primarily on how the data were collected. This is a study design step rather than an analysis step.
crumbs: 38  Part 2: Testing Assumptions of Linear Models

title: Part 2: Testing Assumptions of Linear Models
text:
Continuous response
Core
↑ top
The response variable should be continuous, e.g. mass, temperature, distance. Standard linear models assume that the response can vary continuously around the value predicted by the model. Binary responses, categorical responses and counts generally require different types of model.
crumbs: 38  Part 2: Testing Assumptions of Linear Models

title: Part 2: Testing Assumptions of Linear Models
text:
Normally distributed residuals
Core
↑ top
The residuals — the differences between the observed values and the values predicted by the model — should be approximately normally distributed.
Let’s go back to our first linear model from Practical 4 (Part 2: Hypothesis Testing) - for the hypothesis that minimum temperature is different at sites where the bee H. tumulorum is present than at sites where it is absent.
We can read the data frame we applied in Practical 4 and refit the linear model.

# Read the presence / absence data frame
ht_df <- read_csv("data/ht_df.csv")

# Refit the linear model
linear_model_ht <- lm(min_temp_coldest_month ~ detected,
  data = ht_df,
)
print(summary(linear_model_ht))

The residuals are the differences between the observed values and the values predicted by the linear model.
In the case of a t-test, the predicted values are just the means for each group - shown here where the blue line intercepts 0 (absent) and 1 (present). The residuals are the differences between the observed values and these means - so the distances between the tips of the blue line and the black dots.

The mean minimum temperature when H. tumulorum is absent is 0.1128519, the residuals for sites where H. tumulorum is absent are the observed values minus 0.1128519.
The mean minimum temperature when H. tumulorum is present is 1.3747955, the residuals for sites where H. tumulorum is present are the observed values minus 1.3747955.

We can also access the fitted (predicted) values directly from the model using the function fitted(). In this example they are not especially interesting, because there are only two possible fitted values: the mean minimum temperature for sites where H. tumulorum is absent and the mean for sites where it is present.
Nevertheless, let’s put our fitted and residual values into a data frame, to make our diagnostic plots easier.
We’re going to do this several times, so let’s write a function to make it easier. We can also add two more outputs of the model which we will need for later plots:

Standardised residuals - these express each residual relative to its expected variability, making residuals easier to compare with one another, and can be extracted using the R function rstandard().
Square root of absolute value of standardised residuals.

This function takes the linear model fitted to the data as its input and returns a data frame of the diagnostic statistics.

Note

In your pollinators_assumptions.qmd Quarto file, write a function named get_diagnostic_stats() which takes a fitted linear model as its input and creates and returns a data frame, using the function tibble(), with the following columns:

fitted - the predicted values based on the model, accessed by running fitted() on the fitted model.
residual - the residuals of the fitted model, accessed by running residuals() on the fitted model.
standardised_residual - the standardised residuals of the linear model, run rstandard() on the fitted model.
sqrt_abs_standardised_residual the square root (sqrt()) of the absolute value (abs()) of the standardised residual.







Note



You can create a data frame and directly populate the columns with values obtained by running a function. For example, if I wanted to create a data frame containing the exponentials and logs of the values in my vector x_vec, I could do the following:
The functions exp() and log() calculate the exponential and natural logarithm of a value, respectively.

AnswerAnswer







get_diagnostic_stats <- function(linear_model) {
  diag_stats <- tibble(
    fitted = fitted(linear_model),
    residual = residuals(linear_model),
    standardised_residual = rstandard(linear_model),
    sqrt_abs_standardised_residual = sqrt(abs(standardised_residual))
  )
  return(diag_stats)
}

title: Part 2: Testing Assumptions of Linear Models
text:
Q-Q Plot
↑ top
A Q–Q (quantile–quantile) plot compares two distributions by plotting their quantiles against each other. In this case, the quantiles of the residuals are compared with the theoretical quantiles of a normal distribution. If the residuals are approximately normally distributed, the points should approximately follow the straight line.
To plot the Q-Q plot, we can use the functions stat_qq() and stat_qq_line(). stat_qq() creates the Q–Q plot and stat_qq_line() adds a reference line showing the pattern expected if the residuals follow the theoretical distribution.

ggplot(ht_diagnostics, aes(sample = residual)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line() +
  ggtitle("Q-Q plot - \nMinimum Temperature vs Presence / Absence of H. tumulorum") +
  xlab("Theoretical residuals under normal distribution") +
  ylab("Observed residuals") +
  theme_minimal()








If the points lie approximately along a straight line, the data are reasonably consistent with a normal distribution. Small deviations are expected, particularly at the ends of the plot. Clear systematic patterns, such as strong curvature or points far from the line, suggest that the normality assumption may not be appropriate.
Here the points lie reasonably close to the straight line, so there is no strong evidence that the residuals deviate from a normal distribution.
crumbs: 38  Part 2: Testing Assumptions of Linear Models

title: Part 2: Testing Assumptions of Linear Models
text:
How normal is normal?
Extension
↑ top
Linear models are generally robust to moderate deviations from normality, particularly with larger sample sizes. However, substantial deviations from normality or extreme outliers may make hypothesis tests and confidence intervals less reliable.
What does this actually mean?

Writing a function
We are going to repeat the same steps several times in this exercise, so, let’s write another function.
Let’s take a vector of data points as the input to our function, and have the function: * Put the points into a data frame. * Plot a histogram of the distribution of the points. * Draw a Q-Q plot.
I have provided the function below, but please try to read and understand it.






Note



I have used the patchwork package, which allows us to combine multiple ggplot plots into a single figure.
After loading patchwork, we can combine two plots next to each other in one figure using +:

library(patchwork)



Note that in this exercise we are just looking whether a set of data points is normally distributed, rather than specifically residuals, so we don’t need our diagnostic statistics.

diag_normal <- function(data_points) {
  # Make the data frame
  df_points <- tibble(observations = data_points)
  # Plot a histogram of the distribution of the points
  histo <- ggplot(
    df_points,
    aes(x = observations)
  ) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 25) +
    ggtitle("Distribution of points") +
    xlab("Measurement") +
    ylab("Frequency") +
    theme_minimal()
  # Plot the Q-Q plot
  qq <- ggplot(
    df_points,
    aes(sample = observations)
  ) +
    stat_qq() +
    stat_qq_line() +
    ggtitle("Q-Q plot") +
    xlab("Theoretical quantiles") +
    ylab("Observed quantiles") +
    theme_minimal()
  return(histo + qq)
}


Normal distribution
First, let’s simulate a sample of 30 data points drawn from a normal distribution. Let’s say these are moustache lengths from a sample of schnauzer dogs and they have a mean of 20 cm and a standard deviation of 5 cm.






Figure 38.1: A schnauzer. Source









ExerciseExercise 2 - Sample drawn from a normal distribution






Extension
In your prac6_exercises.qmd Quarto file:

Generate 30 data points from a normal distribution with mean 20cm and standard deviation 5cm.
Pass your simulated data to the diag_normal() function to plot its distribution and Q-Q plot.

Repeat the analysis with 100 and 1000 data points.






AnswerAnswer







# Generate data
moustache_lengths <- rnorm(30, 20, 5)

# Run diag_normal
norm_30 <- diag_normal(moustache_lengths)
print(norm_30)








Repeat the analysis with 100 data points.

moustache_lengths <- rnorm(100, 20, 5)

norm_100 <- diag_normal(moustache_lengths)
print(norm_100)








Repeat the analysis with 1000 data points.

# Generate data
moustache_lengths <- rnorm(1000, 20, 5)

norm_1000 <- diag_normal(moustache_lengths)
print(norm_1000)
















With only 30 data points, the shape of the sample may not look particularly normal, even though the data were explicitly drawn from a normal distribution. The Q–Q plot may also show noticeable deviations from the line simply due to random sampling. As the sample size increases to 100 and then 1000, the shape of the sample should generally become more clearly normal and the points on the Q–Q plot should tend to follow the line more closely.


Mixed populations
Now, let’s say some schnauzers have a gene mutation which causes excessive moustache growth - on average, their moustaches are 20cm longer than standard schnauzers. This mutation occurs in 10% of dogs.






Figure 38.2: A schnauzer with a long moustache. Source









ExerciseExercise 3 - Mixed populations






Extension
In your prac6_exercises.qmd Quarto file:

Generate 900 data points from a normal distribution with mean 20cm and SD 5cm.
Generate 100 data points from a normal distribution with mean 40cm and SD 10cm.
Combine these points into a single vector
To do this, you can use the function c(), for example if your vectors are named short_hair_dogs and long_hair_dogs you could combine them as follows

all_dogs <- c(short_hair_dogs, long_hair_dogs)

Pass your simulated data to the diag_normal() function to plot its distribution and Q-Q plot.







AnswerAnswer







# Generate data
moustache_lengths_short <- rnorm(900, 20, 5)
moustache_lengths_long <- rnorm(100, 40, 10)

moustache_lengths_mixed <- c(moustache_lengths_short, moustache_lengths_long)

# Run diag_normal
mixed_diag <- diag_normal(moustache_lengths_mixed)
print(mixed_diag)
















This time, you should be able to see the systematic deviation from normality towards the right-hand side of the Q–Q plot. Unlike the small random deviations we saw when sampling from a normal distribution, a number of consecutive points systematically move away from the line.


Skewed data
Now, let’s see what happens if our data is skewed. For example, most of our dogs have been to the hairdresser for a trim, with a few exceptions, so the data is skewed to the right (Note: A right skew means that the right-hand tail of the distribution is longer; most observations are therefore towards the left.)






Figure 38.3: A schnauzer with a neat trim. Source



This data would not be an exponential distribution - these dogs’ moustache lengths are not the waiting times between events in a Poisson distribution. However, an exponential distribution is a good shortcut to a right-skewed distribution.






ExerciseExercise 4 - Skewed data






Extension

Pass your simulated data to the diag_normal() function to plot its distribution and Q-Q plot.







AnswerAnswer







# Generate data
moustache_lengths_skewed <- rexp(1000, 0.05)

# Run diag_normal
skewed_diag <- diag_normal(moustache_lengths_skewed)
print(skewed_diag)
















Right-skewed data produces a characteristic systematic curve in the Q–Q plot. The largest observations lie increasingly above the Q–Q line, reflecting the long right tail of the distribution. Left-skewed data produces the opposite pattern.


Data with few extremes
Some non-normal distributions are symmetric but have fewer extreme observations than a normal distribution. These are described as having lighter tails than the normal distribution, or as being platykurtic.
Perhaps very long and very short moustaches have gone out of style. We can recreate this using a uniform distribution.






ExerciseExercise 5 - Data with few extremes






Extension
In your prac6_exercises.qmd Quarto file:

Generate 1000 data points from a uniform distribution with a minimum of 10 and a maximum of 30.
Pass your simulated data to the diag_normal() function to plot its distribution and Q-Q plot.







AnswerAnswer







# Generate data
moustache_lengths_few_extremes <- runif(1000, 10, 30)

few_extremes_diag <- diag_normal(moustache_lengths_few_extremes)
print(few_extremes_diag)
















This is known as an S-shape curve and is indicative of the results having fewer extreme values than would be expected for a normal distribution.


Data with lots of extremes
Some non-normal distributions are symmetric but have more extreme observations than a normal distribution. These are described as having heavier tails than the normal distribution, or as being leptokurtic.
Perhaps very long and very short moustaches have come back into style amongst a few fashionable dogs. We can recreate this using a t-distribution with low degrees of freedom.






ExerciseExercise 6 - Data with many extremes






Extension
In your prac6_exercises.qmd Quarto file:

Generate 1000 data points from a t-distribution with 3 degrees of freedom.
Pass your simulated data to the diag_normal() function to plot its distribution and Q-Q plot.







AnswerAnswer







# Generate data
moustache_lengths_many_extremes <- rt(1000, 3)

# Rescale
moustache_lengths_many_extremes <- (moustache_lengths_many_extremes * 2) + 30

# Run diag_normal
many_extremes_diag <- diag_normal(moustache_lengths_many_extremes)
print(many_extremes_diag)








This is another S-shaped curve in the opposite direction, and is indicative of the results having more extreme values than would be expected for a normal distribution.








Notice that we can now repeat the same analysis on different datasets with a single function call, rather than repeating all of the code used to construct the plots.

Constant variance of residuals
Constant variance (or homoscedasticity) is the assumption that the amount of unexplained variation is roughly the same across the range of values predicted by the model.
For our model comparing sites where H. tumulorum was detected or not detected, there are only two fitted values: the mean for each group. Therefore, we can initially investigate this assumption simply by comparing the spread of residuals in the two groups.

ggplot(
  ht_diagnostics,
  aes(x = residual)
) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 15) +
  facet_wrap(~detected) +
  ggtitle("Distribution of residuals between groups\nMinimum Temperature vs Presence / Absence of H. tumulorum") +
  xlab("Residual (°C)") +
  ylab("Frequency") +
  theme_minimal()








These look reasonably similar, especially given the number of observations in each group.
We can also look directly at the standard deviation for the two groups.

title: Part 2: Testing Assumptions of Linear Models
text:
Scale-Location
Recommended
↑ top
An alternative diagnostic is the Scale–Location plot. This plots the square root of the absolute standardised residuals against the fitted values. Standardised residuals express each residual relative to its expected variability, making residuals easier to compare with one another.
In some cases, this makes changes in residual variability easier to see.
We already calculated these values above using our get_diagnostic_stats() function - we extracted them from the model using the R function rstandard(), then applied the abs() function to get the absolute values, then the sqrt() function to get the square root.
We can now plot the square root of the absolute values of the standardised residuals against our fitted values.

ggplot(
  temp_prec_diagnostics,
  aes(x = fitted, y = sqrt_abs_standardised_residual)
) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  ggtitle("Scale - Location - \nAnnual Mean Temperature vs Total Annual Precipitation") +
  xlab("Fitted precipitation (mm)") +
  ylab("√|Standardised residual|") +
  theme_minimal()

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'









Again, this looks like the equal variance assumption has been met.

title: Part 2: Testing Assumptions of Linear Models
section: Linear relationship with continuous explanatory variables
text:
Linear relationship with continuous explanatory variables
Recommended
↑ top
For linear regression, we also assume that the relationship between the response variable and each continuous explanatory variable is appropriately described as linear.
The Residuals vs Fitted plot can be re-used to assess this assumption. If a linear model is appropriate, there should be no systematic pattern in the residuals, and the smoothed line should remain approximately horizontal around zero. A curved pattern suggests that the relationship has not been adequately described by a straight line.
Let’s look at our plant biomass data again:

ggplot(
  plant_biomass_diagnostics,
  aes(x = fitted, y = residual)
) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  ggtitle("Residuals vs Fitted - \nAge vs Plant biomass") +
  xlab("Fitted biomass (g)") +
  ylab("Residual (g)") +
  theme_minimal()

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'









Here, although the variance is not constant, there is no obvious systematic curvature in the residuals. The linearity assumption therefore appears reasonable.
Let’s deliberately simulate a non-linear relationship, by making our y value a function of \(x^2\), plus some random noise.

curved_data <- tibble(
  x = runif(100, 0, 10),
  y = x^2 + rnorm(100, 0, 5)
)

curved_model <- lm(y ~ x, data = curved_data)

If we plot the residual vs fitted plot, it is clear that there is an issue.

curved_diagnostics <- get_diagnostic_stats(curved_model)

ggplot(curved_diagnostics, aes(x = fitted, y = residual)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  ggtitle("Residuals vs Fitted - \nSimulated curved data") +
  xlab("Fitted") +
  ylab("Residuals") +
  theme_minimal()

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'









The smoothed line here is clearly a curve, suggesting that the relationship is not linear. A simple linear model may therefore not fully describe the relationship between these variables.

Do you think there is a linear relationship between the explanatory variables?

Here, the smoothed line shows some curvature rather than remaining completely horizontal around zero. This suggests that the relationship may not be perfectly linear, although the deviations are relatively modest and are particularly pronounced towards the ends of the range where there are fewer observations.

title: Part 2: Testing Assumptions of Linear Models
text:
Influential observations
Recommended
↑ top
The assumptions we have considered so far apply to the model as a whole. However, individual observations can also have a large influence on the results of a linear model.
An observation has high leverage if it has an unusual value, or combination of values, for the explanatory variables.
An observation with high leverage does not necessarily cause a problem. However, an observation that has both high leverage and a large residual may have a substantial influence on the fitted model.
We need to add two more columns to our diagnostics for our temperature / precipitation regression:

Leverage - a measure of the unusualness of the value of the explanatory variable (or combination of variables).
Cook’s distance - a measure of how much the regression would change if this point was not included

We can extract both of these from the model, using the functions hatvalues() for leverage and cooks.distance() for Cook’s distance.

temp_prec_diagnostics_influ <- temp_prec_diagnostics |>
  mutate(
    leverage = hatvalues(lm_temp_prec),
    cooks_distance = cooks.distance(lm_temp_prec),
  )

title: Part 2: Testing Assumptions of Linear Models
text:
Review
↑ top






NoteSummary




Concepts

Diagnostic information, including fitted values, residuals and standardised residuals, can be extracted directly from a fitted linear model in R.
A Q–Q plot can be used to assess whether residuals are approximately normally distributed; systematic departures from the reference line can indicate departures from normality.
A Residuals vs Fitted plot can be used to assess both constant variance and whether a continuous relationship is appropriately described as linear.
A Scale–Location plot can also be used to assess constant variance. (Recommended)
Leverage and Cook’s distance can be extracted from a fitted model to help identify potentially influential observations. (Recommended)
R can automatically produce the standard diagnostic plots for a fitted linear model using plot().

title: Part 3: Can we break a t-test?
text:
Scenarios
In this part of the practical, you will need one Quarto document:
A standard two-sample t-test assumes that the populations being compared are normally distributed and that their residuals have equal variance, but the t-test is often described as robust to violations of these assumptions. What does this actually mean?
Let’s investigate two sets of hypotheses, in one we will simulate a true difference in means and in the other we will not.
Extension
↑ top
crumbs: 39  Part 3: Can we break a t-test?

title: Part 3: Can we break a t-test?
text:
Scenario 1

Null hypothesis: The mean running speed of orange cats does not differ from the mean running speed of black cats. Population values:
Alternative hypothesis: The mean running speed of orange cats differs from the mean running speed of black cats.
Orange cats: mean speed, 20km/h
Black cats: mean speed, 20km/h



Scenario 2

Null hypothesis: The mean running speed of dogs through a course does not differ depending on whether there is a biscuit at the end of the course.
Alternative hypothesis: The mean running speed of dogs through a course differs depending on whether there is a biscuit at the end of the course.

Population values:

Biscuit absent: mean speed, 20km/hr
Biscuit present: mean speed, 24km/hr

For the cat data, the null hypothesis is true, so the proportion of significant results estimates a Type I error rate.
For the dog data, the alternative hypothesis is true, so the proportion of non-significant results estimates a Type II error rate.
crumbs: 39  Part 3: Can we break a t-test?

title: Part 3: Can we break a t-test?
text:
Helper functions
We are going to perform the same steps lots of times, so we need a function.






ExerciseExercise 1 - Writing a helper function






Extension
Create a new Quarto file, break_t.qmd.






NoteInclude this code



Include this code at the top of your break_t.qmd Quarto file.

library(tidyverse)
library(gt)
library(patchwork)



In your break_t.qmd Quarto file:

Write a function named compare_vectors for which the input is two vectors of measurements. The function should:

Create a data frame with two columns, “group” and “measurement”, where each vector contributes one group. As our groups won’t always be the same size, a good option is to create one data frame per group then combine them with bind_rows().
Create a summary data frame containing the mean and standard deviation of each group
Perform an equal variance t-test comparing the measurements for the two groups.
Fit a linear model to the measurements for the two groups.
Put the residuals from the linear model into the long format data frame.
Plot a histogram showing the distribution of the residuals in each group.
Return a list (see Returning multiple outputs from a function) containing:

df - The data frame
summ_df - The summary data frame
t_test - The t-test result
linear_model - The fitted linear model
distri - the plotted distribution









AnswerAnswer







compare_vectors <- function(vector1, vector2) {
  # Create the data frame
  v1_df <- tibble(
    group = "group_1",
    measurement = vector1
  )
  v2_df <- tibble(
    group = "group_2",
    measurement = vector2
  )
  comp_df <- bind_rows(v1_df, v2_df)

  # Create a summary data frame
  summ_df <- comp_df |>
    group_by(group) |>
    summarise(
      group_mean = mean(measurement),
      group_sd = sd(measurement)
    )

  # Do the t-test
  t_test <- t.test(measurement ~ group,
    data = comp_df,
    var.equal = TRUE
  )

  # Fit the linear model
  linear_model <- lm(measurement ~ group, data = comp_df)

  # Put the residuals from the linear model into the
  # data frame
  comp_df <- comp_df |> mutate(
    residuals = linear_model$residuals
  )

  # Plot a histogram showing the distribution of the
  # residuals in each group.
  distri <- ggplot(comp_df, aes(x = residuals)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 15) +
    facet_wrap(~group) +
    ggtitle("Distribution of residuals") +
    xlab("Residual") +
    ylab("Number of observations") +
    theme_minimal()

  # Put the results into a list
  results <- list(
    df = comp_df,
    summ_df = summ_df,
    t_test = t_test,
    linear_model = linear_model,
    distri = distri
  )
  # Return the list
  return(results)
}









This function will be useful for thoroughly examining a single dataset, however we also want to repeat our analysis on multiple simulated datasets and store only the t-test results.
We can use a shortened version of this function in this case.

compare_vectors_short <- function(vector1, vector2) {
  # Create the data frame
  v1_df <- tibble(
    group = "group_1",
    measurement = vector1
  )
  v2_df <- tibble(
    group = "group_2",
    measurement = vector2
  )
  comp_df <- bind_rows(v1_df, v2_df)

  # Do the t-test
  t_test <- t.test(measurement ~ group, data = comp_df, var.equal = TRUE)

  # Return the t-test p-value
  return(t_test$p.value)
}

We also need an empty data frame in which to store our results.

comparison_df <- tibble()

title: Part 3: Can we break a t-test?
text:
Distributions of p-values
When we repeat a statistical test many times, we can examine the distribution of the p-values it produces.
When the null hypothesis is true and the test is working correctly, p-values should be approximately uniformly distributed between 0 and 1. For example, around 5% should be less than or equal to 0.05, giving the expected 5% type I error rate.
For example, here is a very clean scenario of two fairly big, normally distributed groups with the same mean and variance.

ps <- c()
for (i in seq_len(10000)) {
  group_1 <- rnorm(100, mean = 10, sd = 5)
  group_2 <- rnorm(100, mean = 10, sd = 5)

  t_test <- t.test(group_1, group_2, var.equal = TRUE)
  ps <- c(ps, t_test$p.value)
}
p_df <- tibble(pval = ps)

ggplot(p_df, aes(x = pval)) +
  geom_histogram(boundary = 0, binwidth = 0.05) +
  ggtitle("Distribution of p-values when the null hypothesis is true - Simulated") +
  xlab("p-value") +
  ylab("Number of simulations") +
  theme_minimal()








When the alternative hypothesis is true, we expect more small p-values. The stronger the evidence the test is able to detect, the more strongly the distribution will be concentrated towards zero.
For example, here is a very clean scenario of two fairly big, normally distributed groups with a different mean and the same variance.

ps <- c()
for (i in seq_len(10000)) {
  group_1 <- rnorm(100, mean = 10, sd = 5)
  group_2 <- rnorm(100, mean = 13, sd = 5)

  t_test <- t.test(group_1, group_2, var.equal = TRUE)
  ps <- c(ps, t_test$p.value)
}
p_df <- tibble(pval = ps)

ggplot(p_df, aes(x = pval)) +
  geom_histogram(boundary = 0, binwidth = 0.05) +
  ggtitle("Distribution of p-values when the alternative hypothesis is true - Simulated") +
  xlab("p-value") +
  ylab("Number of simulations") +
  theme_minimal()








Therefore, if we are running many tests we can use p-value distributions to investigate whether a statistical test is behaving as expected, rather than judging it from the result of a single test.

8 - Conclusion
When the groups have both unequal variances and unequal sample sizes, the diagnostic plots show the difference in variance, but may not look dramatically worse than when the sample sizes were equal.
However, the p-values produced when the null hypothesis is true are no longer uniformly distributed. Instead of the approximately flat distribution seen in the previous examples, the p-value distribution is curved, with relatively few very small p-values. The type I error rate is therefore lower than the expected 5%. In this example, the t-test has become too conservative: it rejects the null hypothesis less often than it should.
Importantly, unequal sample sizes and unequal variances interact. Neither caused a major problem on its own in our previous examples, but together they can make the standard t-test unreliable.
This also demonstrates why diagnostic plots should not be treated as a simple pass/fail test: the plots do not necessarily look dramatically different even though the behaviour of the statistical test has changed.

This shows that even with our relatively small sample sizes, the t-test is robust to some violations of its assumptions - at least in these very controlled simulations. However, combinations of violations can have a much greater effect on the behaviour of the test.
We have also demonstrated that the diagnostic plots are useful but they are not definitive - sometimes the test performs well even if they look quite questionable.

title: Part 3: Can we break a t-test?
text:
Review
↑ top






NoteSummary




Concepts

Repeated simulation can be used to investigate how a statistical test behaves under known conditions. (Extension)
When the null hypothesis is true and a statistical test is behaving as expected, p-values should be approximately uniformly distributed between 0 and 1. (Extension)
The proportion of significant simulated results when the null hypothesis is true can be used to estimate the Type I error rate. (Extension)
The proportion of non-significant simulated results when the alternative hypothesis is true can be used to estimate the Type II error rate. (Extension)
Statistical power is the probability of correctly rejecting the null hypothesis when the alternative hypothesis is true. The Type II error rate is therefore (1 - ). (Extension)
A statistical test is robust to a violation of an assumption if it continues to behave reasonably well when that assumption is not met. (Extension)
The t-test can be robust to some violations of normality or equal variance, but its behaviour depends on the particular data and combination of violations. (Extension)
Unequal sample sizes are not themselves a violation of the assumptions of a t-test, but unequal sample sizes combined with unequal variances can cause problems for a standard equal-variance t-test. (Extension)
Diagnostic plots can help identify violations of model assumptions, but should not be treated as simple pass/fail tests. (Extension)

title: Part 4: Generalised Linear Models - Binomial
text:
Binomial response variables
In this part of the practical, you will need two Quarto documents:
As you may have noticed, all of the statistical tests introduced in Practical 4 (except for chi-squared) expect a continuous response variable.
A standard linear model assumes that the response variable is continuous, with observations normally distributed around an expected value. A linear combination of the explanatory variables determines this expected value.
However, not all response variables are continuous or normally distributed. As you learned in the lectures, a generalised linear model (GLM) extends the idea of a linear model to response variables with other distributions.
Core
↑ top
In Part 2: Hypothesis Testing, we treated the presence or absence of a species as our explanatory variable when asking whether mean temperature differed between sites where a species was present and absent. We then used our model to predict mean temperature in the presence of this species in Part 6: Using models to make predictions.
However, we may instead want to ask: does the probability of species presence change with temperature?
In the case of H. tumulorum we would therefore have the following hypotheses:
In this case, detection of H. tumulorum becomes our response variable and minimum temperature becomes our explanatory variable.
Our response variable is binary: at each site H. tumulorum was either detected (1) or not detected (0). We can model this using a binomial distribution, where \(p\) represents the probability of detection. We therefore need our predicted values of \(p\) to lie between 0 and 1.

title: Part 4: Generalised Linear Models - Binomial
section: Why not use a linear model?
text:
Why not use a linear model?
Extension
↑ top
Let’s try just using a linear model. First, we need to load our H. tumulorum dataset. We should also use the as.integer() function to convert our logical (TRUE / FALSE) detected column into a numerical column with 1 for detected and 0 for not detected.
Then we can apply our linear model, with minimum temperature as the explanatory variable and detection of H. tumulorum as the response.

# Load data, convert detected to integers
ht_df <- read_csv("data/ht_df.csv") |>
  mutate(detected_01 = as.integer(detected))

# Apply linear model
lm_binary <- lm(detected_01 ~ min_temp_coldest_month, data = ht_df)

# Display linear model
summary(lm_binary)


Call:
lm(formula = detected_01 ~ min_temp_coldest_month, data = ht_df)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-0.97623 -0.39746  0.08645  0.35050  0.71455 

Coefficients:
                       Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)             0.32815    0.05817   5.641 2.92e-07 ***
min_temp_coldest_month  0.24330    0.04249   5.726 2.07e-07 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.4217 on 74 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.307, Adjusted R-squared:  0.2977 
F-statistic: 32.79 on 1 and 74 DF,  p-value: 2.073e-07


Now let’s try to use this model to predict the presence or absence of H. tumulorum at 0°C.

df_unknown <- tibble(min_temp_coldest_month = 0)

pred <- predict(lm_binary, newdata = df_unknown)
print(pred)

        1 
0.3281477 


Our model predicts a 32.81% probability of detecting H. tumulorum at this temperature. This seems feasible.
Let’s try some more extreme temperatures.






ExerciseExercise 1 - Predictions using a linear model






Extension
If you haven’t already, create a new Quarto file, glms.qmd.

In your glms.qmd Quarto file, use predict() with this model to predict the probability of detecting H. tumulorum when the minimum temperature in the coldest month is:

pred <- predict(lm_binary, newdata = df_unknown)
print(pred)

        1         2 
-2.104826  5.194096 










OK, so H. tumulorum will be present at -21% of sites at -10°C and 519% of sites at 20°C - this is not working.
Let’s plot our real data against our model nevertheless:.

ggplot(
  ht_df,
  aes(x = min_temp_coldest_month, y = detected_01)
) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  ggtitle("H. tumulorum detection and minimum temperature\n- Observed and Fitted") +
  xlab("Minimum temperature of coldest month (°C)") +
  ylab("H. tumulorum detected")

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'









A linear model can predict any numerical value, whereas a probability must always lie between 0 and 1 (0–100%). We therefore need a model that retains the useful linear relationship with our explanatory variable, but converts its predictions onto a scale appropriate for a probability.

title: Part 4: Generalised Linear Models - Binomial
text:
Link functions in binomial GLMs
Core
↑ top
A link function transforms the expected value of the response so that it can be modelled as a linear combination of the explanatory variables.
In a binomial GLM, the logit link function transforms probabilities into log-odds.
\[
\operatorname{logit}(p) = \ln\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)
\]






ExerciseExercise 2 - Write a log-odds function






Core
In your prac6_exercises.qmd Quarto file, write a function to calculate the log-odds from a probability. In R log() is the natural logarithm.
Use your function to calculate the log-odds for a sequence of probabilities from 0 to 1, with increment 0.1 (you can generate this with seq(0, 1, 0.1)). Observe what happens to the log-odds as the probability increases.






AnswerAnswer







# Write the function
calc_log_odds <- function(prob) {
  odds <- prob / (1 - prob)
  log_odds <- log(odds)
  return(log_odds)
}

# Apply the function to the sequence
lo_vec <- c()
for (val in seq(0, 1, 0.1)) {
  lo <- calc_log_odds(val)
  lo_vec <- c(lo_vec, lo)
}
print(lo_vec)

 [1]       -Inf -2.1972246 -1.3862944 -0.8472979 -0.4054651  0.0000000
 [7]  0.4054651  0.8472979  1.3862944  2.1972246        Inf


There is an increase in log-odds as probability increases.








The natural logarithm of the odds (log-odds) can take any value from \(-\infty\) to \(\infty\). We can therefore model the log-odds as a linear combination of our explanatory variables.

title: Part 4: Generalised Linear Models - Binomial
text:
Fitting binomial GLMs in R
If we use a GLM instead of a linear model, it estimates the linear relationship between minimum temperature and presence / absence on the log-odds scale.
We can apply a GLM in R using the glm() function. We use the argument family = binomial to specify that we want to predict a binomial response. Otherwise, the function is applied in the same way as a linear model, but with glm() instead of lm().






ExerciseExercise 3 - Fit a GLM






Core
If you haven’t already, create a new Quarto file, glms.qmd.






NoteInclude this code



Include this code at the top of your glms.qmd Quarto file.

library(tidyverse)
library(gt)



In your glms.qmd Quarto file, use glm() to test whether the probability of detecting H. tumulorum is associated with minimum temperature in the coldest month.
Use:

detected as the response variable
min_temp_coldest_month as the explanatory variable
family = binomial to fit a binomial GLM

Save your model as glm_ht and examine it using summary().






AnswerAnswer







glm_ht <- glm(detected ~ min_temp_coldest_month,
  data = ht_df,
  family = binomial
)
summary(glm_ht)


Call:
glm(formula = detected ~ min_temp_coldest_month, family = binomial, 
    data = ht_df)

Coefficients:
                       Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)             -1.2589     0.4516  -2.787 0.005314 ** 
min_temp_coldest_month   1.6535     0.4268   3.874 0.000107 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 105.31  on 75  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance:  75.69  on 74  degrees of freedom
AIC: 79.69

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 5










We would report these findings as follows:

There was strong evidence that minimum temperature in the coldest month was associated with the probability of detecting H. tumulorum (binomial GLM, \(\beta\) = 1.65, \(z\) = 3.87), \(p\) = 0.0001. The positive coefficient estimate for min_temp_coldest_month indicates that H. tumulorum is more likely to be detected at sites with higher minimum temperatures.

\(\beta\) = 1.65 tells us that for every 1°C increase in minimum temperature, the log-odds of detecting H. tumulorum increase by 1.65.
We can exponentiate this to get the odds ratio:

beta <- glm_ht$coefficients[2]
expo <- exp(beta)
print(expo)

min_temp_coldest_month 
              5.225079 


So, for every 1°C increase in minimum temperature, the odds of detecting H. tumulorum are multiplied by approximately 5.2.
Let’s plot our data and our GLM prediction.
To plot the predicted values we use geom_smooth(), as we did for linear models, but with the arguments method = "glm" and method.args = list(family = binomial).

ggplot(
  ht_df,
  aes(
    x = min_temp_coldest_month,
    y = detected_01
  )
) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "glm",
    method.args = list(family = binomial)
  ) +
  ggtitle("H. tumulorum detection and minimum temperature - Observed and Fitted") +
  xlab("Minimum temperature of coldest month (°C)") +
  ylab("Probability of detection") +
  theme_minimal()

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'









As you can see, the prediction is limited to probabilities between 0 and 1.

title: Part 4: Generalised Linear Models - Binomial
text:
Making predictions






ExerciseExercise 4 - Make predictions using a GLM






Core
In your glms.qmd Quarto file, use your GLM to predict the probability of detecting H. tumulorum at the following temperatures:

0°C
1°C
2°C

By default, predict() returns predictions from this model on the log-odds scale. The argument type = "response" applies the inverse link function and returns predictions on the original response scale — in this case, probabilities.






AnswerAnswer







# Make a data frame of the temperatures for which
# we want to predict probabilities
df_unknown <- tibble(
  min_temp_coldest_month = c(0, 1, 2)
)

# Predict the probability of presence or absence at these
# temperatures
pred <- predict(
  glm_ht,
  newdata = df_unknown,
  type = "response"
)

# Put the results in a data frame
pred_df <- tibble(
  min_temp = c(0, 1, 2),
  predicted_prob = pred
)
gt(pred_df)







min_temp
predicted_prob

0.5973837

0.8857500















So, there is a 22.12% probability of seeing H. tumulorum with a minimum temperature of 0°C, a 59.74% probability at 1°C and an 88.57% probability at 2°C.
Let’s go back to our extreme temperatures, -10°C and 20°C, and do the same thing again.

df_extreme <- tibble(
  min_temp_coldest_month = c(-10, 20)
)

pred <- predict(
  glm_ht,
  newdata = df_extreme,
  type = "response"
)

pred_df <- tibble(
  min_temp = c(-10, 20),
  predicted_prob = pred
)
gt(pred_df)







min_temp
predicted_prob

These values, essentially 0 at -10°C and 1 at 20°C may still be incorrect, but they are at least valid probabilities. Our model describes the relationship supported by the observed data, which has a minimum temperature of -2.29°C and a maximum temperature of 3.49°C. There is no guarantee that the same relationship continues beyond this range. Making predictions outside the observed range is called extrapolation, and these predictions can be highly unreliable.
For example, let’s predict the probability of finding H. tumulorum at 1000°C.

df_extremer <- tibble(
  min_temp_coldest_month = 1000
)

pred <- predict(
  glm_ht,
  newdata = df_extremer,
  type = "response"
)

pred_df <- tibble(
  min_temp = 1000,
  predicted_prob = pred
)
gt(pred_df)







min_temp
predicted_prob

According to our model, we are guaranteed to find H. tumulorum at this temperature.

Using the logit function forces the predicted probability to be between 0 and 1, however it doesn’t guarantee it is correct.

text:
Multiple predictors
Recommended
↑ top
Additional predictors and interactions can be added to GLMs exactly as we added them to linear models in Multiple linear regression.






ExerciseExercise 5 - Fitting a GLM with multiple predictors






Recommended
In your glms.qmd Quarto file, apply a single binomial GLM to assess the following hypotheses, based on the data in data/site_metadata.csv.

Annual mean temperature

Null hypothesis: At the average latitude, the probability of Halictidae being the dominant insect family is not associated with annual mean temperature.
Alternative hypothesis: At the average latitude, the probability of Halictidae being the dominant insect family is associated with annual mean temperature.



Latitude

Null hypothesis: At the average annual mean temperature, the probability of Halictidae being the dominant insect family is not associated with latitude.
Alternative hypothesis: At the average annual mean temperature, the probability of Halictidae being the dominant insect family is associated with latitude.



Interaction

Null hypothesis: The relationship between annual mean temperature and the probability of Halictidae being the dominant insect family does not depend on latitude.
Alternative hypothesis: The relationship between annual mean temperature and the probability of Halictidae being the dominant insect family depends on latitude.

You will need to add a column to site_metadata with 1 if the value of the column dominant_family is Halictidae and 0 otherwise. You will also need to centre your annual_mean_temp and latitude columns around 0 by subtracting the column mean from each value.
Draw a conclusion based on the summary of the fitted model.

site_metadata <- read_csv("data/site_metadata.csv")
site_metadata <- site_metadata |>
  mutate(
    dom_hali = as.integer(dominant_family == "Halictidae"),
    cent_temp = annual_mean_temp - mean(annual_mean_temp),
    cent_lat = latitude - mean(latitude)
  )


glm_hali <- glm(dom_hali ~ cent_lat * cent_temp,
  data = site_metadata,
  family = binomial
)

section: Estimating model parameters using maximum likelihood
text:
Estimating model parameters using maximum likelihood
Extension
↑ top
R uses maximum likelihood to estimate the parameters for the model.
Let’s fit a two-parameter model to some simple data. Seagulls like to steal chips, and are more common near to the sea. Let’s see if there is an association between being nearer to the sea and having your chips stolen.






Figure 40.2: A seagull stealing a chip Source



You’ve been provided with a (imaginary) dataset in data/seagulls.csv showing the distance from the sea of an individual eating chips in metres, and whether or not their chips were stolen.






ExerciseExercise 6 - Fit a binomial GLM






Extension
In your prac6_exercises.qmd Quarto file:

Read the data frame data/seagulls.csv.
Plot a box plot with chips_stolen on the x axis and distance_from_sea on the y axis.
Fit a binomial GLM with chips_stolen as the response variable.
View the GLM output with summary() and draw a brief conclusion.







AnswerAnswer






Read the data frame data/seagulls.csv.

seagulls <- read_csv("data/seagulls.csv")

Plot a box plot with chips_stolen on the x axis and distance_from_sea on the y axis.

ggplot(seagulls, aes(
  x = chips_stolen,
  y = distance_from_sea,
  fill = chips_stolen
)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  ggtitle("Distance from the sea and chip theft - Observed") +
  xlab("Chips stolen") +
  ylab("Distance from sea (m)")








Fit a binomial GLM with chips_stolen as the response variable.
View the GLM output with summary()

seagull_glm <- glm(chips_stolen ~ distance_from_sea,
  data = seagulls,
  family = binomial
)
print(summary(seagull_glm))


Call:
glm(formula = chips_stolen ~ distance_from_sea, family = binomial, 
    data = seagulls)

Coefficients:
                  Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)   
(Intercept)         1.3711     0.6889   1.990   0.0466 * 
distance_from_sea  -0.5219     0.1612  -3.238   0.0012 **
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 61.086  on 49  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 45.130  on 48  degrees of freedom
AIC: 49.13

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 5


Draw a brief conclusion

The estimated coefficient for distance from the sea is -0.522. As distance from the sea increases, the log-odds of having your chips stolen by a seagull therefore decreases (\(p\) = 0.0012). We therefore reject the null hypothesis and conclude that there is evidence of an association between distance from the sea and the probability of having your chips stolen by a seagull.









In this case, R will have estimated both \(\beta_0\) (1.3711) and \(\beta_1\) (-0.5219) using maximum likelihood estimation. This process finds the values of the model parameters that make the observed data most likely.
To understand how this works, let’s fix \(\beta_0\) at 1.3711 and calculate the likelihood of the observed data for a range of possible values of \(\beta_1\), from -1 to +1.
The model we are using is therefore:
\[
\operatorname{logit}(p_{\text{stolen}}) =
1.3711 + \beta_1 \times \text{distance from sea}
\]
We can then try a range of values of \(\beta_1\) and see which value gives us a model with the highest likelihood of our observed data.
For each observation in the data frame, we calculate the probability of the outcome that was actually observed, given its distance from the sea and the value of \(\beta_1\) being tested. We then combine these probabilities to calculate the likelihood of the complete dataset.
For convenience, we use the logarithms of the probabilities. This allows us to add log-probabilities rather than multiplying together many very small probabilities. The value of \(\beta_1\) that gives the highest log-likelihood will also give the highest likelihood.
For each value of \(\beta_1\) we will:

Use the model equation and each observed distance_from_sea value to calculate the log-odds of chips being stolen.
Convert the log-odds to a probability using the inverse logit equation:

\[
p = \frac{e^{\text{log-odds}}}{1 + e^{\text{log-odds}}}
\]

For rows where chips_stolen is TRUE, add the log of the probability of the chips being stolen, \(\log(p)\), to the total log-likelihood.
For rows where chips_stolen is FALSE, add the log of the probability of the chips not being stolen, \(\log(1-p)\), to the total log-likelihood.
Select the value of \(\beta_1\) that gives the highest log-likelihood.


possible_beta1s <- seq(-1, 1, by = 0.01)
log_likelihoods <- c()
b0 <- coef(seagull_glm)["(Intercept)"]

for (beta in possible_beta1s) {
  # Calculate log-odds using this possible coefficient
  log_odds <- b0 + beta * pull(seagulls, distance_from_sea)

  # Convert log-odds to probability
  probs <- exp(log_odds) / (1 + exp(log_odds))

  # Filter the data frame to only rows where chips
  # were stolen and add a row with the probability
  # of this happening under the model
  chips_stolen <- seagulls |>
    mutate(
      probs = probs,
      log_probs = log(probs)
    ) |>
    filter(chips_stolen == TRUE)

  # Filter the data frame to only rows where chips
  # were not stolen and add a row with the probability
  # of this happening under the model
  chips_not_stolen <- seagulls |>
    mutate(
      probs = (1 - probs),
      log_probs = log(probs)
    ) |>
    filter(chips_stolen == FALSE)

  # Calculate the log likelihood of the observed data
  tot_stolen <- chips_stolen |>
    pull(log_probs) |>
    sum()
  tot_not <- chips_not_stolen |>
    pull(log_probs) |>
    sum()
  log_likelihood <- tot_stolen + tot_not

  # Add this to our vector of log likelihoods
  log_likelihoods <- c(log_likelihoods, log_likelihood)
}

# Put the results into a data frame
df_likelihood <- tibble(
  beta = possible_beta1s,
  log_likelihood = log_likelihoods
)
gt(head(df_likelihood))

We can also plot our estimates.

Our maximum likelihood estimate of \(\beta_1\) is -0.52, very similar to the estimate in the model of -0.5219.
Note that maximising the likelihood and maximising the log-likelihood will identify the same value of \(\beta_1\). Log-likelihood is generally more convenient to work with because it allows products of many small probabilities to be replaced by sums of their logarithms, avoiding extremely small numbers.

b0 <- coef(seagull_glm)["(Intercept)"]

for (beta in possible_beta1s) {
  # Calculate log-odds using this possible coefficient
  log_odds <- b0 + beta * pull(seagulls, distance_from_sea)

  # Convert log-odds to probability
  probs <- exp(log_odds) / (1 + exp(log_odds))

  # Filter the data frame to only rows where chips
  # were stolen and add a row with the probability
  # of this happening under the model

  chips_stolen <- seagulls |>
    mutate(probs = probs) |>
    filter(chips_stolen == TRUE)

  # Filter the data frame to only rows where chips
  # were not stolen and add a row with the probability
  # of this happening under the model
  chips_not_stolen <- seagulls |>
    mutate(probs = (1 - probs)) |>
    filter(chips_stolen == FALSE)

  # Calculate the likelihood of the observed data
  tot_stolen <- chips_stolen |>
    pull(probs) |>
    prod()
  tot_not <- chips_not_stolen |>
    pull(probs) |>
    prod()

  likelihood <- tot_stolen * tot_not

  likelihoods <- c(likelihoods, likelihood)

title: Part 4: Generalised Linear Models - Binomial
text:
Parameter space
Extension
We are looking for the most likely value of a single parameter, so we can test a suitable range of possible values. However, we have used R’s estimate for \(\beta_0\). Without this, we would need to find the combination of \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) that gives the highest likelihood of observing our data, requiring us to search across a two-dimensional parameter space.
With additional parameters, the number of dimensions increases and the search becomes increasingly complex.
In practice, glm() uses an optimisation algorithm to find the combination of parameter values that maximises the likelihood, rather than testing every possible combination.

title: Part 4: Generalised Linear Models - Binomial
text:
Assumptions
Core
↑ top
Some assumptions are common to all GLMs and some are specific depending on the type of response variable.
For all GLMs we assume:

Independence of observations - this is mostly a study-design/data-structure issue.
Linearity on the link scale - GLMs assume that the linear predictor is linear with respect to the explanatory variables

For binomial GLMs we additionally assume that the response is compatible with a binomial distribution (see The binomial distribution).
crumbs: 40  Part 4: Generalised Linear Models - Binomial

title: Part 4: Generalised Linear Models - Binomial
text:
Review
↑ top






NoteSummary




Concepts

A binomial GLM can be fitted in R using glm() with family = binomial.
The response variable for a binomial GLM can be represented as 0 and 1, for example absence and presence.
The coefficients returned by a binomial GLM are on the log-odds scale; exponentiating a coefficient gives an odds ratio.
A fitted binomial GLM can be plotted using geom_smooth() with method = "glm" and method.args = list(family = binomial).
By default, predict() returns predictions from a binomial GLM on the log-odds scale; type = "response" returns predicted probabilities.
Predictions from a binomial GLM will remain between 0 and 1, but predictions made outside the observed range of the explanatory variables are extrapolations and may still be unreliable.
Multiple explanatory variables and interactions can be included in a binomial GLM using the same formula syntax as a linear model. (Recommended)
glm() estimates model coefficients using maximum likelihood. (Extension)
Maximum likelihood estimation finds the model parameter values under which the observed data are most likely. (Extension)
GLMs use maximum likelihood to estimate their coefficients. (Extension)
Log-likelihood is generally more convenient than likelihood because products of many small probabilities become sums of their logarithms. (Extension)
With multiple model parameters, estimation involves finding the combination of parameter values that maximises the likelihood across a multidimensional parameter space. (Extension)



Functions



Function
What it does




glm()
Fits a generalised linear model.

title: Part 5: Generalised Linear Models - Poisson
text:
Poisson GLMs
In this part of the practical, you will need one Quarto document:
Core
↑ top
A binomial GLM is appropriate when the response variable represents one of two possible outcomes. A Poisson GLM can be used to model count data when a Poisson distribution (Comparing real, simulated and expected data - discrete distributions) is appropriate. In a Poisson GLM, we model how \(\lambda\), the expected count, changes with our explanatory variables.
As with the binomial GLM, the model coefficients are estimated using maximum likelihood. The likelihood is now calculated using the Poisson rather than the binomial distribution, but the principle is the same: R finds the combination of parameter values that makes the observed data most likely.
Note: Although Poisson GLMs are used for count data, not every count response is adequately described by a Poisson model. We will discuss this below in Assumptions of Poisson GLMs.
crumbs: 41  Part 5: Generalised Linear Models - Poisson

title: Part 5: Generalised Linear Models - Poisson
text:
Log-link function
Core
↑ top
By default, a Poisson GLM uses a log link function, which models the logarithm of the expected count, \(\lambda\), as a linear function of the explanatory variables, with \(\beta_0\) as the intercept and \(\beta_1\) as the coefficient for the explanatory variable.
\[
\log(\lambda) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x
\] The inverse of this is:
\[
\lambda = e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x}
\] This transformation ensures that the expected count is always positive, even though the linear predictor can take any value.
crumbs: 41  Part 5: Generalised Linear Models - Poisson

title: Part 5: Generalised Linear Models - Poisson
text:
Fitting Poisson GLMs in R
Core
↑ top
Let’s use a Poisson GLM to test the following hypotheses:

Null hypothesis: There is no association between the number of non-Apidae insect species and the expected number of Apidae species found at a site.
Alternative hypothesis: There is an association between the number of non-Apidae insect species and the expected number of Apidae species found at a site.

First we need to read our data, and add a column containing the number of non-Apidae species at each site.

site_metadata <- read_csv("data/site_metadata.csv")
site_metadata <- site_metadata |>
  mutate(n_non_apidae = n_unique - n_apidae)

Now we are ready to fit the GLM. This is very similar to fitting a binomial GLM, except we use the argument family = poisson for the Poisson model.






ExerciseExercise 1 - Fitting a Poisson GLM






Core
In your glms.qmd Quarto file, use a GLM to test whether the number of Apidae species at a site is associated with the number of non-Apidae insect species.
Use:

n_apidae as the response variable
n_non_apidae as the explanatory variable
family = poisson to fit a Poisson GLM

Store your model in a variable, glm_apidae, and examine it using summary().






AnswerAnswer







glm_apidae <- glm(
  n_apidae ~ n_non_apidae,
  family = poisson,
  data = site_metadata
)

summary(glm_apidae)


Call:
glm(formula = n_apidae ~ n_non_apidae, family = poisson, data = site_metadata)

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)  2.100522   0.080032  26.246  < 2e-16 ***
n_non_apidae 0.020057   0.002673   7.503 6.23e-14 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for poisson family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 180.30  on 75  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 123.59  on 74  degrees of freedom
AIC: 455.22

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4










The estimated coefficient for the number of non-Apidae species is 0.02. This coefficient is positive, indicating that sites with more non-Apidae insect species are expected to also contain more Apidae species.
The Poisson GLM uses a log link, so the coefficients represent changes in the log of the expected count. We can exponentiate the coefficient to make it easier to interpret:

print(exp(coef(glm_apidae)["n_non_apidae"]))

n_non_apidae 
    1.020259 


For each additional non-Apidae species, the expected number of Apidae species is therefore multiplied by 1.02, corresponding to an increase of approximately 2%.
The p-value associated with this coefficient is 6.23e-14. We therefore reject the null hypothesis and conclude that there is evidence of an association between the number of non-Apidae insect species and the expected number of Apidae species found at a site.
Let’s plot the data and our model, as usual. geom_smooth() transforms the fitted values back from the log scale to the response scale, so the fitted line shows the expected number of Apidae species.

ggplot(
  site_metadata,
  aes(x = n_non_apidae, y = n_apidae)
) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "glm",
    method.args = list(family = poisson)
  ) +
  ggtitle("Apidae and non-Apidae species richness - Observed and Fitted") +
  xlab("Number of non-Apidae species") +
  ylab("Number of Apidae species") +
  theme_minimal()

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

Prediction

Remember to use type = "response" to return the prediction as an expected count rather than on the log scale.
