title: Part 5: Generalised Linear Models - Poisson
text:
Assumptions of Poisson GLMs
Core
↑ top
As well as the assumptions we discussed in Assumptions, for Poisson GLMs, we additionally assume that:

The response is compatible with a Poisson distribution (see Part 3: Using simulation to understand data).
The variance of the response, conditional on the explanatory variables, is equal to its mean.

The relationship between the variance of the response and the mean can be calculated from our model.
Two statistics are commonly used:

Pearson dispersion
\[
\hat{\phi}_{P} =
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} r_{P,i}^{2}}
{n-p}
\]
where \(r_{P,i}\) is the Pearson residual for observation \(i\), \(n\) is the number of observations and \(p\) is the number of model parameters.
We can extract the residuals directly from the fitted GLM using the residuals() function with the argument type = "pearson".

resid <- residuals(glm_apidae, type = "pearson")

The sum of the squares of these values is \({\sum_{i=1}^{n} r_{P,i}^{2}}\).
\((n - p)\) is the residual degrees of freedom, which we can also access from the model, as e.g. glm_apidae$df.residual.






ExerciseExercise 3 - Calculating Pearson dispersion






Core
In your glms.qmd Quarto file, write a function named pearson_dispersion to calculate the Pearson dispersion of a GLM, where the input is the fitted GLM and the output is the Pearson dispersion. Apply it to your fitted Apidae GLM.






AnswerAnswer







pearson_dispersion <- function(fitted_glm) {
  resid <- residuals(fitted_glm, type = "pearson")
  ss <- sum(resid^2)
  df <- fitted_glm$df.residual
  disp <- ss / df
  return(disp)
}
p_disp_apidae <- pearson_dispersion(glm_apidae)
print(p_disp_apidae)

[1] 1.347039












Deviance dispersion
\[
\hat{\phi}_{D} =
\frac{D}
{n-p}
\]
where \(D\) is the residual deviance, \(n\) is the number of observations and \(p\) is the number of model parameters.






Figure 41.1: Deviance Source



The residual deviance is a measure of how much mismatch remains between the observed data and the fitted GLM. The deviance dispersion is the residual deviance divided by the residual degrees of freedom.
It’s based on likelihood, comparing the fitted model with a hypothetical saturated model — a model with enough parameters to fit the observations perfectly. We will come back to this later when we compare models.
We can access the residual deviance using e.g. glm_apidae$deviance.
As we know, \(n - p\) is the residual degrees of freedom, which we can access from the model as e.g. glm_apidae$df.residual.






ExerciseExercise 4 - Calculating deviance dispersion






Core
In your glms.qmd Quarto file, write a function named deviance_dispersion to calculate the deviance dispersion of a GLM, where the input is the fitted GLM and the output is the deviance dispersion. Apply it to your fitted Apidae GLM.






AnswerAnswer







deviance_dispersion <- function(fitted_glm) {
  devi <- fitted_glm$deviance
  df <- fitted_glm$df.residual
  disp <- devi / df
  return(disp)
}
d_disp_apidae <- deviance_dispersion(glm_apidae)
print(d_disp_apidae)

[1] 1.67018










In general, we want both of these statistics to be close to 1. Values substantially greater than 1 can indicate overdispersion - the variance in the data is greater than the model expects. Values substantially less than 1 can indicate underdispersion - the variance in the data is less than the model expects.
Let’s fit another GLM to demonstrate how this can impact our model.






ExerciseExercise 5 - Fitting a Poisson GLM and checking dispersion






Core

Alternative hypothesis: There is an association between the number of unique flower species at a site and the number of unique insect species.

Using your functions from the previous exercises, calculate the Pearson dispersion and deviance dispersion of the model. Do you think the data is overdispersed?

print(summary(glm_unique_spp))

    data = site_metadata)

(Intercept)      3.295700   0.042666  77.244   <2e-16 ***
n_unique_flowers 0.014282   0.001453   9.827   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for poisson family taken to be 1)

Calculate the Pearson dispersion.

Visualising overdispersion
Extension
↑ top
Our dispersion statistics suggest that the observed insect counts vary more than we would expect under our fitted Poisson model. We can use simulation to visualise what this means.
The fitted values from our model are the expected counts (\(\lambda\)) for each site. If the Poisson model is appropriate, we can use these values to simulate the sort of counts we would expect to observe under the fitted model.






ExerciseExercise 6 - Visualising overdispersion






Extension
In your glms.qmd Quarto file:

Use fitted() to extract the expected insect count for each site from your fitted Poisson GLM.
Use rpois() to simulate one new insect count for each site (so set n to be the number of sites), using the fitted values as the values of \(\lambda\).
Create a data frame containing:

the fitted count for each site
the observed insect count
the simulated insect count

Calculate the difference between the fitted count and the observed count and add this as a column, observed_difference.
Calculate the difference between the fitted count and the simulated count and add this as a column, simulated_difference.
Plot these differences as a box plot.

What does this tell you about the variation in the observed data compared with the variation expected under the fitted Poisson model?






AnswerAnswer






Use fitted() to extract the expected insect count for each site from your fitted Poisson GLM.

# Extract expected counts from the fitted model
fitted_counts <- fitted(glm_unique_spp)

Use rpois() to simulate one new insect count for each site, using the fitted values as the values of \(\lambda\).

simulated_counts <- rpois(
  n = length(fitted_counts),
  lambda = fitted_counts
)

Create a data frame containing: the fitted count for each site, the observed insect count, the simulated insect count

dispersion_df <- tibble(
  fitted = fitted_counts,
  observed = site_metadata$n_unique,
  simulated = simulated_counts
)

Calculate the difference between the fitted count and the observed count and add this as a column, observed_difference.
Calculate the difference between the fitted count and the simulated count and add this as a column, simulated_difference.

dispersion_df <- dispersion_df |>
  mutate(
    observed_difference = observed - fitted,
    simulated_difference = simulated - fitted
  )

Plot these differences as a box plot.

# Convert to long format for plotting
dispersion_long <- dispersion_df |>
  select(observed_difference, simulated_difference) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "data",
    values_to = "difference"
  )

# Plot
ggplot(dispersion_long, aes(x = data, y = difference, fill = data)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  ggtitle("Variation around fitted insect species richness") +
  xlab("Data") +
  ylab("Difference from fitted count") +
  theme_minimal()








Clearly, our data are more dispersed than the model predicts.










Accounting for overdispersion
One way to account for overdispersion is to use a quasi-Poisson model. A standard Poisson model assumes:
\[
\operatorname{Var}(Y) = \mu
\]
A quasi-Poisson model introduces an additional dispersion parameter, \(\phi\):
\[
\operatorname{Var}(Y) = \phi\mu
\]
When \(\phi > 1\), this allows the variance to be greater than the mean.






Figure 41.2: Quasi-modo Source



In R, we can fit this model by replacing family = poisson with family = quasipoisson.

glm_unique_spp_quasi <- glm(
  n_unique ~ n_unique_flowers,
  family = quasipoisson,
  data = site_metadata
)

summary(glm_unique_spp_quasi)

    data = site_metadata)

Residual deviance: 432.37  on 74  degrees of freedom

ExerciseExercise 7 - Examining quasi-Poisson output






Extension
Compare the output from the Poisson and quasi-Poisson models.

What has happened to the coefficient estimates?
What has happened to their standard errors?
What has happened to the p-value for n_unique_flowers?
Has accounting for overdispersion changed your conclusion about the association between flower and insect species richness?







AnswerAnswer







The coefficient estimates are identical, but their standard errors are larger in the quasi-Poisson model. The quasi-Poisson model accounts for the additional variation in the data, and therefore gives us less certainty about the estimated coefficients.
The p-value for n_unique_flowers has increased from <2 × 10-16 to 6.5 × 10-5, although there is still strong evidence of an association between flower and insect species richness.

This does not change our conclusion, but accounting for the overdispersion gives us a more appropriate estimate of the uncertainty around the coefficients.

Review
↑ top






NoteSummary




Concepts

A Poisson GLM can be fitted in R using glm() with family = poisson.
Poisson GLM coefficients are on the log scale; exponentiating a coefficient gives the factor by which the expected count changes for a one-unit increase in the explanatory variable.
predict() with type = "response" can be used to obtain predicted expected counts on the original count scale.
Pearson dispersion can be calculated from the Pearson residuals and residual degrees of freedom of a fitted GLM.
Deviance dispersion can be calculated from the residual deviance and residual degrees of freedom of a fitted GLM.
Dispersion values can be used to assess whether the observed variation is consistent with that expected under a fitted Poisson model.
Expected counts can be extracted from a fitted Poisson GLM and used to simulate new Poisson-distributed observations, allowing the observed variation to be compared with variation expected under the model. (Extension)
If the data are overdispersed, a quasi-Poisson GLM can be fitted using family = quasipoisson. (Extension)

title: Part 6: Choosing a model
text:
Choosing a model
In this part of the practical, you will need one Quarto document:
Core
↑ top
When we fit a model, we generally aim for the simplest model that adequately fits the data. We can therefore simplify a model by removing explanatory variables, provided that doing so does not significantly worsen the fit of the model. The simplest model which adequately fits the data is known as the minimal model.
The approaches we use for model comparison apply to both linear models and to both binomial and Poisson GLMs, although the specific statistical test used to compare nested models differs between linear models and GLMs.
For linear models, the residual sum of squares (RSS) measures the discrepancy between the observed values and those predicted by the model. For GLMs, the equivalent role is played by deviance (see Assumptions of Poisson GLMs) - a measure of how much mismatch remains between the observed data and the fitted GLM - or, in other words, of how well the model fits the data. In both cases, simplifying a model will generally worsen its fit, and we can test whether this worsening is sufficiently large to justify retaining the more complex model.

title: Part 6: Choosing a model
text:
Septin dataset
Core
↑ top
We will use a dataset based on this article, published in Nature Communications in 2024. These authors developed a tool to determine the spatial distribution of components inside cells using 3D image analysis. This is based on a measure, \(P_n\), of how polar the distribution of a protein is within a cell.

low \(P_n\) → protein distributed relatively symmetrically → less polar
high \(P_n\) → protein concentrated asymmetrically toward one part of the cell → more polar.

Using their tool, they characterised the distribution of 6 members of a family of proteins called Septins, which are involved in cellular compartmentalisation, in haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) from young mice (aged 10–18 weeks) and aged mice (aged 80+ weeks). They found that most Septins had a lower \(P_n\) in aged HSCs, indicating a less polar distribution, and that the organisation of the Septin network was altered with age. This is shown in their Figure 3B.
The data is in your data/septin.csv folder.
We will use the Septin dataset to determine if the \(P_n\) of the six Septin proteins can be used to predict if an HSC is young or old, and to explore the methods of establishing a minimal model.

title: Part 6: Choosing a model
section: Nested models and backwards stepwise elimination
text:
Nested models and backwards stepwise elimination
Core
↑ top
One model is nested within another if the simpler model can be obtained just by removing one or more terms from the more complex model.
For example, in the following example model 1 is nested within model 2.

model_1 <- lm(y ~ temperature, data = ...)
model_2 <- lm(y ~ temperature + rainfall, data = ...)

Similarly, in the following case, model 1 is nested within model 2, because model 2 expanded to y ~ temperature + rainfall + temperature:rainfall, where temperature:rainfall is the interaction.

model_1 <- lm(y ~ temperature + rainfall, data = ...)
model_2 <- lm(y ~ temperature * rainfall, data = ...)

We can manually remove elements from a nested model and see how the model is affected.
There are various options to choose which element to remove, including:

Sequentially removing the element with the highest p-value - the element with the least significant effect on the model fit.
Removing the element whose removal results in the lowest AIC - a statistic which specifically balances how well the model fits with the complexity of the model.

Let’s fit a GLM to the Septin dataset with Is_Old as the binary response variable and all six septin levels as continuous explanatory variables. We will consider only additive effects at this stage, not interactions.
Please create a new Quarto file, septin.qmd.






NoteInclude this code



Include this code at the top of your septin.qmd Quarto file.

library(tidyverse)
library(gt)

# Read the file
septin <- read_csv("data/septin.csv")

# Fit the GLM
model_1 <- glm(Is_Old ~ Septin1 + Septin2 + Septin6 + Septin7 + Septin9 + Septin11, septin, family = binomial)

# Summarise

title: Part 6: Choosing a model
text:
Likelihood-Ratio tests
Core
↑ top
As we removed explanatory variables from our model, the residual deviance increased. However, this does not tell us whether the increase in deviance is large enough to indicate that removing a variable has significantly worsened the fit of the model.
For nested GLMs, we can test this using a likelihood-ratio test (LRT). The null hypothesis is that the simpler model fits the data adequately compared with the more complex model. A significant result therefore indicates that removing the variable has significantly worsened the fit of the model. The test is based on the ratio of the likelihood of our observed data given the two different models.
For our nested GLMs, the difference in residual deviance between two adjacent points is identical to the likelihood-ratio test statistic.
The test statistic for a likelihood ratio test is:
\[
LR = 2\left[\log(L_{\text{full}}) - \log(L_{\text{reduced}})\right]
\] We can measure the log-likelihood of a fitted model using the R function logLik().
The test statistics for likelihood-ratio tests are approximately chi-squared distributed, with degrees of freedom as the difference between the residual degrees of freedom for the two models.
\[
df_{\mathrm{LR}} = df_{\mathrm{reduced}} - df_{\mathrm{full}}
\]






ExerciseExercise 2 - Likelihood-ratio test






Core
In your septin.qmd Quarto file:

Calculate the test statistic for the likelihood ratio test comparing your model_1 and model_2 from the previous exercise.
Find the degrees of freedom for this likelihood ratio test.
Using the cumulative probability function for the chi-squared distribution, pchisq(), calculate the probability that a variable with a chi-squared distribution with these degrees of freedom would be greater than or equal to your calculated value of the test statistic.







AnswerAnswer






Calculate the test statistic for the likelihood ratio test comparing your model_1 and model_2 from the previous exercise.

log_lik_model_1 <- logLik(model_1)
log_lik_model_2 <- logLik(model_2)
test_statistic <- 2 * (log_lik_model_1 - log_lik_model_2)
print(test_statistic)

'log Lik.' 0.3688633 (df=7)


Find the degrees of freedom for this likelihood ratio test.

df1 <- model_1$df.residual
df2 <- model_2$df.residual
df_diff <- df2 - df1
print(df_diff)

[1] 1


Using the cumulative probability function for the chi-squared distribution, pchisq() with the argument lower.tail = FALSE calculate the probability that a variable with a chi-squared distribution with these degrees of freedom would be greater than or equal to than your calculated value of the test statistic.

prob <- pchisq(test_statistic, df = df_diff, lower.tail = FALSE)
print(prob)

'log Lik.' 0.5436245 (df=7)










You should see a non-significant p-value - so removing Septin 11 has not made the model significantly worse.
The test statistic for a likelihood ratio test comparing two models is identical to the difference in deviance between those two models (for a GLM).

print(model_2$deviance - model_1$deviance)

[1] 0.3688633

      breaks = df_septin$degrees_of_freedom,
      name = "Model",
      labels = paste0("Model ", seq(1, 7))
    )

  ggtitle("Residual deviance of nested Septin models") +
  xlab("Residual degrees of freedom") +
  ylab("Residual deviance") +
  theme_minimal()














ExerciseExercise 3 - Find the minimal model






Core
Based on the plot above, which model is our minimal model?






AnswerAnswer






The change between model 4 and model 5 is the first significant change - this is where we removed Septin 6. This means our minimal model is model 4, as removing Septin 6 made the model significantly worse.








For a linear model, the process above is very similar. As for the GLM, we sequentially remove predictors from the model.
Instead of deviance, we use the residual sum of squares (RSS) for each model, sum(residuals(model)^2) to measure model fit. Conveniently but confusingly, you can also use the deviance(model) function in R to get this value from a fitted linear model.
Instead of a likelihood ratio test, we calculate the test statistic F as follows:
\[
F =
\frac{
(RSS_{\mathrm{reduced}} - RSS_{\mathrm{full}}) /
(df_{\mathrm{reduced}} - df_{\mathrm{full}})
}{
RSS_{\mathrm{full}} / df_{\mathrm{full}}
}
\] This statistic follows approximately an F-distribution, so we find the p-value using the function pf(). The degrees of freedom for the F-distribution are as follows:
\[
df_1 = df_{\mathrm{reduced}} - df_{\mathrm{full}}
\]
\[
df_2 = df_{\mathrm{full}}
\]

Removing elements by AIC
Extension
↑ top
Now let’s try finding a minimal model using the AIC (Akaike Information Criterion) rather than p-value to choose which explanatory variables to remove.
The AIC for a model is calculated based on its log likelihood and \(k\), the number of parameters in the model. It is implemented in the R function AIC().
\[
AIC = -2\log(L) + 2k
\] We can calculate the AIC of a model directly:

aic_septin_m1 <- AIC(model_1)
print(aic_septin_m1)

[1] 960.9955


This just tells us the AIC of the model, not the contribution of each variable. If we want to know how the AIC would change if we removed each variable in turn, we can use the function drop1().

aic_drop1 <- drop1(model_1)
print(aic_drop1)

In the following exercise, we will use AIC for model selection with a linear model, whereas earlier we used likelihood-ratio tests and p-values with a GLM. Both approaches can be used for model selection with either linear models or GLMs, although the statistical test used to compare nested models differs between the two types of model.

title: Part 6: Choosing a model
text:
Review
↑ top






NoteSummary




Concepts

A complex model can be simplified by fitting a series of nested models, each with one or more terms removed.
For fitted GLMs, residual deviance can be extracted and compared between models to see how model fit changes as terms are removed.
Two nested GLMs can be compared using a likelihood-ratio test to test whether removing a term significantly worsens model fit.
For nested GLMs, the likelihood-ratio test statistic can be calculated either from the models’ log-likelihoods or from the difference in their residual deviances.
For linear models, nested models can be compared in a similar way using their residual sums of squares and an F-test.
AIC can also be used to compare models; drop1() can be used to examine how removing each individual term would change the AIC. (Extension)
Backwards stepwise selection can be automated in R using step() with direction = "backward". (Extension)

title: Part 7: Power Analysis

Power Analysis
In this part of the practical, you will need one Quarto document:
Extension
↑ top
Before collecting data, we need to consider whether our experiment will have enough observations to detect an effect if one really exists. The statistical power of a hypothesis test is the probability that it will correctly reject the null hypothesis when a real effect of a specified size exists.
It is affected by:
We therefore need to decide:
Power analysis functions all operate under the assumption that the data you will collect will meet all of the assumptions of your chosen statistical test perfectly.
Power analysis should be carried out early, before we perform our data collection. We are learning about it late in the practical not because you do it last, but because it’s helpful to understand the various hypothesis tests first.
For simple standard tests, R provides analytical power functions. For more complicated models, power can be estimated by simulation.

title: Part 7: Power Analysis
text:
T-test power analysis
Extension
↑ top
Let’s say that we are designing a study to determine if people diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma differ in age from people diagnosed with lung squamous cell carcinoma.
We have identified data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) to use as test data to help us design our new study. TCGA is a real cancer genomics research project which collected and analysed thousands of matched pairs of tumour and normal tissue samples from the same individuals, across 33 types of cancer. The samples were compared in terms of their genome, transcriptome, epigenome and proteome.






Figure 43.1: The Cancer Genome Atlas Source



For the purpose of designing our study, we only want to look at data showing the age of participants diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma and lung squamous cell carcinoma.
You have been provided with a CSV file with the following columns:

Patient_ID: A unique ID for each patient.
Cancer_Type: The type of cancer they were diagnosed with.
Cancer_category: A broader category of where in the body their cancer was diagnosed.
N_Severe_Mutations: Total number of severe mutations in any gene identified in this individual.
N_Severe_Driver_Mutations: Total number of severe mutations in cancer driver genes identified in this individual.
Age: Age in years.
Sex: Sex, male or female.
Tumour_Stage: Stage of the tumour at the time of the study.
Genetic_Ancestry: broad categorisation of genetic ancestry.

First, let’s read the data frame and filter to include only Lung_Adenocarcinoma and Lung_Squamous_Cell_Carcinoma.

by_indiv <- read_csv("data/by_individual.csv")
lungs <- by_indiv |>
  filter(Cancer_Type %in% c("Lung_Adenocarcinoma", "Lung_Squamous_Cell_Carcinoma"))

Before using these data to estimate a plausible effect size for our new study, we should first establish whether they provide evidence of a difference in age between the two cancer types.

ttest_lungs <- t.test(Age ~ Cancer_Type, lungs, var.equal = TRUE)
print(ttest_lungs)


    Two Sample t-test

data:  Age by Cancer_Type
t = -3.3708, df = 931, p-value = 0.0007803
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group Lung_Adenocarcinoma and group Lung_Squamous_Cell_Carcinoma is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -3.2796537 -0.8660109

         mean in group Lung_Adenocarcinoma 
                                  65.20619 
mean in group Lung_Squamous_Cell_Carcinoma 
                                  67.27902 


The difference is highly significant, with a p-value of 7.80e-04.
We can calculate the standardised effect size, Cohen’s d, from the data.

cd <- cohens_d(
  Age ~ Cancer_Type,
  data = lungs,
  pooled_sd = TRUE
)
print(cd)

Cohen's d |         95% CI
--------------------------
-0.22     | [-0.35, -0.09]

- Estimated using pooled SD.


Our estimated standardised effect size is -0.22.
Based on our table above, this is a small effect.
Now we have this value, we have an idea about what might be a reasonable effect size to see in our own study. We can then calculate the number of participants we would need to have an 80% probability of detecting an effect of this size. We need to use the absolute value of Cohen’s d.

abs_cd <- abs(cd$Cohens_d)
power_test <- pwr.t.test(
  d = abs_cd,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  power = 0.8,
  type = "two.sample"
)
print(power_test)

              d = 0.2208845
      sig.level = 0.05

    alternative = two.sided

NOTE: n is number in *each* group


To have 80% power to detect an effect of this size at a significance level of 0.05, we would need at least 323 individuals in each group.

title: Part 7: Power Analysis
text:
Anova power analysis
Power analysis for ANOVA follows a very similar process to for a t-test.
The differences are:

Instead of Cohen’s D, we calculate Cohen’s f using the function cohens_f(). This function runs directly on the fitted ANOVA rather than on the data, so we would do e.g. cf <- cohens_f(anova). We can retrieve the value as e.g. cf$Cohens_f (note the capital C).
The power analysis is performed using the function pwr.anova.test(), with four arguments:

f - Cohen’s f
sig.level - the desired significance level
power - the desired power
k - the number of groups in the ANOVA

title: Part 7: Power Analysis
text:
Simulation-based power analysis
Extension
↑ top
For more complicated statistical models, there may not be a simple analytical function for calculating power. Instead, we can estimate power using simulation. We repeatedly simulate datasets containing an effect of a specified size, analyse each simulated dataset using our planned statistical test or model, and record whether the effect is detected. The proportion of simulated experiments in which the effect is detected provides an estimate of the power of the proposed study. By repeating this process for different sample sizes, we can estimate the sample size required to achieve our desired power.
Simulation-based power analysis is particularly useful for more complicated models, including GLMs, where power may depend on several features of the proposed experiment.
Let’s say we’re planning an experiment to determine if toast will land butter-side-down when dropped. We have two groups of participants, those who consider themselves to be lucky and those who consider themselves to be unlucky. We would consider a difference of 20 percentage points in the probability of the toast landing butter-side-down between these groups to be an effect worth detecting.






Figure 43.2: A disaster Source



For our power analysis, we will assume that toast dropped by lucky participants has a 40% probability of landing butter-side-down, compared with 60% for unlucky participants.
We can then determine how many people we would need to recruit to each group using simulation.
Let’s simulate group sizes of between 5 and 300, with an interval of 20.

For each group size, we will run 1000 simulations, in which we generate two random binomial datasets, one with a probability of 0.4 (lucky) of the toast landing butter-side-down and one with a probability of 0.6 (unlucky).
We can then compare these groups using a GLM with the model toast_bsd ~ luck, where toast_bsd is 1 when the toast landed butter-side-down and 0 when it landed butter-side-up, and luck is 1 for lucky and 0 for unlucky.
We can extract our p-value from the model using summary(model)$coefficients[2, 4] and determine if this is less than our significance threshold of 0.05.
The smallest group size for which the estimated power reaches at least 80% is our estimated required sample size.


# Vector to store the percentages for all groups sizes
perc_vec <- c()

# Try each group size from 5 to 300 with interval 20
for (group_size in seq(5, 300, 20)) {
  # Vector to store the results for this group size
  sig_vec <- c()
  # Simulate 1000 times
  for (j in seq_len(1000)) {
    # Lucky with 0.4 BSD probability
    lucky <- rbinom(group_size, 1, prob = 0.4)
    # Unlucky with 0.6 BSD probability
    unlucky <- rbinom(group_size, 1, prob = 0.6)
    # Put each into a data frame
    df_lucky <- tibble(
      luck = 1,
      toast_bsd = lucky
    )
    df_unlucky <- tibble(
      luck = 0,
      toast_bsd = unlucky
    )
    # Combine the data frames
    df_comb <- bind_rows(df_lucky, df_unlucky)
    # Fit the GLM
    model <- glm(toast_bsd ~ luck,
      family = binomial,
      data = df_comb
    )
    # Extract the p-value
    pval <- summary(model)$coefficients[2, 4]
    # Check if it is significant
    is_sig <- pval <= 0.05
    # Add TRUE or FALSE to the vector
    sig_vec <- c(sig_vec, is_sig)
  }
  # Calculate the percentage of significant p-values
  perc <- sum(sig_vec) / 1000
  # Add it to the vector
  perc_vec <- c(perc_vec, perc)
}

Let’s put the results in a data frame.

power_df <- tibble(
  group_size = seq(5, 300, 20),
  power = perc_vec
)

title: Part 7: Power Analysis
text:
Fixed sample sizes
Bonus
↑ top
In the example above, we started with an effect that we wanted to be able to detect and used power analysis to determine the sample size that we would need.
However, in real experiments there may be practical limits on the number of observations that we can collect. In this case, we can instead use power analysis to investigate how large an effect we would be able to reliably detect with the sample size available to us.
Imagine that we can recruit a maximum of 100 lucky and 100 unlucky participants for our toast-dropping experiment. We will continue to assume that toast dropped by lucky participants has a 0.4 probability of landing butter-side-down.






ExerciseExercise 2 - Calculating detectable effect size with fixed sample size

In your power.qmd Quarto document:

What happens when there is no difference between the two groups? Why is the proportion of significant results close to 0.05?






AnswerAnswer






Create a sequence of probabilities between 0.4 and 0.8, with an interval of 0.02. These will represent different possible probabilities of toast landing butter-side-down for the unlucky group.

probs <- seq(0.4, 0.8, 0.02)

Adapt the simulation above so that the group size is always 100, but the probability for the unlucky group changes in each iteration of the outer loop.
For each probability, simulate the experiment 1000 times and calculate the proportion of experiments in which the GLM detects a significant effect at a significance level of 0.05.

# Vector to store the percentages for all powers
perc_vec_fixed_sample <- c()

# Try each probability for unlucky from 0.4 to 0.8
for (prob in probs) {
  # Vector to store the results for this probability
  sig_vec <- c()
  # Simulate 1000 times
  for (j in seq_len(1000)) {
    # Lucky with 0.4 BSD probability
    lucky <- rbinom(100, 1, prob = 0.4)
    # Unlucky with prob BSD probability
    unlucky <- rbinom(100, 1, prob = prob)
    # Put each into a data frame
    df_lucky <- tibble(
      luck = 1,
      toast_bsd = lucky
    )
    df_unlucky <- tibble(
      luck = 0,
      toast_bsd = unlucky
    )
    # Combine the data frames
    df_comb <- bind_rows(df_lucky, df_unlucky)
    # Fit the GLM
    model <- glm(toast_bsd ~ luck,
      family = binomial,
      data = df_comb
    )
    # Extract the p-value
    pval <- summary(model)$coefficients[2, 4]
    # Check if it is significant
    is_sig <- pval <= 0.05
    # Add TRUE or FALSE to the vector
    sig_vec <- c(sig_vec, is_sig)
  }
  # Calculate the percentage of significant p-values
  perc <- sum(sig_vec) / 1000
  # Add it to the vector
  perc_vec_fixed_sample <- c(perc_vec_fixed_sample, perc)
}

Review
↑ top






NoteSummary




Concepts

Power analysis can be carried out in R by specifying an effect size, desired power and significance level to calculate the required sample size. (Extension)
Effect sizes can be estimated from existing or pilot data in R (or otherwise) and then used as inputs to a power calculation. (Extension)
Different statistical tests use different effect-size measures and corresponding power-analysis functions. (Extension)
For more complicated models, power can be estimated by simulation: repeatedly simulate the proposed experiment, fit the planned model, and calculate the proportion of simulations in which the effect is detected. (Extension)
Repeating a simulation-based power analysis across different sample sizes allows the required sample size for a specified power to be estimated. (Extension)
If sample size is fixed, the simulation can instead be repeated across different effect sizes to estimate the smallest effect that can be reliably detected. (Bonus)

title: Part 8: P-values and Multiple testing
text:
P-value distributions
In this part of the practical, you will need one Quarto document:
Extension
↑ top
As we discussed in Distributions of p-values, when the null hypothesis is true and the assumptions of a statistical test are met, p-values from repeated tests are expected to be uniformly distributed between 0 and 1.
We can understand where this uniform distribution comes from by considering cumulative probabilities. For any value drawn from a continuous probability distribution, we can calculate the proportion of the distribution expected to be less than or equal to that value. If we repeat this for many values drawn from the distribution, these cumulative probabilities are uniformly distributed between 0 and 1.
If we draw values from a standard normal distribution, pnorm() gives the probability of obtaining a value less than or equal to each observation. Across many observations, approximately 5% of these probabilities will fall between 0 and 0.05, 5% between 0.05 and 0.10, and so on.
A p-value is calculated from the cumulative probability of a test statistic under the null hypothesis. For example, for a lower-tailed test, the p-value is the probability of obtaining a test statistic less than or equal to the observed value. Therefore, p-values under the null hypothesis are also expected to be uniformly distributed between 0 and 1.
This is known as the probability integral transform - if \(X\) is a continuous random variable with cumulative distribution function \(F_X\), then the random variable \(Y = F_X(X)\) has a uniform distribution between 0 and 1.
We can reproduce this in R.
Two interesting (optional) further reading articles about p-values are the American Statistical Association statement on p-values here and this article by Greenland in 2018.

title: Part 8: P-values and Multiple testing
text:
Multiple testing
Extension
↑ top
If we perform many tests for which the null hypothesis is true, and the assumptions of the tests are met, approximately 5% of the tests will produce \(p \le 0.05\) purely by chance. This corresponds to the 5% Type I error rate when we use a significance threshold of 0.05.
If we’re only doing one or two tests, this is often deemed to be acceptable. However, when we perform many tests it becomes a problem.
In this article, Austin et al. (2006) demonstrate the problem of multiple testing using an intentionally implausible example. They classified more than 10 million people according to astrological sign and tested whether astrological signs were associated with 223 common reasons for hospitalisation.
Their initial analysis identified apparently significant associations between astrological signs and hospitalisation. They then tested selected associations in an independent validation dataset and found that, for example, Sagittarians had a significantly increased risk of humerus fracture, with \(p = 0.0125\), while Leos had a significantly increased risk of gastrointestinal haemorrhage \(p=0.0483\). However, after correcting for the large number of statistical comparisons being made, none of the associations remained statistically significant.

Multiple testing exercise
We can reproduce this ourselves with our pollinator dataset.
Let’s add an imaginary column, vibes, to our site_metadata data frame, in which each site is assigned a score based on the extent to which the volunteer felt good vibes when they collected the sample. This variable is normally distributed, with mean 50 and standard deviation 30.

site_metadata <- read_csv("data/site_metadata.csv")
site_metadata <- site_metadata |>
  mutate(
    vibes = rnorm(nrow(site_metadata), mean = 50, sd = 30)
  )

Next, let’s take every species which was observed in at least 10 sites.

insect_counts <- read_csv("data/insect_counts.csv")
species_over_10 <- insect_counts |>
  filter(n_observed > 0) |>
  count(species) |>
  filter(n >= 10) |>
  pull(species)







ExerciseExercise 2 - Multiple testing






Extension
In your multiple_testing.qmd Quarto file, for each pollinator species observed at least 10 times, we are going to test whether its presence or absence is associated with vibes.
For each species:

Filter the insect_counts data frame to contain only that species. The result will have one row per site.
Create a column in the same data frame, detected, which is TRUE when n_observed > 0 and FALSE otherwise.
Inner join this data frame to site_metadata to add the vibes variable.
Use a t-test with equal variance to compare vibes between sites where the species was and was not detected.
Extract the p-value from the t-test and append it to a vector.

Once you have the p-values for all 86 species:

Put them into a data frame and plot them as a histogram.
Calculate the proportion which are \(\le\) 0.05.
Identify any species for which presence/absence was significantly associated with vibes.

Your for loop to do this should be structured as follows, so that spp has the value of each species in turn.

for (spp in species_over_10) {
  # Do the steps
}







AnswerAnswer







pvals <- c()
for (spp in species_over_10) {
  # Filter the insect_counts data frame to contain only that species.
  # The result will have one row per site.
  pres_abs <- insect_counts |>
    filter(species == spp)

  # Create a column in the same data frame, `detected`,
  # which is TRUE when n_observed > 0 and FALSE otherwise.
  pres_abs <- pres_abs |>
    mutate(detected = n_observed > 0)

  # Inner join this data frame to site_metadata to add the vibes variable.
  pres_abs_site <- inner_join(pres_abs, site_metadata)

  # Use a t-test with equal variance to compare vibes
  # between sites where the species was and was not detected.
  ttest <- t.test(vibes ~ detected, data = pres_abs_site, var.equal = TRUE)

  # Extract the p-value from the t-test and append it to a vector.
  pvals <- c(pvals, ttest$p.value)
}

title: Part 8: P-values and Multiple testing
text:
Family-wise error rate
Extension
↑ top
The family-wise error rate (FWER) is the probability of making at least one Type I error across a whole set (family) of statistical tests.
For example, in our pollinator vibes experiment above, if all the null hypotheses are true (which they should be), we expect approximately 5% of our tests to produce a false positive.
The FWER is the probability that at least one of our 86 tests will produce a false positive.
If we assume that the tests are independent, the FWER can be calculated as:
\[
\mathrm{FWER} = 1 - (1 - \alpha)^n
\]
Where \(\alpha\) is our p-value threshold and \(n\) is the number of tests.






ExerciseExercise 3 - Family-wise error rate






Extension
In R, in your multiple_testing.qmd Quarto file, calculate FWER for our example above, where alpha is 0.05 and n is 86.






AnswerAnswer







fwer <- 1 - (1 - 0.05)^86
print(fwer)

[1] 0.9878597


There is a 98.79% probability that at least one test will be significant.
crumbs: 44  Part 8: P-values and Multiple testing

title: Part 8: P-values and Multiple testing
text:
Multiple testing corrections
Extension
To avoid this issue, there are various corrections we can apply, which basically lower the threshold at which we consider a p-value to be significant.
The simplest of these is a Bonferroni correction, in which you divide the acceptable p-value by the number of tests.
So, in our case:

pthresh <- 0.05 / 86
print(pthresh)

[1] 0.0005813953


This controls our FWER at no more than 5%, meaning that the probability of obtaining at least one false positive across the whole set of tests is no greater than our “acceptable” 5% threshold.

b_fwer <- 1 - (1 - pthresh)^86
print(b_fwer)

[1] 0.04878441


This correction is easy to understand but can be brutal in terms of increasingly the type II error rate.
A less conservative alternative is a Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) correction. Instead of controlling FWER, this method works to control the false discovery rate (FDR) — the expected proportion of significant results which are false positives. The method can therefore tolerate more false positives when there are more significant results (as, for example, 5% of 100 significant results is larger than 5% of 5 significant results). This allows the threshold p-value to become less stringent when there is evidence for a larger number of genuine effects.
To illustrate this, I will simulate 1000 t-tests each on three pairs of datasets with the following properties:

0% true effects
10% true effects
20% true effects

First, I will write a function to perform a t-test on two samples of 1000 observations drawn from a normal distribution with standard deviation 16. One sample will always have mean 20, the other will have a probability prob of having a mean of 20 and a probability of 1 - prob of having a mean of 18.

run_t <- function(prob) {
  # Set the mean of the two groups
  # Group 1 always has a mean of 20
  group1_mean <- 20

  # Group 2 has a probability prob of having a mean of 20
  # and a probability 1 - prob of having a mean of 18
  group2_mean <- sample(c(20, 18), size = 1, prob = c(prob, 1 - prob))

  # Generate the two samples, drawn from a ND with sd 16
  pop1 <- rnorm(1000, mean = group1_mean, sd = 16)
  pop2 <- rnorm(1000, mean = group2_mean, sd = 16)

  # Put both into a data frame
  df_pop1 <- tibble(pop = 1, value = pop1)
  df_pop2 <- tibble(pop = 2, value = pop2)
  df_comb <- bind_rows(df_pop1, df_pop2)

  # Run the t-test
  ttest <- t.test(value ~ pop, data = df_comb, var.equal = TRUE)

  # Put the result into a data frame, including whether there
  # was a real effect
  res_df <- tibble(
    pvalue = ttest$p.value,
    true_effect = group2_mean == 18
  )
  # Return the t-test p-value
  return(res_df)
}

Now I will simulate 1000 pairs of samples for each scenario:

0% true effects: Both samples always have mean 20
10% true effects: Sample 1 always has mean 20, sample 2 has a mean of 20 90% of the time and of 18 10% of the time.
20% true effects: Sample 1 always has mean 20, sample 2 has a mean of 20 80% of the time and of 18 20% of the time.


# Make empty data frames to store the results
results_0 <- tibble()
results_10 <- tibble()
results_20 <- tibble()

# Run the function 1000 times for each pair of means
for (i in seq_len(1000)) {
  results_0 <- bind_rows(results_0, run_t(1))
  results_10 <- bind_rows(results_10, run_t(0.9))
  results_20 <- bind_rows(results_20, run_t(0.8))
}

Now we can plot our p-values in each scenario.

# Make one data frame for all three sets of results
df_probs <- bind_rows(
  mutate(results_0, scenario = "0% true effects"),
  mutate(results_10, scenario = "10% true effects"),
  mutate(results_20, scenario = "20% true effects")
)

# This is just to make FALSE show at the bottom
# of the plot and TRUE at the top instead of
# the other way around
df_probs <- df_probs |>
  mutate(
    true_effect = factor(
      true_effect,
      levels = c(FALSE, TRUE)
    )
  )

# Plot the p-values
# position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE) - generates
# the stacked effect with FALSE at the bottom
ggplot(df_probs, aes(x = pvalue, fill = true_effect)) +
  geom_histogram(
    boundary = 0,
    binwidth = 0.05,
    position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~scenario) +
  ggtitle("Distribution of p-values with different proportions of true effects - Simulated") +
  xlab("p-value") +
  ylab("Number of tests") +
  theme_minimal()








Here, for the bar between 0 and 0.05, the blue part of the bar represents true positives: tests where there really is a difference between the populations and we have correctly rejected the null hypothesis. The red part represents false positives: tests where there is no real difference, but we have nevertheless obtained a p-value below 0.05.
The proportion of our significant results that are false positives is the false discovery proportion (FDP). The false discovery rate (FDR) is the expected FDP over repeated experiments.
For the remaining bars, the blue part represents false negatives, where there is a true effect but our test has failed to detect it. These are our Type II errors.
Let’s calculate the FDP for each of our three simulations - the proportion of our significant results which are false positives






ExerciseExercise 4 - Calculate FDP






Extension

  filter(pvalue <= 0.05) |>
  group_by(scenario) |>
  summarise(FDP = sum(true_effect == FALSE) / n())
gt(FDP)

When there are no true effects, every significant result is necessarily a false positive, so the FDP is 1. As the number of genuine effects increases, more of our significant results are true positives and the FDP decreases.
We could reduce the number of false positives by applying a Bonferroni correction. Since we have performed 1000 tests, this would give us a significance threshold of:
\[
\frac{0.05}{1000} = 0.00005
\]
Let’s see what effect this would have on the number of false positives and false negatives in our simulations.






ExerciseExercise 5 - Calculate false positive and false negative rates






Extension
In your multiple_testing.qmd Quarto file, based on the df_probs data frame, calculate the false positive and false negative rates with a Bonferroni correction applied, so that only p-values less than 0.05/1000 are considered to be significant.






AnswerAnswer






False positives:

  group_by(scenario) |>
  summarise(
    n_false_pos = sum(
      pvalue <= (0.05 / 1000) & true_effect == FALSE

The Bonferroni correction is extremely effective at preventing false positives. However, this comes at a cost: the much lower p-value threshold also means that many genuine effects are no longer considered significant. In other words, reducing our type I error rate has substantially increased our type II error rate.
This illustrates why Bonferroni correction can be overly conservative when we are performing large numbers of tests and expect some genuine effects to be present.
The BH procedure first ranks the p-values from lowest (most significant) to highest (least significant). For each p-value, it calculates a threshold:
\[
p_{\mathrm{threshold}} = 0.05 \times \frac{\mathrm{rank}}{\mathrm{number\ of\ tests}}
\]
For the smallest of our 1000 p-values, this threshold is therefore \(0.05/1000\). However, the threshold becomes progressively less stringent as we move through the ranked p-values.
We can calculate these thresholds for each of our three simulations.

df_bh <- df_probs |>
  group_by(scenario) |>
  arrange(pvalue, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    rank = seq_len(n()),
    thresh = 0.05 * (rank / n()),
    sig = pvalue <= thresh
  )

In each scenario, the threshold p-value would be the highest ranking p-value which is \(\le\) its threshold - in our case this is the highest ranking row in which sig is TRUE. This will not work for 0% true effects as there will usually be no rows that meet these criteria.
Let’s find the highest p-value which was lower than its threshold for 10% and 20% true effects.

threshold_df <- df_bh |>
  group_by(scenario) |>
  filter(sig) |>
  summarise(
    threshold_p = max(pvalue)
  )

Compared with the Bonferroni correction, the BH procedure generally allows us to retain more of the genuine effects, at the cost of accepting that some false positives may remain. Rather than attempting to eliminate false positives entirely, it controls their expected proportion among the results we call significant.
This makes FDR-controlling approaches particularly useful when large numbers of tests are performed and we expect that some of the tested effects are genuinely present.
We can perform BH correction automatically in R.

df_bh <- df_bh |>
  group_by(scenario) |>
  mutate(
    corrected_pvalue = p.adjust(pvalue, method = "BH")
  )

  group_by(scenario) |>
  summarise(
    n_false_pos = sum(
      corrected_pvalue <= 0.05 & true_effect == FALSE
    )
  )

title: Part 8: P-values and Multiple testing
text:
Review
↑ top






NoteSummary




Concepts

The distribution of p-values expected under the null hypothesis can be investigated in R by simulating data and calculating cumulative probabilities.
The family-wise error rate can be calculated from the significance threshold and the number of tests being performed. (Extension)
A Bonferroni correction can be applied by dividing the desired significance threshold by the number of tests. (Extension)
The numbers of false-positive and false-negative results produced by different significance thresholds can be calculated when the true status of simulated effects is known. (Extension)
The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure can be implemented by ranking p-values and calculating a different threshold for each rank. (Extension)
Multiple-testing corrections can be applied automatically to a set of p-values in R using p.adjust(). (Extension)
